name: CCAR-F Core Bank
description: 210 blueprint-weighted items for Claude Certified Architect - Foundations, written against the official Exam Guide v1.0 and current Anthropic documentation. Every item is framed in one of the six published exam scenarios and tagged to a verbatim task statement.

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
items.stem:
The support resolution agent runs on a hand-written driver against the Claude API. Support ops report that roughly one conversation in twelve ends immediately after the first tool call, leaving the refund unprocessed. The driver's inner loop is:

    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results_for(resp)})
    if any(block.type == "text" for block in resp.content):
        break

What is the correct fix to the termination logic?

options.text: Keep the text check but require the text block to contain an agreed completion phrase such as "resolution complete" or "no further action required", so the loop exits only on an explicit narrative signal from the model.
Branch on the response's stop_reason instead: keep iterating while stop_reason is "tool_use" and stop when it is "end_turn".
Cap the loop at eight tool round trips and treat exhaustion of that cap as the normal end of a conversation, logging any run that finishes earlier for manual review.
Move the decision into the tool layer by having process_refund and escalate_to_human return a workflow_complete flag that the driver reads out of the tool result payload.

items.explanation: An assistant response can carry text and tool_use blocks together, and Claude very often narrates before it calls a tool, so the presence of text says nothing about completion. The documented loop control is stop_reason: a response requesting a client tool has stop_reason "tool_use" and one or more tool_use blocks; the loop terminates when the response comes back with no tool calls and stop_reason "end_turn".

rationales.A: This is the anti-pattern the exam guide names explicitly: parsing natural language signals to determine loop termination. Phrase matching is brittle across paraphrase, translation and refusals, and it still misses turns where Claude narrates and then calls a tool.
rationales.C: An iteration cap is a runaway safety bound, not a stopping mechanism. Using it as the primary terminator guarantees either premature truncation of long cases or wasted round trips on short ones, and the guide names arbitrary iteration caps as an anti-pattern.
rationales.D: This pushes control flow into tool payloads that the model must remember to set, reintroducing a probabilistic signal in place of the deterministic protocol field the API already provides on every response.

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution

options.text: A message with role "tool" whose content array holds an object of type "tool_result" with the fields name, call_id and output carrying the file contents.
A message with role "assistant" that repeats the tool_use block and adds a sibling "tool_result" block containing the file contents, so the pair stays in one turn.
A message with role "user" whose content array holds a "tool_result" block with tool_use_id set to "toolu_01Xy9" and the file contents in its content field.
A message with role "user" whose content array holds a "function_result" block with the function name "read_module" and the file contents in its result field.

items.explanation: Tool results are returned to Claude in a new user message containing a tool_result block. Its required field is tool_use_id, which must match the id of the tool_use block being answered; content is optional and carries the payload, and is_error is an optional boolean. The Claude API has no tool or function message role.

rationales.A: There is no "tool" role in the Claude API, and the field names are wrong: the correlation field is tool_use_id, not call_id, and the payload field is content, not output. This shape belongs to a different vendor's API.
rationales.B: Tool results are supplied by the caller, so they belong in a user message. Putting a tool_result inside the assistant message would misattribute the tool output to the model and breaks the required tool_use then tool_result message pairing.
rationales.D: There is no "function_result" content block type, and results are correlated by the tool_use block's id rather than by tool name, which would be ambiguous whenever the same tool is called twice in one turn.

sources.title: Handle tool calls - Claude Docs

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution

options.text: Add "is_error": false to the tool_result block, because the API requires the flag to be present explicitly whenever the same user message also carries narrative text alongside the result.
Send the narrative text as its own user message first and the tool_result as a second user message, so that each block type occupies a message of a single kind.
Move the narrative text into the preceding assistant message as an extra text block, leaving the user message holding only the tool_result block for the refund call.
Reorder the content array so the tool_result block comes first and the narrative text follows it inside the same user message.

items.explanation: Ordering is enforced at two levels. The user message carrying tool_result blocks must immediately follow the assistant message that requested the tools, and inside that user message every tool_result block must come before any text block. Text placed ahead of a tool_result produces exactly this 400 error. Swapping the two blocks satisfies the rule with no other change.

rationales.A: is_error is optional and defaults to false; its absence is not what the API is complaining about. The error text names missing tool_result blocks immediately after the tool_use, which is a position problem, not a missing-field problem.
rationales.B: Splitting into two user messages leaves a message that is not a tool_result response directly after the tool_use turn, so the same validation still fails. The requirement is about block order inside one message, not about separating message kinds.
rationales.C: This edits a different message than the one at fault. The rule constrains block order inside the user message carrying the results, and the narrative text is permitted there as long as it follows every tool_result block.

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
items.stem: To keep request size predictable, the support agent's driver rebuilds its message list on every iteration: it sends the customer's opening message, the most recent assistant turn, and the tool_result blocks answering that turn, and drops everything older. No request is rejected and nothing is logged as an error, but transcript review shows the agent calling get_customer three or four times in one conversation and asking the customer for an order number that lookup_order had already returned. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Stop rebuilding the list: append each assistant turn and the tool_result blocks that answer it to the running conversation and re-send the whole history, so every decision the model makes is taken over the results already gathered.
Add a line to the system prompt on each iteration listing the tools already called in this conversation and instructing Claude not to call any of them a second time.

Keep the rebuild and persist the discarded turns to a conversation-scoped store, then expose a recall_history tool that the agent can call with a customer_id whenever it believes an earlier lookup is missing from what it can currently see.
Replace the fixed three-message window with a token-budgeted one that retains the most recent 20,000 tokens of history, so many more results survive while the request size stays bounded.

items.explanation: The agentic loop's contract is that tool results accumulate. Each result is appended to the conversation history and the whole history is re-sent on the next iteration, which is what lets the model incorporate new information into its reasoning and choose the next action. A driver that discards earlier turns leaves the model with no record of what it has already established, and the repeated lookups and the re-asked question are the visible cost of that. Requests stay valid because the surviving assistant turn is still answered correctly, which is why nothing errors.

rationales.B: This asks the model to compensate for missing context with an instruction, and it can convey only that a call was made, never what the call returned. The agent would stop repeating get_customer and start guessing at the record it can no longer see.
rationales.C: A recall tool makes the accumulated context optional and model-initiated, so the agent has to notice something is missing before it can ask for it. The failure being measured is precisely that it does not notice.
rationales.D: A larger window postpones the same loss rather than removing it, and a window that trims from the front will eventually cut between an assistant tool_use turn and the user message answering it, turning a silent quality problem into a 400 error.

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
items.stem: The research coordinator is built on the Agent SDK. Long literature runs now finish with a ResultMessage whose subtype is error_max_turns, and the pipeline crashes when it reads result off that message. An engineer proposes raising maxTurns from 40 to 300 for every run and treating the last assistant message the stream yielded as the report. How should the team read and handle this outcome?

options.text: error_max_turns is the ordinary way a completed run reports that it used its allotted turns; the final report is still on the result field and the crash is only a null-handling bug in the pipeline, which should be resolved by defaulting the field to an empty string before it is read.
Raising the limit to 300 for all runs is the documented remedy, because maxTurns is the mechanism the SDK provides for deciding when an agent has finished its task.

The run is incomplete: result is populated only when subtype is success, so the pipeline should read session_id from the result message and resume that session with a higher turn limit to let the run finish.

Replace the subtype check with a count of AssistantMessage objects seen in the stream, and treat the run as finished once no new tool_use block has appeared for two consecutive messages, reading the report off the last of them.

items.explanation: ResultMessage.subtype is the primary termination check and takes success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution or error_max_structured_output_retries. The result field carrying the final text is present only on success; every subtype still carries total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns and session_id. error_max_turns therefore means the agent was cut off mid-task, and the documented recovery is to resume the session with more headroom rather than to treat the truncated run as finished.

rationales.A: Only a success subtype carries result. Treating error_max_turns as a normal completion ships truncated research as if it were a finished report, which is the more damaging failure of the two.
rationales.B: maxTurns is a runaway bound, not a completion signal; it defaults to no limit, and raising it blindly for every run removes the protection without addressing why particular runs overshoot.
rationales.D: This reintroduces stream-shape heuristics in place of the protocol field. Turn counts and message shapes vary with parallel tool calls and background subagents, and the check would misfire on any turn where Claude narrates between tool batches.

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
items.stem: Your team is putting production bounds on the developer-productivity agent before enabling it for the whole engineering org. Which TWO statements about maxTurns and maxBudgetUsd in the Agent SDK are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.text: maxTurns counts tool-use round trips only; the final text-only turn that produces the answer is not counted against the limit.
Exceeding maxBudgetUsd ends the query with a ResultMessage whose subtype is error_max_budget_usd.
maxTurns defaults to 10 round trips, so an agent left unconfigured will stop on its own before a runaway loop becomes expensive.
maxBudgetUsd measures only the main agent loop's spend; requests made by delegated subagents are accounted separately and do not count against it.
maxTurns is the documented signal for detecting that an agent has completed the task it was given.

items.explanation: maxTurns counts tool-use round trips only and defaults to no limit, and maxBudgetUsd caps spend and also defaults to no limit. Hitting either bound produces a ResultMessage with subtype error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd. Both are safety bounds around the loop, not the loop's termination signal.

rationales.C: There is no default turn limit; maxTurns is unset unless you configure it, which is precisely why the docs recommend setting a bound for production agents.
rationales.D: The budget cap is tree-wide: every subagent's own API requests count toward the query's total_cost_usd, and over-limit spawns come back as "Budget limit reached" while running background subagents are stopped.
rationales.E: Completion is detected from ResultMessage.subtype being success, or in the raw API loop from a response with no tool calls; a turn cap only tells you the run was cut short.

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
items.stem: The codebase-exploration agent runs on a hand-written driver against the Claude API. On a wide search Claude returns one assistant turn containing three tool_use blocks, two Read calls and a Grep call. The driver runs them one at a time and sends each result back as its own user message before executing the next. Latency is roughly triple what the team expected, and the first of those requests fails with an error naming tool_use ids found without tool_result blocks immediately after. How should the driver handle a multi-call turn?

options.text: Send the three results as three consecutive user messages in the order the tool_use blocks appeared, so that each result stays adjacent to the call it answers.
Execute all three calls, running the read-only ones concurrently, and return every tool_result in the one user message that immediately follows the assistant turn.
Answer the first tool_use block only and let Claude re-request the other two on the next iteration, which keeps each round trip small and lets the model reprioritise as results arrive.
Instruct the agent in its system prompt to emit at most one tool_use block per assistant turn, so that every call can be answered on its own before the next one is requested.

items.explanation: Claude can request several tools in a single assistant turn. Every tool_use block in that turn has to be answered by a tool_result carrying its id, and all of those blocks belong in the single user message that immediately follows the assistant message, with no other message in between. Executing them one at a time both breaks that rule and serialises work the driver could run concurrently, since read-only calls such as Read and Grep are safe to dispatch together.

rationales.A: Only the first of those three messages sits immediately after the assistant turn. The other two ids are left unanswered in that position, so the request fails the same validation the team is already seeing.
rationales.C: Dropping two of the three calls leaves their ids unanswered, and discarding work Claude has already decided to do adds round trips rather than removing them.
rationales.D: This treats a protocol requirement as a prompting problem. Batching several calls into one turn is what makes a wide search fast, and a prompt instruction is a probabilistic control over something the driver has to get right in any case.

items.objective: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
items.stem: The support agent does not use a model-driven loop. A router executes a fixed sequence for every conversation: get_customer, then lookup_order, then a policy check, then either process_refund or escalate_to_human. Two problems have emerged. Billing disputes with no associated order stall because the router calls lookup_order with an invented identifier, and adding a new tool means rewriting the router and its tests. First-contact resolution is stuck at 61 percent against an 80 percent target. Which architecture best addresses both problems?

options.text: Keep the fixed sequence and extend it with a branch for every request category derived from a taxonomy built out of the last year of support tickets, so uncovered paths shrink over time.
Keep the fixed sequence and enforce each step with tool_choice set to the named tool for that step, so the model can never deviate from the approved order of operations.

Keep the router but have Claude produce the whole plan up front in a single call, then execute that plan step by step without feeding intermediate tool results back into the conversation, which keeps the token cost of a conversation flat and predictable for capacity planning.

Let the model choose the next tool on each iteration by appending every tool_result to the conversation and re-sending it, retaining only the genuinely deterministic requirement, identity verification before a refund, as a programmatic gate.

items.explanation: The blueprint draws the distinction between model-driven decision making, where Claude reasons about which tool to call next from the context it has accumulated, and pre-configured decision trees or fixed tool sequences. Appending each tool_result to the conversation and re-sending is what lets the model adapt to a dispute with no order, and it makes new tools available without a router rewrite. Determinism is preserved only where it is genuinely required, as a programmatic prerequisite gate rather than as a global sequence.

rationales.A: Enumerating categories is the same architecture with more branches. It cannot handle a request shape nobody anticipated, and the maintenance burden that is already blocking the team grows with every added branch.
rationales.B: Forcing a named tool at each step hard-codes the very rigidity that is causing the stalls, and forced tool use has real constraints: it prefills the assistant message so no reasoning text is emitted, and it is unavailable under manual extended thinking and on some models.
rationales.C: Planning once and executing blindly discards the information each tool result carries. The plan cannot react when lookup_order returns nothing, which is exactly the failing case.

items.objective: 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
items.stem: In the research system the document-analysis subagent was given the ability to invoke the web-search subagent directly whenever it finds a dead link, and the synthesis subagent can call document analysis for a second pass. Operations cannot explain why a report took 40 minutes, and each path handles a timeout differently: one retries three times, another returns an empty section. Which change best addresses both complaints, and why?

options.text: Route every delegation and every result through the coordinator in a hub-and-spoke topology, so the full delegation graph is visible in one place and one error policy applies to all of it.
Keep the direct peer-to-peer calls and thread a shared correlation identifier through every subagent prompt so a trace viewer can reconstruct the delegation graph after the fact.
Keep the direct calls and give every subagent the same retry-and-escalate tool, so at least the error behaviour is identical no matter which agent hit the failure.
Have each subagent append its own status lines to a shared scratchpad file that the coordinator reads at the end of the run to assemble a timeline of what happened.

items.explanation: The exam guide describes the coordinator pattern as hub-and-spoke: the coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling and information routing. Routing everything through the coordinator is what buys observability, one consistent error policy and controlled information flow, and it is what lets the coordinator decide whether a failure needs a retry, an alternative source or a partial-coverage annotation.

rationales.B: Correlation identifiers improve after-the-fact tracing but leave the divergent error handling untouched, and the coordinator still cannot intervene while a run is in flight because the calls never pass through it.
rationales.C: Standardising the retry tool makes the behaviour uniform but keeps decision-making distributed, so no single component knows the whole run state or can trade a failed source off against coverage already achieved.
rationales.D: A shared file gives a post-hoc timeline rather than control. Reading it at the end of the run is too late to re-delegate, and concurrent writers make it an unreliable record of ordering.

items.objective: 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
items.stem: The coordinator spawns four search subagents for every research question, each with the prompt "Research this topic and return the best sources you can find." A review of ten runs shows about 60 percent of returned URLs appear in more than one subagent's output, run cost is roughly four times a single-agent baseline, and the breadth of the final report is barely better. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: De-duplicate at the synthesis stage by canonicalising URLs and dropping repeats before the report is written, so the wasted work no longer shows up in the output.
Reduce the fan-out to one search subagent, since the measurements show the extra three are contributing almost nothing beyond what the first one already found.
Partition the search scope in the prompts, assigning each subagent a distinct subtopic or a distinct class of source so the fan-out covers disjoint ground.
Give the four subagents a shared memory store so each can see what the others have already retrieved and skip sources that have already been collected.

items.explanation: Duplication here is a decomposition failure, not an aggregation failure. The blueprint calls for partitioning research scope across subagents to minimise duplication, for example by assigning distinct subtopics or distinct source types to each agent. Four identical prompts converge on the same high-ranking sources, so scope must be made disjoint at delegation time.

rationales.A: De-duplication cleans the report but the four subagents still spend the same tokens and time covering identical ground, so neither the cost nor the coverage problem is addressed.
rationales.B: Collapsing to one agent removes the duplication by removing the parallelism, and it gives up the breadth that fan-out exists to provide once the subagents are actually pointed at different ground.
rationales.D: Subagent memory is scoped per named agent and persists across invocations; it is not a live shared workspace between concurrently running siblings, and coordinating through it would still leave every agent chasing the same subtopic.

items.objective: 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
items.stem: Every question submitted to the research system runs the same pipeline: three web-search subagents, two document-analysis subagents, a synthesis subagent and a report-generation subagent. Median latency is six minutes, which is acceptable for a market landscape review but not for a question such as "who currently chairs the standards body". The team must keep report quality on broad topics unchanged. What should the coordinator do differently?

options.text: Trim the standing pipeline to a single search subagent plus synthesis for all queries and accept slightly thinner coverage on the broad topics in exchange for a large latency win.
Have the coordinator assess what the query actually requires and select which subagents to invoke, reserving the full fan-out for questions that genuinely need multi-source investigation.
Keep the full pipeline but cache completed reports and answer from the cache whenever a new question is sufficiently similar to one already answered.
Keep the full pipeline but set effort to low and reduce each subagent's maxTurns so every stage returns faster without any stage being skipped.

items.explanation: The blueprint asks for coordinator agents that analyse query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke rather than always routing through the full pipeline. A single-fact lookup needs one search and no document analysis; a landscape review needs the whole fan-out. Deciding per query preserves quality where it matters and removes the latency where it does not.

rationales.A: This trades away exactly the capability the system exists for. The broad-topic runs are the ones that justify the architecture, and permanently thinning them to fix short queries is the wrong side of the trade.
rationales.C: Caching helps repeat questions but does nothing for a novel single-fact query, and similarity-based reuse risks answering a new question with a stale report, which is worse than being slow.
rationales.D: Lowering effort and turn budgets degrades every stage including the ones that need depth, and the pipeline still pays the fixed cost of spawning and aggregating stages the query never needed.

sources.title: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
items.stem: Reports from the research system pass the team's coverage rubric only 62 percent of the time. Reviewing the failures, the missing material is almost always a subtopic that was discoverable but was never assigned to any search subagent. The coordinator currently decomposes the question once, fans out, waits for all subagents, calls synthesis and returns. What change most directly raises coverage?

options.text: Close the loop after the fact: once synthesis returns, have the coordinator check the draft against the rubric itself, send narrow follow-up questions back to search and analysis for whatever the draft does not answer, and rebuild the draft, repeating until the rubric is met.
Increase the first fan-out from four search subagents to twelve, so that a wider initial sweep is more likely to touch the subtopics the current decomposition misses.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to end every report with a list of the subtopics it believes were not covered, so a reviewer can judge whether coverage is sufficient before publication.
Raise the coordinator's maxTurns and set its effort to high so it spends more reasoning on the initial decomposition before any subagent is spawned.

items.explanation: The blueprint calls for iterative refinement loops in which the coordinator evaluates synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates to search and analysis subagents with targeted queries, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient. Checking the draft after the evidence is in closes the loop on the failure mode described, because the missing subtopics are the ones that were not visible when the question was first decomposed.

rationales.B: Tripling a decomposition that is systematically too narrow mostly buys more coverage of the subtopics already identified, at three times the cost, and pushes against the concurrency ceiling without adding a mechanism for finding what was missed.
rationales.C: Annotating gaps is valuable reporting but it does not fill them. The rubric failure remains; the reviewer is simply told about it sooner.
rationales.D: More reasoning on the first decomposition may help marginally, but the missing subtopics are typically only discoverable once early results come back, which a single up-front pass cannot exploit.

sources.title: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
items.stem: An engineer is debugging a research run. The document-analysis subagent read about 40 pages of PDFs and its own transcript records every Read call, but the coordinator's transcript contains none of those calls or their contents, only a single paragraph of conclusions delivered as the Agent tool result. The engineer asks whether the coordinator's transcript is being truncated. What is the correct answer?

options.text: The main conversation was compacted part-way through the run, so the older messages holding those file reads were replaced by a summary; raising the compaction threshold will retain them.
The subagent output scan removed the file contents before the coordinator read them, because long document text matches the control-tag patterns that the scan neutralises.
The coordinator's transcript records only the turns counted in its usage field, and subagent turns are excluded from that count, so they are omitted from the log.

Nothing is truncated. A subagent's intermediate tool calls and results stay inside the subagent and only its final message returns to the parent, so anything the coordinator must keep has to be in that final message or written to a file by the subagent.

items.explanation: Context isolation runs in both directions. A non-fork subagent starts fresh, and its intermediate tool calls and results never enter the parent conversation; only its final message returns as the Agent tool result. That is precisely what keeps the coordinator's context small while a subagent reads dozens of files. The design question is therefore what the subagent puts in its last message, or what it writes to a file the coordinator can read afterwards, not which logging setting to change.

rationales.A: Compaction summarises the parent's own history and announces itself with a compact_boundary message in the stream. The subagent's file reads were never in the parent's history, so there was nothing there for compaction to remove.
rationales.B: The output scan neutralises control-tag imitation and turn markers in place and prepends a marker line; it never removes or rewords the subagent's text. It also applies to the final message, not to tool results the parent never receives.
rationales.C: usage is a token accounting field, not a filter on what gets written to a transcript. The parent records what the parent received, and what it received was one Agent tool result.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: A sweep of the monorepo has the developer-productivity coordinator spawn one subagent per service, 26 in all. The run ends with a ResultMessage whose subtype is success, and the final report covers 20 services. Reading back through the message stream, six of the subagent tool results contain nothing but the text "Concurrent subagent limit reached". What happened, and what is the right response?

options.text: Twenty subagents were already running, so the ceiling refused those six spawns and returned that line as a tool result rather than failing the query; raise the concurrency limit, or have the driver spawn in batches under it.

The sweep nested one layer deeper than CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH allows, so the six services at the bottom layer could not be delegated at all; raising the depth setting to 4 restores them.

The query reached its maxBudgetUsd ceiling part-way through the sweep, which stops background subagents that are still running and refuses to spawn any more; those six refusals are the visible edge of the budget cut-off, so raising the budget for this workload will let the whole sweep complete.

A success subtype means all 26 spawns completed, so the six absent services are a synthesis defect: the coordinator dropped their results while assembling the final report, and its prompt should require one section per service spawned.

items.explanation: CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS defaults to 20 subagents running at once and counts every subagent Claude spawns with the Agent tool. At the ceiling Claude Code refuses the spawn and returns "Concurrent subagent limit reached" as that call's tool result, and the query is not ended, which is exactly why this run still reports success and why nothing surfaced as an error. Recovery belongs to the harness rather than to the model: the refusal tells Claude not to retry it, while spawning succeeds again once the running count drops below the limit. A coordinator fanning out wider than the ceiling therefore has to raise the ceiling to match the fan-out, or release its spawns in batches the ceiling can hold.

rationales.B: The depth limit governs nesting, not width. Its default of 3 layers is untouched by a flat 26-way fan-out from a single coordinator, and a subagent stopped by the depth limit does the delegated work itself rather than returning a refusal.
rationales.C: A budget breach announces itself: it returns "Budget limit reached" rather than the concurrency message and ends the query with the error_max_budget_usd subtype. This run ended with success, so no budget cap was reached.
rationales.D: The refusal text is in the stream for those six calls, so their subagents never ran. success only means no turn, budget or execution error ended the query; it says nothing about how many spawns were accepted.

items.objective: 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
items.stem: Your developer-productivity service runs on the Agent SDK with a custom systemPrompt of your own, not the claude_code preset, on an Opus 5 model. Traces show the main agent delegating even single-file edits to subagents, nesting three levels deep, and monthly spend is roughly five times the estimate. The team wants to keep parallel delegation for genuinely independent work. What should you do?

options.text: Switch tool_choice to "none" for the coordinator so it can only produce text, and drive all delegation from your own application code instead of leaving it to the model.

Write the delegation guidance into your custom system prompt yourself, delegate for parallel, isolated-context or independent workstreams and work directly for single-file edits and sequential steps, and set the spawn-depth, concurrency and budget limits, because instructions only steer.
Rely on the damping line that Claude Code adds for Opus 5 models telling Claude not to call the Agent tool unless asked, and confirm it is present by inspecting the system:init message.

Put the spawn tool in disallowedTools so its definition is removed from the request and the coordinator cannot delegate at all, and reintroduce it once the team has agreed a written delegation policy.

items.explanation: Current guidance records that Opus 5 delegates to subagents more readily than prior models. The damping line telling Claude not to call the Agent tool unless asked is added by the claude_code system-prompt preset; with a custom systemPrompt Claude Code does not build its system prompt, so that line is absent and you must supply the guidance yourself. Because instructions only steer, the depth, concurrency and budget limits must be set regardless.

rationales.A: Setting tool_choice to "none" disables tool calling for that agent entirely and pushes the whole orchestration problem into application code, discarding the model-driven delegation the team explicitly wants to keep.
rationales.C: That damping line comes from the claude_code preset. This service supplies its own systemPrompt, so Claude Code does not build the system prompt and the line is not there to rely on.
rationales.D: A bare-name deny removes the Agent tool from the request entirely, so it eliminates the over-delegation by eliminating the parallel independent workstreams the team said it wants to keep, and it leaves the depth, concurrency and budget bounds still unset.

items.objective: 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
items.stem: The support coordinator delegates complex billing investigations to a dedicated subagent. A spend guard in the coordinator's own driver reads the usage field on each ResultMessage and is meant to halt a conversation once its token spend passes a ceiling. The guard never trips, not even on the conversations where a delegated investigation tripled what the run consumed. Which correction makes the guard bound the spend it exists to bound?

options.text: usage omits cache-read tokens by design, so the guard should add the cache-read counters from each AssistantMessage to the totals it already collects.
Derive the figure from num_turns on the result message multiplied by a measured average cost per turn, which absorbs subagent spend without needing per-agent accounting.
Read modelUsage on the result message, which accounts for the whole agent tree, because usage covers only the main agent loop.
Each subagent produces its own ResultMessage, so the guard has to capture and sum those separately from the parent conversation's result.

items.explanation: The usage field on the result message covers only the main agent loop, which is why any conversation that delegated work looks cheap to a guard reading it. modelUsage, or model_usage in Python, is the documented field for whole-tree token and cost accounting, and the same tree-wide total is what maxBudgetUsd enforces through total_cost_usd. A coordinator's guard has to read the tree, because the spend it is meant to bound happens inside the subagents the coordinator spawns.

rationales.A: The gap tracks delegation, not caching, and adding cache counters would not recover tokens spent inside a subagent that the main loop's usage never saw.
rationales.B: An average cost per turn is an estimate rather than an accounting method: turns differ by orders of magnitude in size, and the approach still ignores the delegated work that caused the discrepancy.
rationales.D: Subagents do not surface their own result messages to your application; only their final message returns as the Agent tool result, and their spend is already rolled into the query's tree-wide totals.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: The research coordinator is created with three AgentDefinitions for search, document analysis and synthesis, and is configured with allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "WebSearch"]. In every run the coordinator does all the work itself in one context and never delegates; the transcript records no Agent tool call at all and the run ends normally. What is the minimal fix?

options.text: Add the subagent spawn tool to the allow list - it appears as "Agent" in tool_use blocks and as "Task" in the system:init tools list, so allow both names.
Set background to true on each AgentDefinition, since a coordinator can only reach definitions that are marked as background-capable before the session starts.
Add a subagent_type field to each of the three AgentDefinitions, since the coordinator targets a definition by the subagent_type it declares rather than by its registration key.
Set CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS to 0 for this session, since the delegation machinery ships disabled and that variable is what turns it back on.

items.explanation: Claude spawns subagents through a single tool, and current SDK examples pass allowed_tools including "Agent" alongside Read, Grep and Glob. That same tool is listed as "Task" in the system:init tools list, and older releases emitted "Task" in tool_use blocks, which is why the exam guide states the requirement as allowedTools must include "Task" while the current documentation shows "Agent"; allowing both names is the form that works across versions. With neither name present the coordinator has no approved way to delegate, which matches the silent symptom described.

rationales.B: background controls whether a spawned subagent runs in the background; it has no bearing on whether the coordinator is permitted to spawn one in the first place.
rationales.C: subagent_type is an argument the coordinator supplies when it calls the spawn tool, not a field on AgentDefinition; the definition is keyed by the name it is registered under.
rationales.D: That variable removes the built-in general-purpose agent when set to 1. Leaving it unset or 0 is already the default and does not grant the coordinator the missing spawn tool.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: The developer-productivity coordinator has to audit six services that share no state, and no service's audit depends on another's result. Its transcript shows six assistant turns in a row, each carrying exactly one subagent spawn call, with the coordinator waiting for each subagent's result before it issues the next. Wall-clock time for the audit is the sum of the six runs. What should the coordinator do instead?

options.text: Issue all six spawn calls in a single assistant response, so the six subagents run at the same time and the fan-out costs the time of the slowest audit rather than the sum of all six.
Set run_in_background to false on each spawn call, so the coordinator can dispatch the next one without waiting for the previous subagent to finish.

Raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH so the first subagent can spawn the other five itself, which moves the fan-out one layer down and lets those five run underneath it while the coordinator waits on a single call.
Collapse the six spawns into one general-purpose subagent whose prompt names all six services, so a single run covers the whole audit in one context.

items.explanation: Parallelism comes from where the spawn calls sit, not from how many of them there are. The blueprint states it directly: spawn parallel subagents by emitting multiple spawn calls in a single coordinator response rather than across separate turns. Multiple subagents then run concurrently and independent subtasks finish in the time of the slowest one instead of the sum of all of them. The exam guide names this tool Task; current SDK examples list it as Agent in allowedTools and in tool_use blocks, with Task surviving only in the system:init tools list.

rationales.B: run_in_background set to false is the value that makes the coordinator wait for the result before continuing, which is the behaviour already observed; omitting the field launches a background subagent. Either way the serialisation comes from issuing one call per turn.
rationales.C: Depth governs nesting rather than concurrency, and the default of 3 layers is not what constrains this run. Pushing the fan-out a layer down adds a hop and leaves the coordinator waiting on one call exactly as it does now.
rationales.D: One subagent auditing six services in one context gives up both the parallelism and the context isolation the split exists for, and its single result mixes six audits into one message.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: An unattended refactor run of the developer-productivity agent starts its parent session in acceptEdits so the agent can apply file edits without prompting. A schema-migration subagent is defined with permissionMode set to "default", on the expectation that its Write and Edit calls under db/migrations would still be routed to the operator approval callback. The audit shows those writes executing with no approval step at all. What is happening?

options.text: A subagent's permissionMode is honoured only when the agent is loaded from a .claude/agents/ markdown file; definitions supplied programmatically ignore the field, so the migration agent has to be moved onto disk before its restriction takes effect.

A parent running in acceptEdits, auto or bypassPermissions propagates that mode to every subagent and a per-subagent permissionMode cannot override it, so the migration writes have to be constrained another way, such as a scoped deny rule or a PreToolUse hook.
permissionMode "default" means inherit from the parent; the value that would have restored prompting for this subagent is "plan".
The Python SDK expects this field as permission_mode, so the camelCase spelling was silently ignored when the definition was constructed.

items.explanation: Subagents inherit the parent session's permission mode. An AgentDefinition.permissionMode can override that inherited mode except when the parent is in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits or auto; those three apply to every subagent and cannot be overridden per subagent. acceptEdits auto-approves file edits through Edit and Write, plus filesystem commands such as mkdir, mv and rm, so the migration subagent's writes are approved at the permission-mode step and never reach the callback. Constraining them has to happen through a mechanism that survives the mode, such as a scoped deny rule on the migrations path or a PreToolUse hook.

rationales.A: permissionMode is a documented AgentDefinition field and works for programmatically defined agents; programmatic definitions in fact take precedence over filesystem agents of the same name.
rationales.C: "default" is the ordinary prompting mode rather than an inherit sentinel. The deeper problem is that no per-subagent value helps here, because an acceptEdits parent overrides whatever the definition names, so naming "plan" instead would change nothing about this run.
rationales.D: The Python SDK keeps camelCase for multi-word AgentDefinition fields to match the wire format, so permissionMode is the correct spelling in both SDKs.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: A test-writer subagent is registered with tools set to ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"]. Reviewers report that it produces a careful description of the tests it would add, names the files it would create, and then stops. No error appears in the transcript, no permission prompt was recorded, and the subagent's result comes back as a normal completion. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: The subagent reached its maxTurns limit while planning and returned before it began writing, which is why the result reads as a completed description of intent.
The parent's ask rules queued an approval prompt that a subagent cannot display, so the write call timed out silently and the run continued without it.
Background subagents receive a reduced set of built-in tools from which Write is excluded, so file creation is only possible in a foreground subagent.
A tool left out of a definition's tools list is not present in that subagent's session at all, so Write was never available and Claude worked without it; adding Write and Edit to the list fixes it.

items.explanation: Omitting the tools field gives a subagent every tool available to subagents; listing tools gives it only those. A tool left out is not in the subagent's session at all, so Claude simply works without it, with no permission prompt and no error. The described behaviour, a complete and confident plan with no files created, is the signature of that omission.

rationales.A: A subagent stopped at its turn limit has its Agent tool result marked partial so the parent knows the run is unfinished, which is not what the reviewers are seeing.
rationales.B: There is no silent timeout of this kind; a blocked call surfaces as a denial or an unanswered permission request, and the run would not read as a clean completion.
rationales.C: Write is present in the reduced built-in tool set that background subagents receive; the tools that are always removed from subagents are the interactive and session-control ones such as AskUserQuestion, ExitPlanMode and Workflow.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: Spot checks of published research reports find claims attributed to the wrong paper roughly one time in eight. The document-analysis subagent reads sources correctly, but the coordinator currently passes its findings to the synthesis subagent as a prose paragraph per source. Which TWO changes best preserve attribution through synthesis? (Select TWO)

options.text: Give the synthesis subagent the WebSearch tool so it can look up and confirm the correct citation itself whenever an attribution looks doubtful.
Raise the synthesis subagent's effort setting to high so it spends more reasoning on keeping claims and sources aligned while it writes.
Have the document-analysis subagent return one structured record per claim that keeps the claim text separate from its metadata: source URL or document name, page number and publication date.
Have the coordinator include those structured records in the synthesis subagent's prompt as they were returned, rather than a prose summary of them.
Spawn synthesis as a fork subagent so that it inherits the parent conversation and can therefore read every document-analysis result directly.

items.explanation: Attribution is lost at the boundary where content and metadata are flattened together into prose. The blueprint calls for structured data formats that separate content from metadata, source URLs, document names and page numbers, when passing context between agents, and because the prompt string is the only parent-to-child channel, the coordinator has to carry those records into the synthesis prompt intact rather than paraphrasing them.

rationales.A: This gives a synthesis agent a tool outside its specialisation, which the blueprint warns tends to be misused, and it treats a data-passing defect as a research problem the writer should solve at write time.
rationales.B: More reasoning cannot recover metadata that was never in the synthesis agent's context; the URLs and page numbers were discarded before the agent was invoked.
rationales.E: A fork does inherit the parent transcript, including each subagent's returned claim table, but it does not fix the defect: the records were already flattened into prose before synthesis, and forking discards the context isolation the pipeline depends on and copies the whole parent conversation into the synthesis run.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: An engineer has spent a long session with your agent mapping the shipping-rate engine and now wants to try a speculative redesign in a side conversation. The requirement is that the exploring assistant keeps everything already established in this session, and that the redesign's noisy tool output does not pollute the main conversation. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: Spawn a background general-purpose subagent from this conversation and rely on it seeing the session history, since it is spawned from the same session and inherits its transcript, which keeps a speculative branch out of the main conversation.
Run /compact first to condense the mapping work, then continue in the same conversation so the redesign has the summary available and the transcript stays small.

Start a fork subagent with /subtask, the documented exception to context isolation: it inherits the parent conversation, system prompt, tools, model and message history, while its own tool calls stay out of the main conversation.
Pass --fork-session on its own to branch the current conversation into a separate exploration that starts from the same accumulated state.

items.explanation: A fork subagent is the documented exception to subagent context isolation. It inherits the entire parent conversation, including the system prompt, tools, model and message history, instead of starting fresh, and its tool calls still stay out of the main conversation. That is exactly the combination the engineer needs, and /subtask is how one is started.

rationales.A: A non-fork subagent, background or not, starts with fresh context regardless of which session spawned it; the spawn prompt is the only channel, so the mapping work would have to be re-supplied by hand.
rationales.B: Compaction shrinks the transcript by replacing older messages with a summary, which is a context-budget tactic. It gives no isolation at all: the redesign's exploration lands in the same conversation.
rationales.D: --fork-session takes effect only in combination with --resume or --continue, and it forks a session into a separate process rather than creating an isolated side conversation within the running one.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: A first query() ran a long investigation through your custom "codebase-explorer" subagent, which returned a summary of the module's call graph. An engineer now wants to ask that same subagent a follow-up without repeating the investigation. Which THREE statements are true of resuming it? (Select THREE)

options.text: The same procedure would have worked had the built-in Explore subagent been used for the investigation instead of a custom agent.
Setting background to false on the definition is what causes an agentId to be returned in the first place.
You must capture session_id from the messages and pass it as resume on the second query(), because each query() otherwise starts a new session.
You must parse the agentId out of the text of the spawn tool's result and name that agent ID in the second query's prompt.
Resuming the subagent copies its full transcript into the parent's context window so the parent can read the intermediate tool results.
You must pass the same agents definitions to the second query().

items.explanation: Resuming a subagent takes three things together: capture session_id from the messages, parse agentId out of the text of the spawn tool's result, then in a second query() pass resume with that session ID, name the agent ID in the prompt and supply the same agents definitions. Each query() starts a new session by default, so resuming the session is mandatory to reach the subagent's transcript at all.

rationales.A: The built-in Explore and Plan subagents are one-shot, read-only and return no agentId, so they cannot be resumed. Resumption requires a custom agent or general-purpose.
rationales.B: background controls whether the parent waits for the result; it is not what produces an agentId, which custom and general-purpose subagents return either way.
rationales.E: Resumption continues the subagent's own run. Intermediate tool calls and results stay inside the subagent, and only its final message ever returns to the parent.

items.objective: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
items.stem: Each search subagent in the research system is spawned with a prompt that reads: query the five named databases in this order, take the first ten results from each, and write a 200-word summary of every result. When one of those databases is unreachable, or simply returns nothing on the topic, the subagent comes back with an apology and no findings. Reviewers also note that every report cites the same five sources, including on topics those databases cover badly. How should the coordinator write these subagent prompts instead?

options.text: Keep the procedure and add an explicit fallback branch for each database naming the substitute source to try when it is unreachable, so every failure path is specified in advance.

State what the subagent is trying to find out and what its output has to satisfy - the question being answered, what counts as an acceptable source, how much corroboration a claim needs - and leave the choice of sources and route to the subagent.

Have the coordinator run the five database queries itself and spawn each subagent with the retrieved results already embedded in its prompt, so a subagent never has to reach an unreachable source and the summarising procedure always runs to completion.
Keep the procedure and wrap each database query in a retry policy of three attempts with exponential backoff, so a transient outage no longer ends a subagent's run with nothing to report.

items.explanation: The blueprint asks for coordinator prompts that specify research goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedural instructions, precisely so that subagents can adapt. A procedure encodes one route to the answer: when the route is blocked the subagent has nothing left to do, and where the route is poor it has no licence to choose a better one. Goals plus criteria give it something to satisfy rather than something to follow, and the criteria are also what make the returned work reviewable.

rationales.A: Enumerating fallbacks is the same procedural prompt with more branches. It covers the failure modes someone thought of and none of the others, and it still fixes the source list on topics those five databases cover badly.
rationales.C: This moves the research into the coordinator and leaves the subagents summarising, which removes the parallel investigation the fan-out exists for and routes every query through the one context the architecture is designed to keep small.
rationales.D: Retries address a transient outage, not a database that holds nothing on the topic, and they do nothing about the second symptom: the same five sources appearing in every report regardless of fit.

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: The support agent already has a programmatic gate that blocks process_refund until get_customer has run in the conversation, and it fires correctly. A quarterly audit nevertheless finds four refunds credited to the wrong account: in each case the agent called get_customer for the caller, then called process_refund with a customer_id taken from an order record belonging to a different account. What change closes this hole?

options.text: Strengthen the system prompt with an explicit instruction, reinforced by two worked examples, to reuse the customer_id returned by the most recent get_customer call whenever a refund is issued, and repeat the same requirement in the refund tool description as reinforcement.

Make the gate stateful about identity rather than only about sequence: record the verified customer_id that get_customer returned and have the PreToolUse hook deny process_refund whenever the call's customer_id differs from the recorded value.

Use forced tool selection so that get_customer is always the tool called immediately before process_refund, and have the driver reject any refund attempt not preceded by that call in the same turn, guaranteeing that the freshest identity lookup is the one in scope.
Route every refund through escalate_to_human so a person confirms the account before any money moves, and keep the existing sequence gate as a second line of defence.

items.explanation: The existing gate enforces ordering, which is a weaker property than the policy actually requires. Deterministic compliance means the enforcement predicate has to match the rule: the refund's customer_id must equal the identity that verification returned. Recording the verified value from the get_customer tool result and comparing it in a PreToolUse hook, which runs before every other permission step, makes the check impossible for the model to route around.

rationales.A: Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate, and the audit is already evidence of that rate in production. Where a wrong outcome moves money to the wrong account, guidance is not an adequate control.
rationales.C: Forcing the order of calls re-states the property the gate already enforces. Nothing in it constrains which customer_id the subsequent refund call carries, so the same four failures pass through.
rationales.D: This meets the compliance requirement by abandoning the automation target the agent exists to hit, and it converts a narrow identity check into a human bottleneck on every refund.

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: Your developer-productivity workflow runs in two stages. An exploration agent maps an unfamiliar service and chooses an approach; a second agent then implements it. The implementation agent is invoked with "Implement the plan from the exploration phase" and either re-explores from scratch or writes code against assumptions the exploration phase had already ruled out. What is the right handoff design?

options.text: Compile a structured handoff record listing the files and symbols identified, the constraints discovered, the approach chosen and the acceptance criteria, and pass it in the implementation agent's prompt, because the implementing agent has no access to the exploration transcript.
Raise the exploration agent's maxTurns and let it carry straight on into implementation in the same run, so that no handoff is needed and no context can be lost between the stages.

Have the exploration agent write its complete transcript to a file and instruct the implementation agent to read that file before it starts, so nothing that was discovered is left behind, and any later audit can replay the same file to establish exactly what the exploration phase knew at handoff time.
Record the exploration findings in the project CLAUDE.md so they are re-injected on every request, which makes them available to the implementation stage and to any later session.

items.explanation: The receiving stage starts without the sending stage's transcript, exactly as a human escalation target does, so the handoff has to be a structured summary of what the receiver needs to act: the artefacts identified, the constraints found, the decision taken and how success will be judged. That mirrors the guide's handoff protocol, where the summary carries the identifiers, the root cause and the recommended action rather than a pointer to a conversation the receiver cannot see.

rationales.B: Collapsing the stages removes the handoff by removing the separation that gives the implementation stage a clean context, and long single runs are precisely where turn limits and context degradation start to bite.
rationales.C: A raw transcript is not a handoff artefact: it buries the four things the implementer needs in the exploration noise, and reading it back consumes the context budget the split was meant to protect.
rationales.D: CLAUDE.md is for durable project conventions, not per-task findings. Writing run-specific discoveries there pollutes every future session and still does not tell this implementer which decision applies now.

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: An architecture review of the support agent's enforcement design turns on how the Agent SDK decides whether a tool call may proceed. Which TWO statements about that evaluation are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Hooks are evaluated first, ahead of deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules and the canUseTool callback.
A PreToolUse hook returning a deny decision blocks the call even when the session is running in bypassPermissions.
canUseTool is evaluated first so that application code always gets the opportunity to veto a call before any rule is considered.
Deny rules are evaluated after the permission mode, which is why bypassPermissions overrides them.
Allow rules are evaluated before deny rules, so a bare-name allow entry for Bash overrides a scoped deny rule written against the same tool.

items.explanation: The SDK evaluates a tool request in a fixed six-step order: hooks, then deny rules, then ask rules, then the permission mode, then allow rules, then the canUseTool callback. Because hooks run first, a hook deny blocks the call even in bypassPermissions mode, which is what makes hooks the right place for a control that must never be bypassed.

rationales.C: canUseTool is the last step, not the first, which is why auto-approved calls resolve earlier and never reach it.
rationales.D: Deny rules are evaluated before the permission mode, which is why a scoped deny still refuses matching calls under bypassPermissions.
rationales.E: The documented order puts deny rules second and allow rules fifth. A scoped deny therefore refuses a matching call however permissive the allow list is, which is what makes a deny rule a boundary rather than a preference.

sources.title: Configure permissions - Claude Agent SDK

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: A code-exploration agent must never delete files but must still be able to run the project's test suite through Bash. Two configurations are on the table: disallowed_tools=["Bash"] and disallowed_tools=["Bash(rm *)"]. Which should be chosen and why?

options.text: The bare name, because a bare-name deny leaves the tool available to the model and refuses only the destructive invocations at call time, which is what the requirement describes.

Neither, because deny rules stop applying once the session runs in acceptEdits or bypassPermissions, so the only durable option is a PreToolUse hook that inspects each command string and refuses anything matching rm, git clean or find with -delete.

The scoped rule, because a bare-name deny removes the tool definition from the request entirely so the agent could not run tests at all, while a scoped rule leaves Bash available and refuses only matching calls in every permission mode.

The bare name together with a re-added Bash entry in allowed_tools, so that the deny establishes the default position and the allow rule restores the specific capability the test suite needs without loosening the position for any other command.

items.explanation: The two forms behave differently by design. A bare-name deny removes the tool definition from the request, so Claude never sees the tool and cannot call it for any purpose. A scoped deny leaves the tool available and denies only calls matching the pattern, and it does so in every permission mode including bypassPermissions. Only the scoped form satisfies both halves of the requirement.

rationales.A: This states the semantics the wrong way round. It is the scoped form that leaves the tool available and refuses matching calls; the bare name removes the tool outright.
rationales.B: Deny rules are evaluated ahead of the permission mode and continue to apply under acceptEdits and bypassPermissions alike, so the premise is false and the extra hook machinery is unnecessary here.
rationales.D: Allow rules cannot reinstate a tool that a deny rule has removed, because deny is evaluated first; the agent would still have no Bash tool to call.

sources.title: Configure permissions - Claude Agent SDK

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: When the support agent escalates, its escalate_to_human call currently posts a single line into the queue: "Customer needs help with a refund, please review." Human agents reopen about 70 percent of these asking for basic details, and average handling time after escalation is 11 minutes. What should the escalation payload contain?

options.text: The full raw conversation transcript pasted into the ticket body, so the receiving agent can do their own root cause analysis and recommend an action in their own words, which also preserves the customer's exact wording in case the outcome is disputed later.

A sentiment score for the conversation and an urgency rating derived from it, both produced by a classifier calibrated last year against a labelled sample of pre-migration tickets, so the queue can be ordered before anyone opens a case.

The session_id of the agent run, so the receiving agent can resume that session in Claude Code and page through the tool results the agent saw, including the order record and the policy lookup, before deciding anything themselves.

A short fixed-field record: which account the case belongs to, what actually went wrong, the money at stake, and the step the agent proposes be taken, because whoever picks the ticket up cannot see the conversation.

items.explanation: The guide's handoff protocol for mid-process escalation requires a structured summary containing the customer ID, the root cause, the refund amount and the recommended action, precisely because the human receiving the case cannot see the conversation. Those four fields are what remove the reopen-and-ask cycle the team is measuring.

rationales.A: A transcript is unstructured and long, and it makes the receiving agent redo the analysis the agent already performed, which is the opposite of what a handoff is for.
rationales.B: The calibration is real but the population is not this one: it was fitted on pre-migration tickets, and a score calibrated on a stale population is not a reliable queue order. More fundamentally, neither number says what went wrong or what should be done, so the reopen rate would not move.
rationales.C: Session transcripts are local to the machine that created the session and are not a support tool a human queue can open; a session identifier is not a case summary.

sources.title: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: A single customer message reads: the jacket arrived damaged, the card was charged twice in March, and the address on next month's subscription shipment is the old one. Transcript review shows the agent resolves the damaged item, replies, and never returns to the other two. Roughly one conversation in five contains more than one concern. What design change addresses this?

options.text: Have the agent decompose the message into distinct items, investigate each against the same shared case context, and synthesise one resolution that covers all of them before replying.
Instruct the agent to handle only the first concern in a message and to ask the customer to raise the remaining ones as separate tickets, so each is tracked independently.
Escalate any message containing more than one concern to a human agent, since multi-concern cases are by definition too complex for autonomous first-contact resolution.
Raise maxTurns and give the agent a larger context budget so it has enough room to work through all three concerns before the run ends.

items.explanation: The blueprint calls for decomposing multi-concern customer requests into distinct items, investigating each in parallel using shared context, and then synthesising a unified resolution. Shared context matters because the same customer and order records serve all three items, and a single synthesised reply is what first-contact resolution actually measures.

rationales.B: Pushing work back onto the customer is a direct hit on first-contact resolution and satisfaction, and it manufactures three tickets out of one conversation the agent was capable of closing.
rationales.C: Multiple concerns is not one of the documented escalation triggers, which are an explicit request for a human, a policy gap or exception, and an inability to make meaningful progress. Escalating on concern count would flood the queue with resolvable cases.
rationales.D: The agent is not running out of room; it stops because it treated the message as a single request. More turns give a partially-scoped conversation more space to remain partially scoped.

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: Two ordering requirements exist in the research pipeline. First, the report-generation subagent should not run before synthesis has returned; when it has happened the report came back empty, the reviewer caught it immediately and the run was retried for a few dollars. Second, every citation in a published report must correspond to a claim that verify_fact confirmed; a violation here reaches customers and has triggered a retraction. Engineering time for enforcement work is limited this quarter. Where should it be spent?

options.text: Put both requirements into the coordinator's system prompt with emphatic wording and a pair of worked examples, then measure adherence over a month before building any enforcement machinery.

Gate both requirements with PreToolUse hooks and additionally deny the report tool until a synthesis manifest file exists on disk, so neither ordering rule can ever be violated by any future caller, and the manifest gives the compliance team a durable artefact to audit after each run.

Enforce the citation rule programmatically with a gate that blocks report publication until verify_fact has confirmed each claim, and leave the subagent ordering to the coordinator prompt, where a violation is caught cheaply and retried.

Reverse that split: gate the subagent ordering with a hook, since it is a deterministic sequencing property a rule can express exactly, and rely on prompt guidance for citations, which is a judgement about evidence the model is better placed to make than a rule is.

items.explanation: Deterministic enforcement is warranted where prompt guidance's non-zero failure rate produces an unrecoverable outcome. A citation that reaches a customer and forces a retraction is that case; an empty report caught by a reviewer and retried for a few dollars is not. Spending the enforcement budget on the gate that prevents the unrecoverable failure, and accepting probabilistic guidance where the failure is cheap and self-correcting, is the judgement the constraint calls for.

rationales.A: Leaving the retraction-grade requirement to wording accepts a known non-zero failure rate on the one outcome the team cannot take back, and a month of measurement is a month of exposure.
rationales.B: Gating everything spends the scarce engineering time on the requirement that already self-corrects, and the extra manifest-file precondition adds a second failure mode with no additional protection against the harm that matters.
rationales.D: This inverts the risk analysis. Sequencing is the cheap failure and citation integrity is the expensive one, so it puts the deterministic control on the wrong requirement.

items.objective: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
items.stem: Team policy is that the migration agent must run pytest -q and see it pass before it may git commit. The check lives in the run's canUseTool callback and it holds for commits the main agent makes. Last month three commits with failing tests still reached the shared branch, every one of them made by a build-fixer subagent the main agent had spawned, in a session whose allowedTools carries a bare Bash entry. Which implementation makes the precondition hold everywhere in the agent tree while keeping the run unattended?

options.text: Narrow the allow list so the commit invocation is covered by a scoped rule rather than by the bare Bash entry, which routes that one command into the callback for inspection.
Move the check into a PreToolUse hook that inspects the command string and denies the commit with a reason when no passing test run is recorded.
Remove Bash from the build-fixer subagent's tools list so it cannot commit at all, and have the main agent make every commit on the subagent's behalf.

Restate the rule in the project CLAUDE.md and repeat it in the build-fixer's AgentDefinition prompt, since a subagent loads project CLAUDE.md through settingSources and would carry the rule into its own run.

items.explanation: A tool call approved at an earlier step never reaches canUseTool, and a bare allow-list entry auto-approves every call to that tool, so a check that lives only in the callback is silently skipped for exactly the calls it needs to see. Hooks are the first step in the evaluation order and a hook denial applies even to a call an allow rule or a permissive mode would otherwise approve, which is why the documentation names a PreToolUse hook as the control for a check that must run on every tool call. The denial reason is also what steers the agent back to running the suite first.

rationales.A: A scoped allow rule still approves matching calls at the allow-rules step, which comes before the callback. Narrowing an allow rule cannot route a call into a step that runs after it; the commit would be auto-approved rather than inspected.
rationales.C: The build-fixer needs Bash to run the very suite it was spawned to repair, and funnelling commits through the main agent gives up the parallel work the split exists for while leaving the precondition itself unenforced.
rationales.D: CLAUDE.md and a subagent prompt are guidance, and the three bad commits are the measurement of guidance's failure rate. A rule the model has to remember is not a precondition the tree cannot violate.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
items.stem: Your developer-productivity agent registers a PostToolUse hook that appends every file path the agent touches to an audit log while engineers explore an unfamiliar codebase. The TypeScript registration is `hooks: { PostToolUse: [ { hooks: [auditLog] } ] }` with no `matcher` property supplied. When will `auditLog` be invoked?

options.text: It will not run at all. A hook entry without a `matcher` is treated as an empty pattern, so the SDK skips the entry at registration and logs a warning naming the event.
It will run only for the built-in file tools Read, Write and Edit, because results from MCP tools are delivered through the separate PostToolUseFailure event instead.
It runs after every PostToolUse event, whatever tool produced the result, because a hook registered with no matcher matches every event of that type, MCP tool results included.
It will run only for tools carrying the `readOnlyHint` annotation, since PostToolUse is evaluated after the SDK has decided which tools may execute in parallel.

items.explanation: A hook's `matcher` filters against the event's target, which for tool events is the tool name, and accepts alternation such as "Write|Edit". A hook registered with no matcher runs for every event of that type, so this callback fires after every tool result in the session.

rationales.A: An omitted matcher is a documented registration form, not an error condition; nothing is skipped and no warning is emitted.
rationales.B: The matcher, not the tool family, decides which results reach a hook. PostToolUseFailure is a distinct event for failed tool executions, not the delivery path for MCP results.
rationales.D: `readOnlyHint` governs whether a tool may execute concurrently with others; it plays no part in hook matching or hook dispatch.
