items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
items.stem: Policy for your support resolution agent says refunds above $500 must be handled by a person. You add a PreToolUse hook matching `process_refund` that reads `input.amount` and blocks anything over the ceiling. The hook must also push the agent onto the `escalate_to_human` path rather than let it retry `process_refund` with a smaller amount. Which hook return value achieves that?

options.text: Return `{ systemMessage: "Refund exceeds the $500 ceiling; hand this case to escalate_to_human." }` so the note is surfaced while the tool call itself proceeds unchanged.
Return `hookSpecificOutput` with `permissionDecision: "deny"` and a `permissionDecisionReason` naming `escalate_to_human` as the required next step.
Return `{ continue: false }` so the turn ends immediately, then have the wrapper application re-prompt the agent with an instruction to call `escalate_to_human`.
Return `hookSpecificOutput` carrying `additionalContext` that restates the escalation policy in full, so the model can pick `escalate_to_human` on its next turn.

items.explanation: A PreToolUse hook expresses its decision inside `hookSpecificOutput`. `permissionDecision: "deny"` blocks the call deterministically, and `permissionDecisionReason` is the channel that tells Claude why it was blocked, which is what lets the agent route to the alternative workflow instead of retrying the same tool.

rationales.A: `systemMessage` is a top-level field surfaced to the user, not to the model, and it does not block anything, so the over-ceiling refund would still execute.
rationales.C: `continue: false` stops the turn rather than redirecting it, discarding the in-flight work and pushing the recovery logic outside the agent where the conversation context is lost.
rationales.D: Appending context informs the model but never blocks a call. The refund would run before the added context could influence any later decision.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization

options.text: `updatedInput` is honoured only on PostToolUse, where it rewrites the recorded tool input after execution; a PreToolUse hook may inspect the input but can never modify it.
`permissionDecision` has to be omitted for input rewriting to take effect, and `updatedInput` must be returned as a serialised JSON string rather than as an object.
The hook needs `permissionDecision: "ask"` so that the SDK re-serialises the modified input before presenting the call, whereas `"defer"` merely postpones the permission prompt.
`updatedInput` must sit inside `hookSpecificOutput`, not at the top level, and `"defer"` discards `updatedInput` and ends the query so it can be resumed later.

items.explanation: Two documented rules combine here. `updatedInput` is a field of `hookSpecificOutput`; returned at the top level it is simply not read, so the original input flows through. And `"defer"` ends the query for later resumption and ignores `updatedInput` outright, which accounts for the early termination. Omitting `permissionDecision` entirely is legal and lets the rewritten input pass through normal permission evaluation.

rationales.A: PreToolUse is exactly the event that can rewrite a call's input before it executes; PostToolUse acts on the result, after the tool has already run.
rationales.B: There is no requirement to omit `permissionDecision` for a rewrite, and `updatedInput` is an object, not a JSON string. This misdiagnoses both symptoms.
rationales.C: `"ask"` routes the call to a permission prompt rather than enabling a rewrite, and `"defer"` does more than postpone a prompt: it ends the query.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
items.stem: Three document-analysis MCP servers feed your research system. One returns publication dates as Unix epoch seconds, one as ISO 8601 strings, and one as numeric status codes when a date is missing. A fourth date format arrives from the built-in `Read` tool, which the agent uses to pull the corpus index out of a local `corpus-index.csv`. The synthesis subagent regularly misreads epoch integers as page counts. One hook has to normalise all four sources. Which hook configuration puts a single normalised shape in front of the model?

options.text: A single PostToolUse hook whose matcher names the three MCP tools and `Read` alike, returning `updatedToolOutput` with the raw payload replaced by a copy in which every date has been rewritten to ISO 8601.

A PostToolUse hook matching those MCP tools that returns `additionalContext` holding a conversion table that maps epoch seconds, ISO 8601 strings and each server's numeric status codes onto a single documented date convention.

A PostToolUse hook matching those MCP tools that returns `updatedMCPToolOutput`, the field reserved for rewriting results that arrived from an MCP server, with all three date representations converted to ISO 8601.
A line in the coordinator's system prompt instructing every subagent to convert timestamps to ISO 8601 before including them in the message it returns to the coordinator.

items.explanation: A hook's matcher is tested against the tool name, so one alternation pattern can cover `mcp__`-prefixed tools and a built-in such as `Read` together. `updatedToolOutput` then replaces a tool's output before Claude reads it and works for any tool in both SDKs, so that single hook normalises all four sources and the model only ever sees ISO 8601 dates.

rationales.B: `additionalContext` appends to what Claude sees; the raw, unnormalised payload is still in view, so the misreading can continue.
rationales.C: `updatedMCPToolOutput` replaces MCP tool output only, so it cannot touch the `Read` result whatever its matcher says, and it is the deprecated predecessor of `updatedToolOutput`.
rationales.D: A prompt instruction is probabilistic guidance. Normalisation that downstream reasoning depends on should be a deterministic transformation in a hook.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
items.stem: Two PreToolUse hooks match `process_refund` in your support agent: a `fraudCheck` hook that returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` for flagged accounts, and a `businessHours` hook that returns `permissionDecision: "allow"` while the escalation desk is staffed. On one call `fraudCheck` denies and `businessHours` allows. Which TWO statements about how the SDK resolves this are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Hooks are evaluated in registration order and the first decision returned is final, so listing `businessHours` ahead of `fraudCheck` would let the refund through.
The allow short-circuits the remaining permission steps, so any deny rules and ask rules configured for `process_refund` are skipped for this call.
Because one hook returned allow, the conflict is handed to the `canUseTool` callback, which arbitrates between the two hook results before the tool runs.
Both hooks run in parallel when the event fires and their completion order is not guaranteed, so each hook must reach its decision independently of the other.
The refund is blocked: for permission decisions the most restrictive result applies, so a single deny holds regardless of what any other matching hook returned.

items.explanation: When an event fires, all matching hooks run in parallel and completion order is non-deterministic, so each callback must be written to act independently. For permission decisions the most restrictive result applies, which means one deny blocks the tool call whatever the other hooks returned.

rationales.A: There is no first-wins ordering between hooks; they run concurrently and the results are combined by restrictiveness, not by registration position.
rationales.B: A hook allow does not skip the deny and ask rules that follow it in the permission evaluation order; those steps still run.
rationales.C: `canUseTool` is the last step of permission evaluation, not an arbitrator for hooks, and the deny has already resolved the call before it could be reached.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
items.stem: Your codebase-exploration agent has hooks that call an internal policy service, which became slow this week. Engineers see two different symptoms. In one run a `Bash` command never executed at all and Claude received a tool result saying the hook did not respond. In another run a `Grep` result reached the model normally and the turn continued, even though the hook logged a timeout. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: The difference is the tool rather than the event: `Bash` is state-modifying so it runs sequentially and a hook timeout aborts it, while read-only tools such as `Grep` are dispatched concurrently and bypass hook evaluation entirely.
The difference is the matcher: a hook registered with an alternation matcher is given a larger timeout budget by the SDK than one registered against a single tool name.

Hook timeout behaviour is event-specific: a timed-out PreToolUse hook means the tool does not run and Claude is told the hook did not respond, while a timed-out PostToolUse hook keeps the tool result and the turn continues.
The first run exhausted the hook retry budget and the second did not; the SDK retries a timed-out hook twice before deciding whether to drop the pending tool call.

items.explanation: Timeout handling depends on which event the hook is registered against, because the events sit at different points in the turn. A PreToolUse hook is a gate, so a timeout means the tool does not run and Claude receives a result saying the hook did not respond. A PostToolUse hook runs after execution, so a timeout leaves the tool result intact and the turn carries on.

rationales.A: Read-only tools are not exempt from hooks; the parallel-execution grouping decides concurrency, not whether hook callbacks fire.
rationales.B: Matcher shape has no effect on timeout budget. A matcher only decides which events a hook sees.
rationales.D: There is no documented hook retry budget; the divergence is between the PreToolUse and PostToolUse events, not between attempts.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
items.stem: An unattended overnight backlog run of the support agent is configured with `permission_mode="bypassPermissions"` and `allowed_tools=["Read", "mcp__support__lookup_order"]`. A `canUseTool` callback rejects any `process_refund` call above $500. The morning audit finds refunds of $1,200, $900 and $760 were approved without review. The run must stay fully unattended, and every tool other than `process_refund` must keep executing without being routed through an approval path. Which fix BEST guarantees the threshold check runs on every `process_refund` call?

options.text: Add `"mcp__support__process_refund"` to `allowed_tools` so the callback is actually invoked for that tool, since only tools named in the allow list are routed through `canUseTool`.

Replace the callback with a scoped deny rule such as `disallowed_tools=["mcp__support__process_refund(amount:*)"]`, since scoped deny rules leave the tool available and are enforced in every permission mode including bypassPermissions.
Drop `permission_mode` back to `"default"` for the overnight run so that every unlisted tool raises a permission prompt which the `canUseTool` callback can then answer on the operator's behalf.
Move the threshold check into a PreToolUse hook that inspects the outgoing call's `amount` and returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` above the ceiling, an interception no run configuration can waive.

items.explanation: Two things separate a hook from the check that failed here. The ceiling was written as an application-level veto, and this run pre-approves the tools it uses, so every refund resolved before the veto could speak -- the silent bypass the documentation warns about for a check that must run on each call. What TS 1.5 asks for instead is interception: a PreToolUse hook sees the outgoing `process_refund` request with its `amount` still in hand, applies the $500 rule to that value, refuses the calls that break policy, and its refusal is not something the run's configuration can waive. Every other tool keeps its automatic approval, so the backlog run stays unattended and nothing else is routed through an approval path.

rationales.A: This makes the problem worse. An allow rule pre-approves the tool at an even earlier step, so the call is resolved before `canUseTool` is consulted.
rationales.B: A deny rule matches on tool name and call shape, not on a numeric comparison, so a rule of this form cannot express the $500 threshold and would block far more or far fewer refunds than the policy intends.
rationales.C: This does reach the callback for `process_refund`, but it also routes every other tool that `allowed_tools` does not name -- `Write`, `Bash`, `Edit` and the rest -- through `canUseTool`, so the callback becomes the approval path for the whole run instead of one business-rule check, and the unattended bypass configuration is abandoned.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
items.stem: Your developer-productivity agent must enforce six things while engineers explore an unfamiliar codebase: log every file path touched, block writes outside an allow-listed directory, redact secrets from tool output, run a lint gate before any commit, record per-tool latency, and prefer British spelling in generated code comments. One engineer wants all six written as sentences in the system prompt to keep the agent simple; another objects that six hook callbacks would crowd out the context window engineers need for exploration. Which response is correct?

options.text: Write all six into the system prompt. Hook definitions are merged into the system prompt at session start anyway, so both placements cost the same per request and prompt text is easier to maintain.

Put the five that must hold on every call into hooks and leave only the spelling preference in the prompt: a hook is a deterministic guarantee where a prompt instruction is probabilistic compliance, and hooks run in your application's own process rather than inside the agent's context window, so they consume no context.

Put all six into hooks, and accept the cost: each callback's return value is appended to the transcript as a synthetic user message, so the exploration budget has to be sized for six hooks as well as the files being read.

Write all six into the system prompt except the audit log, since hooks execute inside the MCP server process that owns the matched tool and so cannot see built-in tool calls such as Read, Grep and Write at all.

items.explanation: Two separate facts settle this. A business rule that must hold on every call belongs in a hook because a hook gives a deterministic guarantee while a prompt instruction gives only probabilistic compliance; the house spelling preference is the one item here that tolerates probabilistic handling. And hooks run in your application process, not inside the agent's context window, so they do not consume context. Registering them costs nothing in the transcript by itself, and only what a hook deliberately returns, such as `additionalContext` or a replaced tool output, enters what Claude reads.

rationales.A: Hook definitions are never injected into the system prompt, so the two placements do not cost the same, and a prompt sentence buys probabilistic compliance where a path allow-list or a lint gate needs a guarantee.
rationales.C: Hook return values are not appended to the transcript as synthetic messages, so there is no per-hook exploration cost to size for, and a stylistic preference does not need a deterministic gate in the first place.
rationales.D: Hooks are an SDK-level interception point covering built-in and MCP tools alike; they do not run inside MCP server processes, so a hook sees Read, Grep and Write perfectly well.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: An engineer asks your agent to add comprehensive tests to a nine-year-old billing service. There is no existing test suite, coupling between modules is unknown, and dependency injection is done through an undocumented registry. Which decomposition strategy fits this task?

options.text: Dynamic decomposition: map the module structure, identify the highest-impact untested areas, then build a prioritised plan whose later subtasks come from the dependencies discovered.
A fixed four-stage prompt chain settled up front -- enumerate source files, write unit tests, write integration tests, emit coverage -- run once with no branch points.
A single prompt carrying the full repository tree and every source file, asking for one complete test plan plus the generated test files in a single response.
A pipeline that walks the source files in alphabetical order and writes one test file per source file, so the run is reproducible and can resume from the last completed file.

items.explanation: This is the canonical open-ended investigation task: the right subtasks are not knowable before work starts because the coupling and the injection registry have to be discovered. Adaptive decomposition maps structure first, identifies high-impact areas, then produces a prioritised plan that keeps adapting as dependencies surface.

rationales.B: A chain fixed before exploration bakes in assumptions about a codebase nobody has mapped yet, and it has no mechanism for reacting to a dependency found in stage two.
rationales.C: One enormous prompt invites attention dilution across hundreds of files and produces a plan with no intermediate output anyone can inspect or correct.
rationales.D: Alphabetical order is reproducible but arbitrary. It ignores impact and coupling, so effort lands on trivial modules while the risky ones stay untested.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: Every section of your research report is produced by a fixed three-call chain: an outline call, a drafting call that consumes the outline, and a formatting call that consumes the draft. The application discards the outline and the unformatted draft the moment the next call returns, logs neither, and branches on neither. The team's complaint is latency and cost per section. What does current guidance say about this chain?

options.text: Run the three calls concurrently rather than sequentially, since the outline, the draft and the formatting are independent once the section topic has been chosen.
Keep the chain as it stands, because splitting the work across separate calls is what keeps each stage's instructions unambiguous and merging them would reintroduce instruction conflicts.
Collapse it into a single call: explicit chaining earns its cost only when an intermediate output is inspected or a specific pipeline structure has to be enforced, and neither applies here.
Replace the three calls with three specialised subagents, one per stage, so that only the finished section returns to the coordinator's context.

items.explanation: With adaptive thinking and subagent orchestration Claude handles most multistep reasoning internally, so explicit prompt chaining is worth its cost only when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure. Here the outline and the raw draft are thrown away unread, so the chain buys neither observability nor enforced structure and is paying three round trips for what one call would do.

rationales.A: The stages are strictly ordered: the draft consumes the outline and the formatting consumes the draft, so they cannot run concurrently.
rationales.B: A single request can carry several clearly scoped instructions. Chaining is not what disambiguates them, and current guidance treats it as a cost to justify rather than a default.
rationales.D: Delegating each stage to its own subagent preserves the same three-stage split and adds delegation overhead, while still producing intermediate results nobody reads.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: A new research run must screen 900 conference abstracts, score each against six criteria, then cluster the survivors. The current coordinator delegates one subagent per abstract. Runs die part way through, the coordinator's context fills with per-abstract scores long before clustering starts, and restarts repeat completed work. What is the right architectural change?

options.text: Raise `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` above its default of 20 and set `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` to 5 so the coordinator can nest a second tier of dispatcher agents.
Move the fan-out into a dynamic Workflow, where the script holds the loop and the per-abstract results live in script variables, leaving only the clustering step in Claude's context.
Keep the coordinator but give each scoring subagent `memory: "project"` so its scores persist to disk between invocations and the coordinator can read them back on a later turn.
Keep the coordinator and raise `max_turns` while setting each subagent's `effort` to "low", so all 900 delegations fit inside one query without exhausting the turn budget.

items.explanation: The choice of decomposition mechanism turns on who holds the plan. With subagents Claude decides turn by turn and every intermediate result lands in a context window; subagents are documented for a few delegated tasks per turn. A dynamic Workflow puts the loop, the branching and the intermediate results in script variables, so Claude's context holds only the final answer, and workflows are the documented primitive for dozens to hundreds of agents per run.

rationales.A: Raising the caps lets more subagents run at once but does nothing about the coordinator's context filling with 900 scores, which is the actual failure.
rationales.C: Subagent memory persists material for a named agent across invocations; it does not move the coordinator's aggregation burden out of its context window.
rationales.D: Turn budget is not the constraint. Lowering effort degrades scoring quality while the context and restart problems remain untouched.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: One of your research system's report types is a regulated quarterly compliance review whose aspects never change: extract each source's claims, check every claim against the same six criteria, assemble the citation table, then draft the report. External auditors read the intermediate claim list and the criteria scorecard from every run and compare them quarter on quarter. Hoping for speed, the team replaced that fixed sequence with adaptive decomposition, letting the coordinator generate whatever subtasks each run's early findings suggest. The finished reports still read well, but two runs over the same corpus now emit different intermediate artefacts and the auditors can no longer compare a run against its predecessor. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep adaptive decomposition and add a line to the coordinator's system prompt telling it to emit a claim list and a criteria scorecard on every run, so the artefacts come back without losing the flexibility.

Return this report type to the fixed sequential pipeline: its aspects are known in advance, its steps have to run in one order, and each stage must emit the same inspectable artefact every time, which is what prompt chaining is for. Reserve adaptive decomposition for the open questions whose subtasks nobody can name up front.

Keep adaptive decomposition but run each review twice over the same corpus and report only the material that appears in both passes, so reproducibility comes from agreement between the two runs rather than from a fixed sequence.
Keep adaptive decomposition and archive the coordinator's full transcript for every run, so the auditors can reconstruct which subtasks actually ran instead of relying on a fixed set of artefacts.

items.explanation: Adaptive decomposition earns its keep when the subtasks cannot be known before work starts. This workload is the opposite case: a predictable multi-aspect review whose aspects are fixed, whose order is fixed, and whose intermediate outputs are themselves a deliverable that has to be comparable across runs. That is precisely the shape a fixed sequential pipeline is for, and choosing adaptive decomposition for it traded away the reproducibility the audit depends on for flexibility the task never needed.

rationales.A: A prompt instruction gives probabilistic compliance. The coordinator can still pick different subtasks each run, so the two named artefacts vary in coverage and content even when both files are produced, which is exactly what the auditors cannot work with.
rationales.C: Two passes double the cost and still fix no set of stages. Agreement between two independently varying plans is not the same as one defined sequence emitting the same artefact at the same point every run.
rationales.D: Archiving records what happened; it does not make two runs comparable. The auditors need identical stages producing identical artefact shapes, not a transcript of a differently shaped plan each quarter.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: Your CI job triages every red nightly build. It reads the build log, asks Claude for a triage plan -- an ordered list of investigation subtasks -- and then works that list to the end before posting its report. Two failures recur. When an early subtask establishes that the assertion broke because a schema migration changed a shared fixture, the job still walks the remaining planned subtasks through modules that can no longer be implicated. And leads the build log never mentioned, surfaced only by those subtasks, are never investigated at all. What should change?

options.text: Regenerate the plan as the run proceeds: after each subtask returns, derive the remaining subtasks from what it established rather than from the opening log.
Keep the single up-front plan but make it exhaustive, enumerating a subtask for every module the failing test transitively touches, so nothing that could be implicated is left off the list.
Keep the up-front plan and dispatch its subtasks concurrently to subagents, then have the coordinator reconcile their findings in one closing pass so that no subtask waits on the one before it.
Drop the planning step and hand a single call the build log and the repository, letting it investigate however it sees fit and report whatever it concludes, so that no stale list can constrain it.

items.explanation: Adaptive decomposition means the plan is produced by the run rather than before it: what each step discovers is what generates the next subtask. This job plans once, from the opening log, then executes that list as though it were a fixed pipeline, so a finding that invalidates the plan cannot redirect it and a lead the log never named has no way into it. Feeding each subtask's result back into the choice of the next one is what lets an investigation plan adapt as evidence accumulates, and it keeps every intermediate finding inspectable, which is the condition under which splitting work across separate calls earns its cost.

rationales.B: A longer list is still a list fixed before the evidence exists. It buys breadth at a large cost per build and still cannot drop the subtasks that the first finding has just ruled out.
rationales.C: Running the planned subtasks at once removes the dependency adaptation needs: a subtask cannot be shaped by a finding that is still in flight beside it, and the plan being reconciled is the wrong plan.
rationales.D: The problem is a plan that never updates, not the existence of a plan. One unstructured call gives up the intermediate findings the team inspects and leaves the triage impossible to audit.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: Your support agent resolves billing disputes through a fixed five-step chain: verify identity, list recent orders, classify the dispute, compute an adjustment, draft the reply. A review of 300 transcripts shows about a third of disputes need work the chain has no step for (chasing a carrier claim, reading a warranty exception, pulling a promotion's terms), and the agent forces those into the compute-an-adjustment step. Which decomposition change is most appropriate?

options.text: Extend the fixed chain with a dedicated step for chasing a carrier claim, a step for reading warranty exceptions and a step for pulling promotion terms, keeping a single deterministic pipeline that every dispute walks end to end in the same order.

Collapse the five steps into one prompt carrying the whole policy manual, the customer's order history and the warranty schedule, so the agent decides for itself which parts of the process apply to a given dispute and in what order.

Keep the fixed prefix (verify, list orders, classify) where the sequence really is deterministic, then switch to adaptive decomposition that generates the remaining subtasks from what classification found.
Keep the chain unchanged and raise the agent's turn budget so it has room to loop back over the compute step repeatedly until the unusual disputes come out correctly.

items.explanation: The two halves of this workflow have different characters. The prefix is genuinely predictable and order-dependent, which is where a fixed chain belongs. What follows classification is open-ended, so the subtasks should be generated from what classification discovered. Matching the pattern to each segment beats forcing one pattern over the whole workflow.

rationales.A: Enumerating dispute types keeps the pipeline rigid and only postpones the problem to the next unclassified case, while making every straightforward dispute walk more steps.
rationales.B: Removing all structure loses the deterministic identity verification that must precede any financial step, and gives up the inspectable intermediate outputs the chain provides.
rationales.D: More turns do not create the missing subtasks. The agent still has no step for chasing a carrier claim, so it keeps forcing the work into the wrong one.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: Before publication, every research report is checked against the same six quality criteria: citation coverage, claim support, source recency, source diversity, contradiction handling and structure. Today a single call receives the finished report and all six criteria together. Across 200 reports the first two or three criteria are reported on consistently, the rest only sometimes, and nobody can tell from the output which criteria were actually applied to a given report. The six are fixed by policy and every report must be checked against all of them. Which decomposition change matches the documented pattern for this workload?

options.text: Make the check a fixed chain, one call per criterion, each call receiving the report plus that criterion alone and emitting its own scorecard, which is stored beside the report.

Let the drafting subagent choose per report which of the six criteria are worth a call, generating the checks from the weaknesses it noticed while writing, so review effort lands where problems are most likely to be.

Keep the single call but number the six criteria in the prompt and require an output row for every one of them, including the criteria where the reviewer found nothing worth reporting, so coverage becomes visible.
Raise the review call's effort setting and give it a larger thinking budget, so all six criteria are weighed properly inside the one pass that already exists.

items.explanation: The criteria are known before the run starts and every report needs all six, which is the predictable multi-aspect review that a fixed sequential chain exists for. Giving each criterion its own call leaves that call one clean task instead of six competing ones, and the per-criterion scorecard is an intermediate output the team keeps, compares and can act on. That is the condition under which an explicit chain earns its extra calls; a chain is the wrong choice only when its intermediates are discarded unread.

rationales.B: Adaptive decomposition is for subtasks nobody can name up front. These six are fixed by policy, and letting the drafting step pick which to run is how a report skips the check it most needed.
rationales.C: A row per criterion makes the gaps countable without closing them. One call is still weighing six criteria at once, so the thin checks stay thin.
rationales.D: More effort inside one call gives no criterion a task of its own, and it produces no per-criterion artefact anyone can store or compare between reports.

items.objective: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
items.stem: Your boilerplate generator produces service scaffolds that compile and pass smoke tests but routinely miss the team's error-handling conventions. Appending "double-check your work against our conventions before answering" to the generation prompt produced no measurable change over 200 runs. Which decomposition change matches the documented pattern for this situation?

options.text: Enable extended thinking on the single generation call so the model reasons about the conventions before emitting the scaffold, then raise the thinking budget until compliance improves.
Split the step into a self-correction chain of separate calls: draft the scaffold, review it against an explicit conventions rubric, then revise using that review.
Raise the session's `effort` setting to "xhigh" so the model spends more of its budget on the generation call and produces a more careful first draft.
Delegate generation to a background subagent with `model: "opus"` so the scaffold is produced outside the main conversation and comes back as a single final message.

items.explanation: Draft, review against criteria, refine is the named prompt-chaining pattern, with each step a separate call so the intermediate review can be logged, evaluated or branched on. Splitting the work gives the review step a clean task and an explicit rubric instead of asking one call to critique its own in-progress output.

rationales.A: Extended thinking lengthens reasoning inside one call; it does not create the separable review step whose output you can inspect and measure.
rationales.C: Raising effort tunes how much budget a call spends. It leaves the structure of the task unchanged, which is the thing that failed.
rationales.D: Moving the same single-step generation into a subagent changes where it runs, not how it is decomposed, so the conventions are still missed.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: An analyst runs a long-running literature review in a local Claude Code session, using it to sanity-check the citations that the multi-agent research pipeline's report-generation subagent produces. The review session has never been renamed. Agent view lists it as `market-research-3f`, the same label `claude agents --json` reports. Running `claude --resume market-research-3f` says no such session was found. Why?

options.text: `--resume` accepts only a session UUID as an argument; every other identifier, including names set with `-n` at startup or with `/rename` during a session, has to be selected through the interactive picker instead of being passed on the command line.
The transcript was pruned by `cleanupPeriodDays` overnight, so the label is still cached in the picker while the underlying JSONL transcript has already been deleted.
Named resumption works only from the Agent SDK's `resume` option; the command line resolves a name only when the session was created in the same terminal.
That is the session's default display name, which labels it in listings of running sessions but is not a resume handle; a name set with `-n` or `/rename`, or the session ID, would resolve.

items.explanation: An unnamed interactive session gets a default display name built from the working-directory name plus a two-character suffix. It identifies the session in listings of running sessions such as agent view and `claude agents --json` output, but is not a resume handle. A name the user set with `-n`, `/rename` or Ctrl+R resolves, as does the generated title Claude Code writes from the first prompt, and so does the session ID itself.

rationales.A: `--resume` accepts a session ID or a session name, and running it with no argument opens the picker; it is not UUID-only.
rationales.B: The session is still listed and still resumable by a valid handle, so nothing has been pruned.
rationales.C: Name resolution is a documented command-line behaviour and is not restricted to the terminal that created the session.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: A nightly support-agent regression suite is launched from a Node script through the Agent SDK with its working directory set to `/srv/support-agent`. The next morning an engineer opens a terminal in that same directory and runs `claude --continue` expecting to inspect the run. Claude loads an unrelated interactive session from two days earlier. What is happening, and what works instead?

options.text: `--continue` skips sessions created by `claude -p` and the Agent SDK; capture the run's `session_id` and pass it to `claude --resume <session-id>`, or use `claude -p --continue`.
`--continue` matches on the exact working-directory string recorded at creation time, so re-running it from the repository root will make the encoded working directory match the SDK run.
SDK sessions are written to a separate store and are never resumable from the command line, so the run has to be replayed by re-executing the script with the same prompt and options.
`--continue` loads the most recently named session, so giving the SDK run a name at launch would make it win the ordering and be selected by `--continue`.

items.explanation: `--continue` loads the most recent conversation in the current directory but deliberately skips background sessions, sessions created with `claude -p` or the Agent SDK, and sessions whose first prompt was `/loop`. Those sessions are still resumable: pass the captured session ID to `claude --resume`, or use `claude -p --continue`, which does include them.

rationales.B: Both runs used the same working directory, so directory encoding is not the discriminator; the session's origin is.
rationales.C: An SDK session is stored like any other and is resumable by ID with `claude --resume <session-id>`.
rationales.D: `--continue` selects by recency within the directory, subject to the exclusions, not by whether a session carries a name.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: Two analysts branch a completed corpus-analysis session to trial competing synthesis strategies, each running `claude --resume corpus-baseline --fork-session` in the same checkout. Each branch writes `reports/synthesis.md`. Both later report that the other branch overwrote their output. What is the misunderstanding?

options.text: `--fork-session` requires a `--session-id` for the new branch. Without one, both forks reuse the parent's session ID and therefore share a single transcript and a single output path.

Forked sessions inherit the parent's permission grants, so each branch auto-approved the other's Write calls; adding a scoped deny rule for `Write(reports/**)` to both branches resolves the collision.
Forking branches conversation history, not the filesystem: a fork's file writes are real and visible to every session in that directory. Isolation needs checkpointing or a worktree.
`--fork-session` has no effect unless it is placed before `--resume` on the command line; as written the flag was ignored, so both analysts simply continued the same session instead of branching it.

items.explanation: Forking creates an independent branch of the conversation, and each fork does get its own session ID while the original's history is untouched. What it does not do is isolate the filesystem: edits a forked session makes are real and visible to any session working in the same directory. Branching file changes needs file checkpointing or a separate worktree.

rationales.A: Each fork receives its own new session ID automatically; no `--session-id` is required, and shared IDs are not what caused the overwrite.
rationales.B: Permission grants are not why the files collided. Both branches were legitimately allowed to write; the problem is that they wrote to one shared path.
rationales.D: Flag order on the command line is not significant. `--fork-session` does need to be combined with `--resume` or `--continue`, and here it was.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: A Python developer-productivity tool has finished a codebase-analysis session whose ID is held in `analysis_id`. It now needs two independent branches to explore competing refactoring approaches, without disturbing the original session's transcript. Which call creates a branch?

options.text: `query(prompt=..., options=ClaudeAgentOptions(fork_session=True))` -- `fork_session` on its own branches the most recent session recorded for the current working directory under `~/.claude/projects/`.
`query(prompt=..., options=ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=analysis_id, fork_session=True))` -- forking requires the session to fork from, and the branch gets its own new session ID.
`client = createSession(parent=analysis_id)` -- the experimental session API returns a child handle whose message history is copied and whose writes never touch the parent transcript.
`query(prompt=..., options=ClaudeAgentOptions(continue_conversation=True, forkSession=True))` -- continue the latest conversation in this directory and set the fork flag alongside it.

items.explanation: In the Python SDK `fork_session=True` only takes effect when it is paired with `resume=<session-id>`. The fork then receives its own session ID while the original session's ID and history stay unchanged, which is exactly what running two independent branches from a shared baseline requires.

rationales.A: `fork_session` on its own does nothing; there is no session to branch from until `resume` names one.
rationales.C: The experimental session API with `createSession()` was removed from the TypeScript Agent SDK in 0.3.142 and has no Python equivalent.
rationales.D: `forkSession` is the TypeScript spelling and is not a Python option, and continuing the latest conversation is not the same as branching a named baseline.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem:
A support-agent triage session was originally started with:

```
claude -n nightly-triage --mcp-config ./support-mcp.json --add-dir /srv/policies
```

It ended in the ordinary manual permission mode, and no settings file on this machine sets `permissions.defaultMode`. The next morning an operator resumes it in a terminal, without `-p`, using `claude --resume nightly-triage` alone, and the name matches exactly one session. The agent has lost capabilities it had the night before. Which TWO of the following are NOT restored by resumption and must be supplied again on the resume command? (Select TWO)

options.text: The MCP servers supplied by `--mcp-config`.
The extra working directories supplied by `--add-dir`.
The conversation history recorded in the session transcript, including every prior tool result.
The model the session was running when it was last active.
The permission mode the session was operating under.

items.explanation: Resuming restores the conversation, the session's model, the agent it was started with, the permission mode, active goals and unexpired scheduled tasks. It does not restore command-line configuration such as `--mcp-config`, `--settings`, `--plugin-dir`, `--fallback-model` or `--add-dir` directories, all of which have to be passed again on the resume invocation.

rationales.C: Conversation history is the core of what a session persists and is restored on resume.
rationales.D: The session's model is restored along with the conversation.
rationales.E: Resuming by an exactly matching name in a terminal without `-p` restores the permission mode the session was in. The documented exceptions cover sessions that ended in bypassPermissions, plan or auto mode, resumption through the session picker, and a `defaultMode` supplied by a settings file, none of which apply here.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: A market-landscape research session ran six weeks ago. Its transcript holds 40 web-search tool results plus a set of findings the team accepted at the time. Leadership now wants an updated report on the same question. Which approach is the more robust one?

options.text: Resume the session and open with an instruction to disregard every tool result older than four weeks, then re-run the searches that still matter to the question.
Resume the session with `--fork-session` so the stale branch is preserved for audit while the fork re-runs the searches over the same inherited conversation history.
Resume the session and run `/compact` first, so the stale search payloads are summarised away and only the accepted findings survive into the working context.
Start a fresh session and pass the captured findings and decisions in as application state in the opening prompt, instead of carrying stale tool results forward.

items.explanation: The documented advice is not to rely on session resume: capture the results you need, such as analysis output, decisions and diffs, as application state and pass them into a fresh session's prompt. Six-week-old search payloads are stale tool results, and a clean session with an injected structured summary is more reliable than asking a resumed agent to reason around them.

rationales.A: The stale payloads stay in context whatever the opening instruction says, and the model can still ground an answer in them.
rationales.B: Forking copies the same stale history into the branch, so the branch inherits the problem it was supposed to avoid.
rationales.C: Compaction summarises rather than removes, and summarisation is exactly where dated figures and their provenance get flattened.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: Yesterday an engineer used your agent to map a legacy payments module, reading 60 files and recording the call graph. Overnight a teammate merged a refactor that touched 9 of those files. This morning the engineer resumes the same session to continue the investigation. What is the most efficient way to make the resumed session correct?

options.text: Name the nine changed files in the first message and ask for targeted re-analysis of those files and anything depending on them, leaving the rest of the map intact.
Rely on resumption to reconcile the difference, since the session records its working directory and re-reads any file whose modification time is newer than the transcript entry that read it.

Abandon the session and start a fresh exploration of all 60 files, because stale file content anywhere in the transcript makes the whole recorded call graph unreliable and cheaper to rebuild than to repair.
Run `/compact` immediately after resuming, so the outdated file contents are summarised out of the working context before the next question is asked and the agent re-reads whatever it still needs.

items.explanation: A session persists the conversation, not the filesystem, so a resumed agent still believes the file contents recorded in its transcript. Telling it exactly which files changed lets it re-read only those and the code depending on them, which is far cheaper than discarding a 60-file map that is 85 percent still valid.

rationales.B: Sessions do not watch the filesystem or compare modification times; nothing triggers a re-read on resume.
rationales.C: Starting over throws away 51 files of still-accurate analysis to fix 9 files, which is disproportionate when the delta is known.
rationales.D: Compaction shortens context; it does not correct wrong file contents, and it can lose the specific details the map depends on.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: A supervisor process records the `session_id` of every support-agent run so failed runs can be resumed and finished later. It works for completed runs, but several runs that end with `ResultMessage.subtype` of `error_max_turns` leave the supervisor with no ID at all. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: `session_id` is present on every result message, including `error_max_turns`, `error_max_budget_usd` and `error_during_execution` results.
A single-shot `query()` yields the final error result message and then raises, so the ID has to be captured inside the message loop rather than after it.
`session_id` is populated only when a run ends with subtype `success`; error results still carry usage and cost fields but no session identifier.
In Python the session ID is a direct field on the init `SystemMessage`, while in TypeScript it is nested inside `SystemMessage.data`.
The supervisor must call `createSession()` before `query()` in order to obtain a session ID it can record up front.

items.explanation: Every result message carries `session_id`, whatever the subtype, alongside `total_cost_usd`, `usage` and `num_turns`; only the `result` text field is limited to successful runs. The reason the supervisor loses the ID is control flow: a single-shot `query()` emits the final error result and then raises, because the underlying process exits non-zero, so any capture written after the loop never executes.

rationales.C: Error results do carry `session_id`. It is the `result` field holding the final text that is present only on success.
rationales.D: This is reversed: TypeScript exposes it as a direct field on the init `SystemMessage`, while in Python it is nested inside `SystemMessage.data`.
rationales.E: The experimental session API with `createSession()` was removed in TypeScript Agent SDK 0.3.142; session IDs are read from messages, not requested in advance.

items.objective: 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking
items.stem: Your support agent runs behind a load balancer across three application servers. A conversation that began on `app-2` is later routed to `app-3`, which calls `query(..., options=ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=session_id))` and fails because the session is unknown. What explains this, and what is the right remedy?

options.text: Session IDs embed the originating host, so every server in the pool has to be started with the same `--session-id` value for the identifier space to be shared.
Resumption across hosts requires `continue_conversation=True` rather than `resume`, since continuing selects the most recent session for the working directory on whichever host serves the request.
Transcripts are local JSONL files under `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`, so `app-3` holds no copy; attach a shared `session_store` adapter or start fresh with a summary.
The encoded working-directory segment differs on each host, so aligning the deployment path across all three servers is sufficient to make the same session ID resolve anywhere in the pool.

items.explanation: Session transcripts are written as JSONL files on the machine that created them, under `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`. Resumption is therefore host-local by default. The documented options are to attach a `session_store` adapter so transcripts live in shared storage, to move the file, or to stop relying on resume and pass a captured summary into a fresh session on whichever host serves the request.

rationales.A: Session IDs do not encode a host, and `--session-id` names a session rather than defining an identifier space shared across machines.
rationales.B: `continue_conversation` reads the same host-local store, so it fails for the same reason; it also selects by recency rather than resuming the specific conversation.
rationales.D: Aligning the path fixes the directory segment but not the missing file. `app-3` still has no transcript for that session ID.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: The support resolution agent's `process_refund` tool carries a well-written five-sentence top-level description covering what the tool does, when it should be used and when it should not. Its `input_schema` declares `amount_minor_units` as an integer and `refund_scope` as a string with the enum values `full_order` and `line_item`, but neither property carries a `description`. Transcripts show the agent passing 49 for a refund of 49.99 in the account currency, and selecting `full_order` on disputes where only one damaged line item was in question. Every call is schema-valid and the tool executes. Which change to the tool definition most directly addresses this?

options.text: Set `strict: true` on the tool and add `"additionalProperties": false` to `input_schema`, so grammar-constrained sampling holds every emitted argument to the declared types, the required fields and the declared enum values before the call is dispatched to the refund service.
Add a `confirm_amount` boolean that the model must set to true once it has re-read the order total, so a deliberate second step stands between reading the order and issuing the refund.

Give each property in `input_schema` its own `description` stating what the parameter means, the unit and format expected, and how the value changes the tool's behaviour, including which scope value covers a single disputed line.

Add few-shot examples to the agent's system prompt showing two correctly argued `process_refund` calls, one for a whole-order refund and one for a single line item, so the model can pattern-match the argument shapes and the scope value from the transcript rather than from the schema it is given.

items.explanation: Anthropic's best practices for tool definitions require the description to explain what each parameter means and how it affects the tool's behaviour, alongside what the tool does, when it should and should not be used, and any caveats. Here the top-level description is already doing the selection work, because the right tool is being chosen every time; the whole failure sits at the parameter layer, where nothing states that the amount is expressed in minor units or which scope value covers a single disputed line. Documenting each property puts that information exactly where the model reads it when it builds arguments, and it is the change that turns a schema-valid call into a semantically correct one.

rationales.A: Strict tool use guarantees only that the emitted input follows the schema: correct types, required fields present, no extra keys. An integer 49 and the enum value `full_order` already satisfy that contract, so grammar-constrained sampling changes nothing. Schema conformance is not semantic correctness.
rationales.B: A model-set confirmation flag rests the check on the same misreading of the field that produced the wrong number, and it adds an unvalidated property instead of telling the model what the existing ones mean.
rationales.D: Prompt examples can help, but the documented order is descriptions first, and for argument shape the tool definition's own `input_examples` field rather than prose in the system prompt. Neither substitutes for stating each parameter's unit and meaning at the layer where the model reads the schema.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: In a multi-agent research system, the document-analysis subagent holds two carefully differentiated tools: `extract_data_points`, whose four-sentence description covers pulling structured figures out of a supplied PDF, and `verify_claim_against_source`, whose description covers checking a single stated claim against one named source and explicitly says it is not a bulk extraction tool. Even so, whenever the coordinator's delegation text contains the word "verify", the subagent opens with `verify_claim_against_source` and loops over claims one at a time, including on tasks that are plainly bulk figure extraction. The subagent's system prompt contains the line "Verify every figure before reporting it." What should the architect examine first?

options.text: The delegation contract between coordinator and subagent, replacing free-text task descriptions with a fixed enum of task types so the coordinator's wording can no longer reach the subagent at all.

The subagent's own system prompt, where a standing instruction built around the word "Verify" can bind that word to the similarly named tool and steer the opening call more strongly than either tool description does.

The `input_schema` of `verify_claim_against_source`, tightening it with `required` and `"additionalProperties": false` so that bulk-shaped calls are rejected and the model is forced to try the other tool.

The two descriptions again, on the principle that ambiguous or overlapping tool descriptions are what cause misrouting between near-identical tools; lengthen both well past four sentences and add to each a negative example showing a request that belongs to the other tool.

items.explanation: The exam guide names system prompt wording as an independent influence on tool selection: keyword-sensitive instructions can create unintended tool associations that override well-written tool descriptions, and reviewing the system prompt for such instructions is a listed skill. Here the descriptions already differentiate the tools and even state the negative boundary, while a literal keyword in the system prompt ('Verify') maps onto a tool name and fires whenever the coordinator uses the same word. Anthropic's tool-use overview separately documents only that system prompt phrasing shifts whether a tool is called at all, noting that a light instruction to use the tools to investigate before responding increases tool use; the keyword-to-tool-name association is the exam guide's own knowledge bullet on the impact of system prompt wording on tool selection.

rationales.A: Constraining the coordinator's vocabulary treats the symptom and destroys the adaptability free-text delegation gives the subagent. The same misrouting returns the moment an enum label or user-supplied string contains the trigger word.
rationales.C: Schema tightening controls the shape of an accepted call, not which tool is chosen. A single-claim verification call is well formed, so a stricter schema rejects nothing.
rationales.D: The two descriptions are already four sentences each and already state the boundary, so overlap is not what is misrouting these calls. More description text does not remove the competing keyword instruction, and the guide's remedy for this symptom is to review the system prompt.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: A developer productivity MCP server has grown to expose `create_branch`, `commit_changes`, `open_pr`, `request_review`, `merge_pr` and `close_pr`, each with a one-line description and each operating on the same pull-request resource with almost the same parameters. Engineers report that the agent calls `open_pr` when asked to request a review and `close_pr` when asked to merge, and the wrong-tool rate has risen with every tool added. Which redesign follows current Anthropic tool-design guidance?

options.text: Split the six tools further into narrower per-state operations such as `open_pr_draft`, `open_pr_ready`, `merge_pr_squash` and `merge_pr_rebase`, so that each tool covers exactly one outcome, no two tools overlap in purpose, and every description can be written for a single unambiguous case.
Keep the six tools and set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` on pull-request turns, guaranteeing that the model calls one of them rather than answering in prose about what it would do.

Keep the six tools and add a seventh routing tool, `choose_git_tool`, that takes the engineer's request as free text and returns the name of the pull-request tool the agent should call next, so the selection decision sits in one place the team can test and version.

Consolidate the related operations behind a single service-namespaced tool such as `github_manage_pull_request` with an `action` parameter enumerating open, request_review, merge and close, documenting each action and its required parameters in one detailed description.

items.explanation: Anthropic's define-tools guidance is explicitly to consolidate rather than proliferate: rather than a separate tool for every action, group them into a single tool with an `action` parameter, because fewer and more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity. It also prescribes service-prefixed namespacing such as `github_list_prs`, which matters more now that tool search matches queries against names and descriptions. These six tools are variants of one operation on one resource, which is exactly the consolidation case.

rationales.A: Further splitting makes the diagnosed problem worse. The tools already overlap in purpose and parameters, so multiplying near-identical definitions increases decision complexity and the number of near-miss candidates the model must discriminate between.
rationales.B: Forcing a tool call guarantees that some tool runs, not that the right one runs. The agent's failure is picking the wrong tool from a confusable set, and forced tool use additionally suppresses the natural-language text the model would otherwise emit before the call.
rationales.C: A routing tool adds a round trip and one more confusable tool while leaving the ambiguous six in place. Tool selection is what the model does natively from names and descriptions, so re-implementing it as a tool call is over-engineering a documented description-level fix.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: The research coordinator connects to two MCP servers at once: an internal corpus server and a public web-index server. Each server independently exposes a tool named `search`, and each name is unique within its own server. After the client aggregates both tool lists, corpus queries start arriving at the web index. According to the MCP specification, what is the correct fix at the aggregating client layer?

options.text: Disambiguate by prefixing each aggregated tool name with a server identifier the client itself controls, because tool-name uniqueness is scoped only to a single server and the `serverInfo` `name` is not guaranteed unique and should not be relied upon.

Use the `serverInfo` `name` returned during initialization as the qualifier for each aggregated tool, since the specification requires that value to be unique across every server a client connects to and expects clients to key their combined tool registry on it.

Have each server return its tools in a stable but distinct order in `tools/list`, which the specification already asks for so clients can cache the list, and key the combined registry on list position so the client can tell the two `search` entries apart when it forwards a call.

Require both servers to declare an `outputSchema` for `search`, so the `structuredContent` each returns has a distinguishable shape and the aggregating client can work out after the fact which server should have handled the query and re-route it there.

items.explanation: The MCP tools specification scopes tool-name uniqueness to a single server and states that a client or proxy aggregating several servers may encounter collisions and SHOULD disambiguate by prefixing with a server identifier, while explicitly warning that the `serverInfo` `name` is not guaranteed unique and should not be relied on for this. Claude Code and the Agent SDK implement exactly this pattern by exposing MCP tools as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`.

rationales.B: The specification says the opposite: `serverInfo` `name` carries no uniqueness guarantee, so building disambiguation on it can produce the same collision it was meant to solve.
rationales.C: Ordering is a caching and prompt-cache concern, not an identity mechanism. Servers are told to return tools deterministically so clients can cache the list; nothing lets a client treat position as a stable identifier across reconnects or list changes.
rationales.D: `outputSchema` describes the shape of a result, and routing is a decision made before a call is issued. Inspecting results to work out which server should have been called is both too late and unreliable.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: A developer productivity agent runs with tool search at its default setting and about 60 MCP tools in its catalogue. One of them, `query_index`, wraps a prebuilt symbol index that resolves definitions and call sites in milliseconds; its description reads "Query the index." Traces show that when engineers ask things like "find everywhere this function is called", `query_index` almost never appears among the tools a search loads, and the agent falls back to shelling out to ripgrep. Which change is the best fix?

options.text: Set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false` so all 60 tool definitions are loaded upfront on every turn, guaranteeing that `query_index` is always visible to the model when it plans a symbol lookup.

Rename the tool `search_symbol_references` and rewrite the description with the concrete keywords engineers use, such as searching a prebuilt symbol index for definitions and call sites by symbol name, file path or language, because names and descriptions are what the tool search matches queries against.
Add `query_index` to `allowedTools` so it runs without a permission prompt, removing the interruption that makes the agent prefer the shell command it can already run unattended.

Detect symbol-shaped requests in the application layer with a keyword matcher and set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "query_index"}` on those turns, forcing the prebuilt index to be consulted whenever the engineer's wording mentions a function, method or class name rather than leaving the decision to the model.

items.explanation: With tool search on, a tool's name and description are not only the selection signal but also the retrieval key: both search variants match against tool names, descriptions, argument names and argument descriptions, and the documented debugging step for a tool Claude never finds is to check exactly those fields and add the keywords users actually type. A tool whose description is three words cannot be retrieved into the small set of tools loaded per search, so it is never a selection candidate at all. Fixing the name and the description repairs discoverability and selection together.

rationales.A: Disabling tool search puts all 60 definitions in context permanently, which sits above the 30-50 range where Anthropic documents tool-selection accuracy degrading and costs roughly 10-20K tokens for 50 tools. It also leaves the uninformative description that caused the model to overlook the tool in the first place.
rationales.C: Permission is a different layer from availability and retrieval. The trace shows the tool is never surfaced, so it is never proposed, and a tool that is never proposed cannot be blocked by a permission prompt.
rationales.D: Forcing a named tool from brittle application-side keyword matching hard-codes routing that the model should be doing, breaks on phrasings the matcher does not anticipate, and suppresses the assistant text the model would otherwise emit before the call.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: The support resolution agent's `process_refund` tool declares `customer_id` as a required string. A programmatic prerequisite already blocks `process_refund` until `get_customer` has returned a verified customer id, and that gate is in place and working correctly. Even so, when a customer opens with "just refund my last order" and no lookup has happened yet, traces show the agent burning turns on `process_refund` calls carrying a plausible but fabricated identifier such as `CUST-000123`, each refused by the gate, instead of calling `get_customer` or asking the customer for an identifier. Which TWO changes reduce the fabrication at the tool-definition layer, following documented guidance? (Select TWO)

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` on every turn so that the model is compelled to call one of the available tools instead of reasoning its way to a value in prose.
Mark `customer_id` as optional so the model is under no pressure to supply a value it has not yet obtained, and let the backend resolve the customer when the field is absent.
Expand the `customer_id` parameter description to state its exact format and to say that the value must come from a prior `get_customer` result and must never be inferred from the conversation.

Expand the `process_refund` tool description itself to state that the tool must only be called after `get_customer` has returned a verified customer, and that the agent must ask the customer for an identifier rather than supply one it has not received.
Set `strict: true` on the tool and pair `required` with `"additionalProperties": false` in `input_schema`, so grammar-constrained sampling holds the generated input to the declared contract.
Set `destructiveHint: true` in the tool's annotations so the client refuses to dispatch the call until a verified customer record exists in the session.

items.explanation: The orchestration gate is the deterministic control and it is already doing its job; what remains is a tool-definition problem, because the tool definition is what the model reads when it decides whether to call a tool and what to put in the arguments. Anthropic's guidance asks a description to cover what the tool does, when it should and should not be used, what each parameter means and how it affects behaviour, and any caveats. A parameter description that gives the exact format and says the value must come from a prior `get_customer` result tells the model where the value is supposed to originate; a tool description that states the prerequisite and instructs the agent to ask the customer rather than invent an identifier closes the same gap at tool level. Together they stop the model proposing calls the gate will only refuse.

rationales.A: Forcing a tool call makes fabrication more likely, not less, because the model must produce a call rather than ask a clarifying question. It also removes the natural-language turn in which the agent would have requested the missing identifier.
rationales.B: Making the identifier optional removes the only signal that verification has happened and lets a refund proceed against an unresolved customer. Optional fields are the right answer for extraction schemas where source documents may genuinely lack a value, not for a required input to a financial operation.
rationales.E: Strict tool use is grammar-constrained sampling, and its documented guarantee is only that the emitted `input` strictly follows `input_schema` and that the tool name is valid: correct types, required fields not omitted. A fabricated identifier is a well-formed string that already satisfies the schema, so it passes untouched, and compelling the required field to be populated arguably makes an invented value more likely rather than less.
rationales.F: Annotations are metadata hints, not enforcement. `destructiveHint` is informational in the Agent SDK, only `readOnlyHint` has functional effect (parallel batching of read-only calls), and the specification tells clients to treat annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the corpus MCP tool `search_corpus` returns, for every hit, more than thirty fields: tokenizer statistics, ACL flags, shard ids and an internal storage reference such as `blob_7f2a::v4`, alongside the matched snippet. There is no title, canonical URL or public identifier in the payload. Two symptoms follow: the synthesis subagent's context fills after a handful of searches, and the citations in generated reports point at blob references that mean nothing to a reader. Which change to the tool's output contract best addresses both?

options.text: Leave the payload as it is and add a PostToolUse hook in the coordinator that strips the tokenizer statistics, ACL flags and shard identifiers from every `search_corpus` result before the model sees them, keeping the server's response generic for the other teams that already consume it.

Leave the payload as it is and instruct the synthesis subagent in its system prompt to read only the matched snippet, to ignore the tokenizer statistics, ACL flags and shard identifiers entirely, and to cite each document by the title it can infer from the snippet text.

Return the same thirty fields but move them out of the text content into `structuredContent` validated by an `outputSchema` declared on the tool, so the text block the model reads stays short, the full record is still available, and no other team's integration has to change.

Return only the high-signal fields the agent needs to decide its next step, and identify each hit by a stable, semantically meaningful identifier such as the document slug or UUID together with its title and canonical URL, rather than by an opaque internal reference.

items.explanation: Anthropic's tool-design guidance is that tool responses should return only high-signal information and should use semantic, stable identifiers such as slugs or UUIDs rather than opaque internal references, because bloated responses waste context and make it harder for Claude to extract what matters. Both symptoms here trace to the same defect in the tool's output contract, and fixing the contract fixes it for every agent that calls the tool, not just this one.

rationales.A: A hook can normalise or trim results and is a legitimate mechanism, but here it leaves a defective contract in place so that every consumer must reimplement the same trimming, and it cannot invent the stable identifier and title that the payload never contained.
rationales.B: A prompt instruction is probabilistic and does not reduce the tokens the payload already consumed by the time the model reads it. It also cannot fix citations, since no citable identifier exists anywhere in the result.
rationales.C: `structuredContent` is server-produced result data, not a way to hide bulk from the model. When it is set, Claude receives the JSON, and text blocks in `content` are not forwarded, so this moves the same thirty fields into the model's view under a different key while still omitting the identifier and title.

items.objective: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
items.stem: The support agent exposes one tool for self-service account work. Its schema is `{"type": "object", "properties": {"instruction": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["instruction"]}` and its description says "Performs an account action described in plain language." It covers shipping-address updates, plan downgrades and account closure. Two incidents have been logged: an account was closed when the customer only asked what closing would involve, and several address updates silently no-opped because the free text did not parse. Which redesign is correct?

options.text: Split it into purpose-specific tools such as `update_shipping_address`, `change_plan` and `close_account`, each with a typed input schema, explicit required fields and its own description, so the boundary between the operations is enforced by the contract rather than by parsing prose.

Keep the single tool and add an `input_examples` array carrying a correctly phrased example instruction for each of the three operations, one for a shipping-address change, one for a plan downgrade and one for an account closure, so the model can pattern-match the phrasing the server's parser accepts.

Keep the single tool and add a `confirm` boolean to the schema alongside `instruction`, requiring the model to set it to true for any instruction it judges irreversible and having the server refuse to act on a closure request that arrives without it, so the destructive case carries a deliberate second signal.

Keep the single tool, set `strict: true`, and grow the description to enumerate every accepted phrasing for each of the three operations along with the phrasings that will be rejected, so the model can map any customer wording onto a form that the server's existing parser reliably handles.

items.explanation: This is the case the exam guide describes as splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts. The three operations have different required inputs, different consequences and different reversibility, and a single free-text `instruction` field gives the model no schema to satisfy and the server nothing to validate. Splitting is the right move when purposes genuinely differ; note that consolidation behind an `action` parameter is the right move in the opposite case, where several tools are variants of one operation over one resource with one contract.

rationales.B: Examples of accepted phrasing make a fragile natural-language parser slightly more likely to succeed, but the contract remains untyped, address updates can still no-op, and nothing distinguishes a question about closing an account from a request to close it.
rationales.C: A model-set `confirm` flag makes the irreversibility check depend on the model's judgement of its own free-text argument. Deterministic protection for a destructive operation belongs in a typed, separately named tool with its own gate, not in a boolean the model chooses to set.
rationales.D: Strict tool use guarantees only that the emitted input matches the schema, and the schema here is a single unconstrained string, so it guarantees nothing useful. Enumerating phrasings in prose scales badly and still leaves three unrelated operations sharing one contract.
