items.objective: 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
items.stem: A team that uses Claude Code daily for refactoring and documentation has let its instruction files grow over two quarters, and memory now takes a noticeable share of the window before any work starts. The tech lead needs the per-file context cost of the instruction files in the running session, because the team is deciding what to trim rather than where the files live. Which step produces that?

options.text: Run /memory, which lists memory file locations across user and project scope and reports the token cost that each one contributes to the session.
Run /context and read the entries listed under Memory files, which report the instruction files loaded into the current session and the context they occupy.
Run /doctor, which validates the repository's Claude Code configuration and reports which instruction files were skipped because they failed to parse.
Restart with claude --debug and read the startup banner, which is the only surface that names the instruction files a session has loaded.

items.explanation: /context is the documented surface for what a session is actually spending: its Memory files section lists the instruction files loaded into the running session together with the context they occupy, which is what a trimming decision needs. If the lead then needs to know when each file loaded and why, the InstructionsLoaded hook logs that per file. Note a divergence worth carrying into practice: the exam guide names /memory for verifying which memory files are loaded, while the current documentation routes loaded-file verification and per-file context cost to /context and leaves /memory as the place to browse and open memory file locations.

rationales.A: /memory lists memory file LOCATIONS across user and project scope, including entries for files that do not exist yet, and lets you open them for editing. It reports no token cost at all, so it cannot tell the team what is worth trimming.
rationales.C: /doctor reports on installation and configuration health and can propose trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md, but it is not the surface that enumerates the instruction files loaded into a specific running session with the context each occupies.
rationales.D: Debug output is not the documented mechanism for this, and the claim that it is the only surface is wrong: /context reports the loaded memory files and their context cost inside the session with no restart required.

tags: scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

items.objective: 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
items.stem: A monorepo team's Claude Code sessions behave inconsistently around one convention: the generated protobuf stubs under gen/ must never be hand-edited. Some sessions honour it, others ignore it, and a colleague working in the same repository sees the opposite pattern. In a session where it was ignored the engineer has already run /context and confirmed that the file carrying the convention is not among the entries under Memory files. He now wants a single listing of every memory file location that can apply to this repository across user and project scope, including any the team has not created yet, so that he can open the right one and move the convention into it. Which step gives him that?

options.text: Run /memory, which lists memory file locations across user and project scope, including entries for files that do not exist yet, and opens any of them for editing.

Run /doctor, which checks installation and configuration health and proposes trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md, so it reports every memory file location the repository could use and flags the ones nobody has created.
Run /context again with the memory section expanded, which adds the user-scope and project-scope locations that were not loaded to the same listing it has already produced for the files that were.

Add the InstructionsLoaded hook to .claude/settings.json, which logs every instruction file location Claude Code considers across user and project scope, including the ones it decided not to load, with a reason recorded for each.

items.explanation: /memory is the command that lists CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and other memory file locations across user and project scope, including user and project CLAUDE.md entries for files that do not exist yet; selecting an entry opens it in the editor and creates it first if it is missing. That inventory of where instructions can live is what a hierarchy problem needs, as distinct from a report of what one session happened to load. The exam guide names /memory for verifying which memory files are loaded and diagnosing inconsistent behaviour across sessions, and the bank keys to the guide; current documentation splits the job and sends the question of which files actually loaded into the running session to /context, which is why the stem has already ruled that step out.

rationales.B: /doctor reports installation and configuration health and can propose trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md, but it does not enumerate the memory file locations available across scopes and it will not open one for editing.
rationales.C: /context reports what the running session loaded and nothing more. A file that never loaded cannot appear there, which is exactly why his first check came back empty, and a second run would tell him no more than the first did.
rationales.D: The InstructionsLoaded hook logs which instruction files loaded, when, and why, which makes it a good tool for debugging path-scoped rules and lazily loaded subdirectory files. It records load events, so it still cannot list a location where no file exists yet.

items.objective: 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
items.stem: A repository's root CLAUDE.md has reached about 1,100 lines: coding standards, a long block of React component examples, the database migration policy, and the release checklist. /context shows memory files taking a substantial share of the window before any work starts, and engineers report that instructions buried in the middle are increasingly missed. A developer proposes splitting the file into four files under docs/claude/ and replacing each section with an @docs/claude/<topic>.md import. Why will that proposal not fix the reported problem, and what will?

options.text: Imports resolve against the working directory rather than the file that contains them, so the four paths would break in any session started below the root; the workable fix is to keep the sections inline and compress each one into a short bulleted summary of no more than a dozen lines.

Imports nest to a maximum depth of four hops and the proposal exceeds it; the workable fix is to flatten the four topics into a single imported file and leave the root CLAUDE.md as a one-line pointer to it.

Imported files are expanded and loaded at launch alongside the file that references them, so the token cost is unchanged; moving the conditional sections into .claude/rules/ files with paths globs is what actually defers loading until Claude works with matching files.

The split does defer loading, because an imported file is read only at the point Claude first needs its subject; the remaining problem is ordering, so the fix is to move the most critical rules to the top of the root file.

items.explanation: @ imports are an organisation tool, not a context-reduction tool: every discovered import is expanded into context at launch alongside the file that referenced it, so four imports cost what four inline sections cost. Path-scoped rules under .claude/rules/ are the mechanism that genuinely defers loading, because a rule with a paths glob enters context only when Claude works with a file that matches.

rationales.A: Relative import paths resolve against the file containing the import, not the working directory, so the paths would be fine. The diagnosis is wrong even though shortening a bloated memory file is sound advice on its own.
rationales.B: The four-hop limit is real but applies to chains of nested imports, not to four sibling imports in one file. Flattening them would not reduce the loaded token count either.
rationales.D: This inverts the documented behaviour: imports are not lazy. Ordering does matter for adherence, but reordering a file that is still fully loaded leaves the context cost exactly where it was.

items.objective: 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
items.stem:
A monorepo's root CLAUDE.md ends with a single import line:

  @~/.company/engineering-standards.md

Engineers clone the standards repository to that path during onboarding. On most machines Claude Code follows those standards. On one engineer's machine it never has, even though the file exists at that path and /memory shows the root CLAUDE.md exactly as expected. The engineer recalls dismissing some dialog during their first session in this repository. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The import resolves outside the working directory, so Claude Code asked once for approval of the external files; the engineer declined, which leaves those imports disabled for the repository and stops the dialog reappearing.

Imports inside a project-level memory file are capped at four hops, and the standards file imports further files that push the chain past the cap on that machine, which silently drops the whole subtree.

A project-level memory file cannot import a path outside the repository at all, so the line resolves to nothing everywhere; the other machines are following a stale copy of the standards that was cached during an earlier session in this repository.
The engineer's user settings set claudeMdExcludes, and because that setting does not merge across scopes it replaces the project value and removes the imported file for that user only.

items.explanation: An import in a project-level memory file whose path resolves outside the working directory is treated as external. Claude Code shows a one-time approval dialog listing those files; declining leaves the imports disabled for that repository and the dialog does not come back, which matches a machine that has never once applied the standards while every other machine does. Imports in user-scope files such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md load without the dialog, which is why the distinction is easy to miss.

rationales.B: The four-hop limit is real, but it would behave the same on every machine that clones the same standards repository. Nothing here is machine-specific, and the stem reports a single-machine failure.
rationales.C: Imports accept both relative and absolute paths, and a home-relative external path is explicitly supported subject to approval. There is also no cached-copy mechanism for memory files.
rationales.D: claudeMdExcludes skips files by absolute-path glob and its arrays MERGE across user, project, local and managed scope rather than replacing one another. It also would not produce the dismissed dialog the engineer remembers.

items.objective: 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
items.stem: An engineer starts Claude Code from the root of a monorepo to explore an unfamiliar service. The repository has a root CLAUDE.md and a packages/checkout/CLAUDE.md documenting that package's error-handling conventions. For the first twenty minutes Claude answers questions about checkout without applying any of those conventions. Once it opens packages/checkout/src/refund.ts to trace a bug, every later suggestion follows them precisely. Which statement explains the behaviour?

options.text: Subdirectory memory files are loaded at launch but placed after the root file, so their instructions are only reached once the conversation already contains a file from that directory.
Only files named .claude/CLAUDE.md load automatically; a CLAUDE.md at the top level of a package directory is treated as ordinary documentation until Claude reads it as a file.
Memory files below the working directory load at launch only when the package is passed with --add-dir; without that flag the package file is picked up at the next compaction instead.
Memory files at or above the working directory load at launch; a CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory below it is included only when Claude reads a file in that subdirectory.

items.explanation: Claude Code loads the CLAUDE.md files in the directory hierarchy at or above the working directory when the session starts. Files in subdirectories below it are deliberately deferred and are included the first time Claude reads a file in that subdirectory, which is exactly the twenty-minute gap described. It is also why a nested CLAUDE.md cannot be relied on to govern files scattered across the tree.

rationales.A: Subdirectory files are not loaded at launch at all, so ordering within the loaded set is not the explanation. Discovered files are concatenated from the filesystem root down to the working directory.
rationales.B: Both ./CLAUDE.md and ./.claude/CLAUDE.md are recognised project memory locations, and a package-level CLAUDE.md is a real memory file rather than documentation. The trigger is reading a file in that directory, not reading the memory file itself.
rationales.C: --add-dir extends file access to directories outside the working tree; it has nothing to do with subdirectories already inside it, and compaction does not pull in unread subdirectory memory.

items.objective: 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
items.stem:
A CI runner checks out the application repository and, separately, the platform team's standards repository at /opt/eng-standards, which carries its own CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/ directory. The review stage runs:

  claude -p "$REVIEW_PROMPT" --add-dir /opt/eng-standards --output-format json

Claude can read files under /opt/eng-standards when asked, but none of the instructions in that directory's CLAUDE.md are being applied to the review. The platform team's runbook says to add CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 to the job environment. Which statement best explains the failure and what that variable changes?

options.text: The flag is the wrong mechanism and the variable is unnecessary: permissions.additionalDirectories in the repository's .claude/settings.json is what both grants access to a directory and loads the CLAUDE.md and rules it contains.

--add-dir grants file access, and by default the CLAUDE.md files in the directories it names are not loaded; the variable is the documented switch that also loads CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/*.md and CLAUDE.local.md from an added directory.

Directories on the command line are loaded as memory only when the run declares them as settings sources; adding --setting-sources project,user promotes them to project sources so they are treated as part of the repository.

Memory files are discovered only in the working directory and the directories above it and no configuration changes that, so the standards checkout has to be vendored into the application repository's tree.

items.explanation: The documented contract for --add-dir is that it grants file access rather than configuration discovery: by default the CLAUDE.md files in an added directory are not loaded, which is exactly the split the stage is seeing, with the files readable and the instructions absent. CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 is the documented switch that also loads CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/*.md and CLAUDE.local.md from those directories, with CLAUDE.local.md skipped when local is excluded from --setting-sources. Skills and commands are the standing exception to the rule: .claude/skills/ and .claude/commands/ are loaded from an added directory with no variable set. Be aware that the environment variable is documentation depth rather than named exam-guide surface: the guide's appendix lists the CLI flags and no environment variables, so what the guide anchors here is the access-versus-configuration distinction, which is the judgement the item turns on.

rationales.A: The permissions.additionalDirectories setting is the persistent form of the same file-access grant. It does not load CLAUDE.md or .claude/rules/ from the directories it names, so swapping the flag for the setting leaves the instructions exactly as absent as they were.
rationales.C: --setting-sources selects which settings scopes are consulted (user, project, local). It does not reclassify directories outside the working tree, and passing it here changes nothing about added-directory memory.
rationales.D: Memory files in ancestor directories of the working directory do load, so the first half is right about the default discovery path, but the claim that no configuration changes it is false. Vendoring another team's repository into the application tree is the wrong remedy for a one-line environment change.

items.objective: 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
items.stem: A team is moving a 200-line reference table of internal service endpoints out of the root CLAUDE.md and into a skill under .claude/skills/. A developer looks the table up perhaps once a week, Claude should never pull it in on its own, and the team wants nothing at all from this skill sitting in context at the start of every session. Which TWO statements about achieving that are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Adding user-invocable: false is what takes the description out of the session-start context, and the skill is then run only when a developer types the command.
Setting context: fork keeps the description out of context at launch, because a forked skill is not registered with the main session until something invokes it.
Omitting the description field from the frontmatter is what keeps the skill out of the session-start listing, since Claude Code then registers it by directory name with no listing entry.
Because the body is reference material rather than a procedure, Claude Code loads it at launch the way it loads a rules file, so a skill saves nothing here until the content is rewritten as steps.

Moved into a skill as it stands, the table itself is already out of the session-start context: only the skill's description is loaded at launch, and the body enters the conversation when the skill is invoked.
Adding disable-model-invocation: true removes the last piece, because a skill carrying that field keeps its description out of context and runs only when a developer types the command.

items.explanation: A skill contributes only its description to the session-start context and loads its body when it is used, which is what takes a weekly-use reference table out of every session without losing it. disable-model-invocation: true goes one step further: its documented effect is that the description is not in context at all and the full skill loads only when a developer types the command, which matches a table Claude should never reach for by itself.

rationales.A: user-invocable: false is the mirror image of what is wanted. It means only Claude may invoke the skill, its description stays permanently in context so Claude knows the skill exists, and Claude Code hides it from the slash menu.
rationales.B: context: fork changes where an invoked skill runs and what context it sees. It has no bearing on what is loaded at session start, and the skill is discovered and listed exactly as before.
rationales.C: Omitting description does not remove the skill from the listing: Claude Code falls back to the first paragraph of the markdown content, so something is still loaded at launch and it is less informative than a written description.
rationales.D: A skill's body loads only when the skill is used, whatever the body contains. Long reference material is an explicitly documented use for skills precisely because it then costs almost nothing until it is needed.

items.objective: 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
items.stem: A team ships /deploy-preview as a project skill at .claude/skills/deploy-preview/SKILL.md, committed to the repository. One engineer wanted a variant that also tails the deployment log, so she copied the directory to ~/.claude/skills/deploy-preview/ and edited it there. Two sprints later the team adds a mandatory approval step to the project skill. Every teammate picks the change up on their next session; on her machine /deploy-preview still runs the old steps with no approval. What explains this, and what is the right correction?

options.text: Project skills take precedence over personal ones, so her copy is inert; the real cause is that skill directories are only scanned at startup, and restarting the session will pick the new step up.
Skills are additive across scopes in the way memory files are, so both bodies are in context and Claude is following the older one; she should delete the approval step from the project skill instead.

Personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/ take precedence over a project skill of the same name, so her copy shadows the team's; she should give the personal variant a different name so both stay addressable.

A personal skill shadows a project skill only when their frontmatter name fields match; hers match by directory alone, so the real cause is that her allowed-tools list omits the tool the new approval step calls.

items.explanation: Skill name collisions resolve enterprise over personal over project, so a personal skill with the same name shadows the team's project skill entirely and keeps doing so through every future change to the repository copy. The documented remedy for a personal variant is to give it a different name, which leaves the team's skill reachable alongside it.

rationales.A: The precedence runs the other way for skills: personal beats project. Claude Code also watches skill directories for live changes, so a restart is not what is missing here.
rationales.B: Additive layering is the CLAUDE.md behaviour, not the skill behaviour. Skills override by name, and weakening the team's skill to accommodate one personal copy is the wrong direction of fix.
rationales.D: For a project or personal skill the command name comes from the directory name, so the collision is real regardless of the frontmatter name. allowed-tools grants permission for a turn and would not silently substitute an older body.

items.objective: 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
items.stem:
A platform team ships two helpers to every engineer through the repository. One is a command file at .claude/commands/scaffold-service.md. The other is a skill at .claude/skills/audit-deps/SKILL.md whose frontmatter reads:

  ---
  name: dependency-audit
  description: Audit third-party dependencies against the approved list
  ---

Both are committed, and both reach every engineer on clone. After pulling, an engineer finds that /scaffold-service and /audit-deps work, while /dependency-audit does nothing and never appears in autocomplete. Which statement accounts for that?

options.text: A command file takes its command name from its file name, and a project skill takes its from the directory holding SKILL.md; in a project skill the frontmatter name is only the display label.

In a project skill the frontmatter name replaces the directory name in the command, so /dependency-audit is the registered form; /audit-deps still answers only because Claude Code keeps the directory name as an alias until the session is restarted.

Claude Code ignores name in a file under .claude/commands/ but honours it in a SKILL.md, and it skips any project skill whose directory name and name field disagree, so this skill was never registered and /audit-deps is resolving to a bundled skill.

A project skill is addressed by a directory-qualified command, so the engineer has to type /skills:audit-deps or /skills:dependency-audit; the bare form is reserved for files under .claude/commands/ and for skills shipped inside a plugin.

items.explanation: For a personal or project skill the typed command comes from the directory holding SKILL.md, so .claude/skills/audit-deps/ produces /audit-deps and the frontmatter name sets only the label shown in skill listings. A file under .claude/commands/ takes its command name from the file name without the extension, so scaffold-service.md produces /scaffold-service, and name and paths are ignored outright in a command file. Both directories are project scope: they are committed and shared with the team through source control, which is why every engineer gets both on clone, whereas the personal equivalents at ~/.claude/commands/ and ~/.claude/skills/ stay on one machine. Only in a plugin skill does name replace the last segment of the command.

rationales.B: That is the plugin-skill behaviour: in a plugin skill the frontmatter name replaces the directory name in the last segment of the command. For a personal or project skill name is a display label, the directory name is the command, and there is no alias that expires at restart.
rationales.C: A mismatch between directory name and frontmatter name is not an error and does not cause a skill to be skipped. The first clause is true as far as it goes, since name is ignored in a command file, but that has no bearing on how a SKILL.md is registered.
rationales.D: Directory qualification such as /apps/web:audit-deps exists only to disambiguate a skill discovered in a nested .claude/skills/ directory below the working directory from one of the same name at the root. It is not the normal invocation form, and plugin skills are namespaced as plugin-name:skill-name.

items.objective: 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
items.stem: An architect maintains /map-service, a skill that walks a service's imports, database calls and queue bindings and prints a full dependency inventory before condensing it into about fifteen lines. The inventory itself runs to several thousand lines. After two or three invocations the main session is crowded with raw inventory, answers about other parts of the codebase get vaguer, and nobody ever reads anything but the summary. Which change to SKILL.md addresses this most directly?

options.text: Set allowed-tools to Read, Grep and Glob so the skill has no way to emit large command output, which keeps the inventory small enough that the main session is not affected by it.
Set disable-model-invocation: true so the skill runs only when a developer types the command, which keeps its output out of any session that did not explicitly ask for a map.
Move the skill body into .claude/rules/ with a paths glob, the documented way to run a skill in an isolated sub-agent context so that its output cannot pollute the main conversation.
Set context: fork, so the skill content becomes the prompt for a subagent with a window of its own and only that subagent's finished result returns to the session.

items.explanation: context: fork runs the skill in a forked subagent whose prompt is the skill content and which has no access to the conversation history, so verbose intermediate output stays in the subagent's window and only the result reaches the main session. That is the documented use for skills producing bulky analysis. Note that since v2.1.218 the fork runs in the background by default and its result arrives later, so background: false is what makes it block the invoking turn.

rationales.A: allowed-tools grants permission for the tools it lists for the invoking turn; it does not restrict what the skill can call, and every other tool remains available under normal permission settings. It also has no bearing on output volume.
rationales.B: The skill is already being invoked deliberately by developers; the problem is what its output does to the session once invoked, which controlling invocation does not touch.
rationales.C: A rules file supplies standing guidance when Claude reads matching files; it runs nothing and isolates nothing. The isolated sub-agent context this option describes is what context: fork provides, and a paths-scoped rule would push the same bulk into the main window involuntarily.

items.objective: 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
items.stem: A team adds context: fork to api-conventions, a skill whose body is purely reference material: endpoint naming rules, the shape of the error envelope, and pagination defaults, with no steps to carry out. Developers who invoke it now get a short and unhelpful reply, and none of the conventions are applied to the code being written afterwards. What is the best explanation and correction?

options.text: A forked skill does not receive the frontmatter allowed-tools grant, so the subagent cannot read the files it needs; restoring it with an explicit list naming Read and Grep will make the fork return usable guidance.

context: fork suits a skill containing an actionable task; a guidelines-only skill hands the subagent reference text with nothing to do, so it returns nothing useful. Remove the field and let the skill load into the main conversation instead.
The fork ran in the background and its result arrived after the developer had already moved on; setting background: false restores the behaviour with no other change to the skill.

Reference material can never be delivered by a skill, so the body must move to .claude/rules/api-conventions.md with no paths field, which is the only mechanism that applies conventions while code is being written.

items.explanation: A forked skill runs in a subagent whose prompt is the skill content, so it needs an actionable task. Guidelines-only content gives the subagent nothing to do and it returns without meaningful output, and because the fork is isolated the guidance never lands in the main conversation where the code is being written. Reference content belongs in a normal skill, whose description-only cost at session start is already small.

rationales.A: allowed-tools is a permission grant for the invoking turn, not something the fork loses; and no tool grant would give a subagent a task when the skill body contains none.
rationales.C: Background execution is real and does change when a result arrives, but making the fork block would still deliver an empty result from a task-free subagent. It fixes the timing, not the cause.
rationales.D: Skills are a perfectly good home for reference material, and a paths-less rule would load unconditionally at launch, adding the very session-start cost that moving content into a skill avoids. The claim that it is the only mechanism is false.

items.objective: 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
items.stem: A /pr-check skill runs inside the pull-request pipeline and its body invokes the project's test runner and type checker through Bash. Which SKILL.md frontmatter field is the one that determines whether those tool calls need separate approval from the pipeline's permission rules?

options.text: argument-hint, which declares the commands a skill expects to run so the permission layer can match them against the rules at invocation time.
disallowed-tools, which narrows the tool pool for the duration of the skill and thereby exempts whatever tools remain from further permission checks.
allowed-tools, the frontmatter field naming the tools Claude may use without a separate approval during the turn that invokes the skill.
context: fork, because a forked subagent is governed by the pipeline's own permission mode rather than the session's and therefore runs its commands unprompted.

items.explanation: allowed-tools is the SKILL.md frontmatter field for a skill's tool access: it names the tools Claude may use during the turn that invokes the skill, so those calls do not have to be settled separately by the pipeline's permission rules, and the setting clears when the next user message is sent. The exam guide describes allowed-tools as restricting tool access during skill execution; the current documentation defines it as a per-turn grant that does not remove any tool, with disallowed-tools as the restricting field. Either framing points at the same field. Note also that a project skill's allowed-tools applies even in a print-mode run in a folder that has never been trusted, so repository skills deserve review before Claude Code is run there.

rationales.A: argument-hint is a hint about expected arguments shown during autocomplete. It has no relationship to tools or permissions.
rationales.B: disallowed-tools is a real frontmatter field, but it removes tools from Claude's available pool while the skill is active. Taking tools away is not what settles whether the remaining ones need approval, and the claim that it exempts the survivors from permission checks is false.
rationales.D: context: fork changes where the skill runs and what context it sees, not which tools it may use; a backgrounded fork actually runs with a narrower tool set.

Claude Certified Architect - Foundations Exam Guide v1.0, Domain 3 objectives

tags: scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

items.objective: 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
items.stem:
The pipeline's /generate-tests skill takes a target path. Its frontmatter is:

  ---
  description: Generate unit tests for a target module
  argument-hint: [target-path]
  ---

A refactor removed the $ARGUMENTS placeholder from the body, and nothing else in the body consumes an argument. The job invokes the skill as /generate-tests src/cart, and the transcript shows Claude Code appending an ARGUMENTS: src/cart line to the end of the rendered skill content because no placeholder received the value. Tests are now generated for whichever module Claude looked at most recently rather than for src/cart. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Put a placeholder back where the body names the module under test, either $ARGUMENTS or the indexed form $0, so the path is substituted at the point the instructions use it rather than trailing the content.

Rely on argument-hint, the frontmatter field that prompts the developer for the required parameter and binds the supplied value to the name written in the hint, so restoring argument-hint: [target-path] restores the binding the refactor removed.

Move the target path out of the invocation and into the frontmatter as a default value, since a body carrying no placeholder is treated as taking no arguments and the appended ARGUMENTS: line is stripped before the content reaches Claude.
Add disable-model-invocation: true so that only the pipeline can invoke the skill, which makes Claude treat the appended ARGUMENTS: line as the authoritative target.

items.explanation: The supplied value does reach Claude: when no placeholder receives an argument, Claude Code appends ARGUMENTS: <value> to the end of the rendered skill content, which is why dropping a placeholder degrades quietly instead of failing. A value trailing the content is far weaker than a value sitting where the instructions need it, so the fix is to restore a placeholder: $ARGUMENTS for the whole argument string as typed, or an indexed form such as $0 for the first argument. Note a divergence to carry into practice: the exam guide describes argument-hint as prompting developers for required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments, while the current documentation defines it as a hint shown during autocomplete only. The bank keys to the guide where the two conflict, and nothing here turns on the difference, because under either reading argument-hint never binds a value into the body.

rationales.B: Under the current documentation argument-hint is autocomplete display text and nothing more; under the exam guide's framing it prompts for a parameter. Neither reading gives it the power to bind a value into the skill body, which is what the broken body needs.
rationales.C: There is no documented frontmatter default for an argument, and the premise is contradicted by the stem itself, which shows the ARGUMENTS: line surviving into the rendered content rather than being stripped.
rationales.D: Restricting who may invoke the skill changes nothing about where the value lands. The pipeline is already the only caller, and the appended line is exactly what is failing to steer the generation.

items.objective: 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
items.stem: A team is adding a /release-staging skill that runs the staging deployment. Two requirements have to be met: Claude must never trigger the skill on its own as a step inside some larger task, and the skill body has to name the branch being released before Claude reads it, so the instructions can refer to that branch explicitly. Which TWO changes meet those requirements? (Select TWO)

options.text: Set user-invocable: false in the frontmatter, which reserves the skill for deliberate developer invocation and removes it from the set Claude can choose automatically.
Set disable-model-invocation: true in the frontmatter, which keeps the skill's description out of context entirely and leaves it invocable only when a developer types the command.
Put !`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` in the skill body, so Claude Code runs the command and substitutes its output into the content before Claude sees it.
Set context: fork together with an agent field, so the deployment runs in a subagent that the main conversation has no way to start by itself.
Add argument-hint: [branch] so the developer is required to supply the branch name, which the skill then treats as the release target.
List Bash(git rev-parse *) in allowed-tools, which causes the branch name to be resolved and inserted into the skill body at invocation time.

items.explanation: disable-model-invocation: true is the documented setting for side-effecting workflows such as deploy or commit: the description is kept out of context so Claude cannot select the skill, and only a developer typing the command can run it. The !`command` syntax is dynamic context injection: Claude Code executes the command and substitutes its output into the skill content before Claude sees it, which is what puts the real branch name in front of the instructions.

rationales.A: user-invocable: false is the mirror image of what is wanted. It means only Claude can invoke the skill, keeps its description permanently in context, and hides it from the slash menu.
rationales.D: context: fork controls where the skill runs and what context it sees. It does not stop Claude from choosing to invoke the skill, and a backgrounded fork would run the deployment outside session checkpoints.
rationales.E: argument-hint is an autocomplete hint only; it does not require an argument. It also does nothing to prevent Claude from invoking the skill on its own.
rationales.F: allowed-tools pre-approves tools for the invoking turn. It grants permission, it does not execute anything, so no branch name would be substituted into the body.

items.objective: 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
items.stem: A pipeline reviews database changes, and the team wants one convention, that migrations are append-only and must never be edited in place, to reach Claude whenever it works with a migration file wherever in the repository that file happens to sit, and to stay out of context the rest of the time. Which file and frontmatter does that?

options.text: A file at .claude/rules/migrations.md whose frontmatter carries description: Migration conventions and glob: **/migrations/*.sql, with the convention written in the body below it.
A file at .claude/rules/sql/migrations.md with no frontmatter at all, relying on the migrations-named path inside .claude/rules/ to scope it to migration work.
A file at .claude/rules/migrations.md whose YAML frontmatter contains paths: ["migrations/*.sql"], with the convention written in the body below it.
A file at .claude/rules/migrations.md whose YAML frontmatter contains paths: ["**/migrations/*.sql"], with the convention written in the body below it.

items.explanation: Path-specific rules live in .claude/rules/*.md and carry a YAML frontmatter paths list of glob patterns. Two details have to be right together: the field is paths, and the pattern has to open with **/ so it reaches migration files at any depth rather than only a directory sitting at the repository root. With both right the rule loads when Claude works with a matching file and stays out of context otherwise.

rationales.A: The frontmatter field that scopes a rule is paths and it takes a list of glob patterns; glob is not a documented key. A rule whose frontmatter carries no paths field loads unconditionally at launch, which is the opposite of what was asked for.
rationales.B: All .md files under .claude/rules/ are discovered recursively, so a subdirectory is an organisational convenience and scopes nothing. With no paths field this rule would load unconditionally at launch in every session.
rationales.C: The field name is right but the pattern is anchored at the repository root, so it matches only a top-level migrations directory and misses migration files sitting elsewhere in the tree. The leading **/ is what makes a pattern independent of directory location.

tags: scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

items.objective: 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
items.stem:
An engineer splits a long CLAUDE.md into topic files under .claude/rules/. One of them is:

  ---
  description: Conventions for the generated GraphQL client
  ---
  Never hand-edit files under packages/gql-client. Regenerate with npm run codegen.

The engineer expected this to cost nothing until somebody touched the generated client. Instead /context shows it present in every session, including sessions that never open that package. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: Rules are evaluated on the first tool call of any kind rather than on file reads, so this file will always appear; moving the text into packages/gql-client/CLAUDE.md is what limits it to sessions started inside that package.

A rule with no paths field loads unconditionally at launch, with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md; adding paths: ["packages/gql-client/**"] is what makes it load only when Claude works with a matching file.
The description field is what makes a rule eligible for eager loading; removing the description leaves only the body, which is then deferred until Claude reads a file the body names.
Files sitting directly in .claude/rules/ always load and only files in subdirectories are path-scoped; moving this one to .claude/rules/generated/gql-client.md defers it until the package is touched.

items.explanation: Omitting paths does not make a rule default-off. A rule without a paths field loads unconditionally at launch with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md, which is why it shows up in every session. Adding a paths list of glob patterns is what converts it into a conditionally loaded rule.

rationales.A: Path-scoped rules trigger when Claude reads a file matching the pattern, not on any tool call. Relocating to a nested CLAUDE.md would also make the convention depend on where the session was started.
rationales.C: description is metadata; it does not control load timing. Removing it would leave the rule loading at launch exactly as before, with less information about what it covers.
rationales.D: All .md files under .claude/rules/ are discovered recursively, so subdirectories are an organisational convenience only. Location within the tree does not scope a rule; the paths field does.

items.objective: 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
items.stem: A repository has .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: ["**/*.test.ts", "**/*.test.tsx"], documenting the required factory helpers and the ban on snapshot tests. In a fresh session a developer asks, without opening anything, what the team's conventions are for writing tests. Claude gives a generic answer that contradicts the rule. Later in the same session, after Claude opens src/cart/cart.test.ts to fix a failure, its suggestions match the rule exactly. Which statement best explains the difference?

options.text: Path-scoped rules load at the start of the first turn that mentions a matching file extension, and the developer's question said tests rather than naming a path, so no pattern was matched.
Rules are evaluated against the files in the current git diff, and nothing matching had been modified when the question was asked, so the rule stayed out of scope until an edit was made.
A path-scoped rule activates when Claude reads a file matching its glob rather than on every prompt, and the developer's question touched no matching file, so the rule was not in context yet.
A rule with more than one glob pattern is activated only after all its patterns have been expanded on first use, and the second pattern delayed activation until a file matched either entry.

items.explanation: Path-scoped rules trigger when Claude reads a file matching one of the patterns, not on every prompt and not on the wording of a question. That makes them ideal for conventions that should govern editing, and a poor fit for guidance a developer expects Claude to be able to recite before any file is opened. Conventions that must be available in conversation from the first turn belong in CLAUDE.md.

rationales.A: Activation is not keyword-driven. Nothing in a prompt's wording loads a rule; reading a matching file does.
rationales.B: There is no documented coupling between rule activation and the git diff. A read of a matching file is what activates the rule, whether or not that file has been changed.
rationales.D: Multiple patterns in a paths list are all live once the rule is discovered; there is no staged activation that waits for a second pattern.

items.objective: 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
items.stem:
An engineer joining an unfamiliar front-end monorepo is exploring it with Claude Code, reading files with Read and Grep before changing anything, and relying on the platform team's rule to surface the local conventions as she goes:

  ---
  description: Front-end source conventions
  paths:
    - "{apps,packages,services,tools,libs,plugins,examples,integrations}/{web,admin,portal,docs,mobile,marketing,internal,legacy,shared,ops}/**/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,mjs,cjs,vue,svelte,astro,css,scss,less,json}"
    - "apps/legacy-portal/**/*.js"
  ---

When she reads apps/legacy-portal/src/main.js the conventions appear. When she reads apps/web/src/App.tsx they never do, even though that path plainly matches the first pattern. The platform team's README quotes the documented constraint it was written against: a rule's whole paths list shares one budget of 1,000 expanded patterns and 4 MiB, each brace group multiplies the number of expanded patterns, and patterns without braces do not count against the budget. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?

options.text: The first pattern's brace groups multiply out past the shared budget, so it is used unexpanded and its literal braces match no real path; splitting it into several narrower patterns brings each within budget and restores matching.
Brace expansion is not supported in rule globs at all, so only the second pattern is a valid glob; every alternative has to be written as its own entry in the paths list for any of them to match.

A brace group may hold at most three alternatives, and every group in the first pattern exceeds that, so the whole pattern is treated as a literal path segment rather than expanded; reducing each group to three alternatives and adding further entries for the remainder makes it match again.

Rule globs are matched relative to the directory the session was started from rather than the repository root, so a pattern that opens with a brace group can only ever match files directly beneath the start directory; running Claude Code from apps/web would make the conventions appear.

items.explanation: Count the alternatives in the first entry: eight directory names, ten area names and thirteen extensions multiply to 1,040 expanded patterns from a single list entry, which is past the 1,000-pattern budget the whole paths list shares. The second entry carries no braces, so it does not count against the budget at all, and that is exactly the asymmetry described: legacy-portal matches while apps/web never does. Claude Code uses any pattern that would exceed the budget unexpanded, at which point its literal braces match no file on disk while the rule's other patterns keep working. Breaking the first entry into several narrower entries keeps each one within budget.

rationales.B: Brace expansion is documented and supported in rule path patterns, including forms such as src/**/*.{ts,tsx}. The second pattern works because it is simple, not because braces are illegal.
rationales.C: There is no three-alternative limit on brace groups, and the stem states the real constraint: a budget shared across the whole paths list, measured in expanded patterns and in bytes. Reducing every group to three alternatives would work only by accident.
rationales.D: Rule patterns are not restricted to files directly beneath the start directory, and the session that failed to pick the rule up is the same one in which the legacy-portal pattern matched successfully, so the start directory cannot be the difference.

items.objective: 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
items.stem: A monorepo's pipeline runs Claude Code on every pull request, and its engineers also use it interactively all day. One cross-cutting constraint is already encoded and working: .claude/rules/integration-tests.md carries paths: ["**/*.integration.test.ts"] and states that those roughly ninety files must run against the docker-compose fixture stack and must never mock the HTTP layer. One set of conventions is left to place. They cover packages/payments and nothing else: its ledger invariants, its money type, and the rule that its handlers must never call the pricing service directly. The payments engineers almost always start Claude Code with packages/payments as their working directory, and they need to be able to ask about the invariants and get a correct answer in the first turn, before any file has been opened. Where do those conventions belong?

options.text: In a section of the root CLAUDE.md headed Payments, so that the conventions reach every session in the monorepo whatever files a given pull request happens to touch.

In .claude/rules/payments.md scoped with paths: ["packages/payments/**"], which keeps every convention in the repository's central .claude/ directory and gives the payments package the same conditional treatment the integration-test constraint already receives.

In packages/payments/CLAUDE.md, a memory file that is loaded at launch for any session started inside that package and is also picked up from a root session as soon as Claude reads one of the files it sits beside.
In a project skill at .claude/skills/payments-conventions/SKILL.md, so the body costs nothing until the conversation turns to ledger invariants.

items.explanation: A CLAUDE.md at or above the working directory is loaded when the session starts, so payments engineers who launch inside packages/payments carry the invariants from the first turn, which is the constraint that separates the options. The same file is also discovered from a root session and included the moment Claude reads a file in that directory, so pipeline runs are covered too. Path-scoped rules remain the right tool for the cross-cutting constraint the stem treats as settled, because those test files are spread across the repository and are only ever reached by being read.

rationales.A: This does put the conventions in every session, and in every session that never goes near payments, which is the always-loaded cost that per-directory memory files and path-scoped rules both exist to avoid. A root CLAUDE.md is for what the whole repository needs.
rationales.B: This is the natural-looking answer and it fails the stated constraint: a path-scoped rule enters context when Claude reads a file matching its glob, not on every prompt, so the first-turn question about ledger invariants would still get a generic answer.
rationales.D: A skill contributes only its description at session start and its body when it is invoked, which is efficient but discretionary. Nothing guarantees Claude reaches for it on the first question, and these conventions need to be standing context rather than an on-demand procedure.

items.objective: 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
items.stem: An engineer keeps a personal checklist for reviewing generated code: always trace the error paths, always look for a missing await, always confirm the test actually asserts something. She works across roughly a dozen repositories and wants Claude Code to apply the checklist in all of them, on her machine only, with one copy to maintain, and she wants each project's own conventions to take priority wherever they conflict with it. Where does the checklist belong?

options.text: In a .claude/rules/ file inside each repository, listed in that repository's .gitignore so the file stays local to her machine and never reaches a teammate.
In a file under ~/.claude/rules/, which applies to every project on her machine and loads before project rules, leaving project rules the higher priority.
In ./CLAUDE.local.md at the root of each repository, which is the documented location for personal instructions that must not be shared with the rest of the team.
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, since user-scope memory applies to every project on the machine and takes priority over any project rule it overlaps with.

items.explanation: User-level rules live in ~/.claude/rules/ and apply to every project on the machine, so there is one copy to maintain. They are loaded before project rules, which is what leaves project rules the higher priority where the two overlap. That satisfies every constraint she stated at once, including the one about deferring to a project's own conventions.

rationales.A: This works only if she remembers to add and gitignore the file in every repository she touches, now and in future, leaving as many copies to maintain as there are checkouts rather than the one she asked for.
rationales.C: CLAUDE.local.md is indeed personal and gitignored, but it is per-repository: a dozen repositories means a dozen copies drifting apart, which is exactly the maintenance she wants to avoid.
rationales.D: The scope is right and the checklist would reach every project, but the precedence claim is backwards: user instructions are loaded before project instructions, which leaves project content the higher priority where the two overlap. Standing review guidance also belongs in a user rule rather than swelling the always-loaded user CLAUDE.md.

items.objective: 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
items.stem: A pull-request review job invokes Claude Code from the repository root. A rule at .claude/rules/security/auth.md, carrying a single entry in its paths list, is never applied even on pull requests whose diff obviously includes files it should match, and the job reports no error. Which TWO of the following would explain that? (Select TWO)

options.text: The rule's one paths entry contains a '[' that cannot be read as a bracket expression, which makes the pattern invalid so that it matches nothing at all.
The rule's frontmatter carries a paths list but no description field, and Claude Code activates a path-scoped rule only once it can tell Claude what the rule covers.
The rule declares both a description and a paths field, and a rule may carry only one of the two, so the conflicting frontmatter is dropped.
The rule file is reached through a symlink into a shared configuration checkout, and symlinked rule files are skipped rather than resolved.
An identically named rule exists at ~/.claude/rules/, and because user rules load first, the project copy is discarded as a duplicate.
The job passes --setting-sources user,local, and project rules are skipped when project is excluded from that list.

items.explanation: Two explanations fit a rule that silently never fires. A pattern containing a '[' that cannot be parsed as a bracket expression is invalid and matches nothing, and with only one entry in the paths list nothing else in that rule can compensate. Separately, project rules are skipped altogether when project is excluded from --setting-sources, which is easy to introduce in a CI invocation and produces no error.

rationales.B: description is optional metadata that records what a rule covers; it is not a condition of activation. A rule carrying a paths list and no description is discovered and loads normally when Claude reads a matching file.
rationales.C: description and paths coexist normally in rule frontmatter; description explains what the rule covers while paths scopes when it loads.
rationales.D: The rules directory supports symlinks for whole directories and for individual files. They are resolved and loaded normally, and circular symlinks are detected and handled.
rationales.E: User-level rules load before project rules and the project copy keeps the higher priority. Neither is discarded as a duplicate.

items.objective: 3.4 Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
items.stem: A developer on the code generation team presses Shift+Tab until the status bar reads 'plan mode on', then asks Claude to work out why an integration test fails about one run in five. Watching the transcript, the developer sees Claude call Read on four source files and then run 'npm test -- --runInBand tests/checkout.spec.ts' followed by 'git log -S retryBudget --oneline'. The developer expected plan mode to prevent any command at all from running. Which statement correctly describes plan mode?

options.text: Plan mode permits the Read tool only. A shell command running at all means the session dropped out of plan mode when the first Bash call was issued, which also means any file edits attempted after that point were applied straight to the working tree.
Plan mode blocks changes to source files, not exploration. Claude can read files and run shell commands to investigate, and edits stay blocked until the developer approves a plan.

Plan mode changes only the shape of the response, requiring Claude to emit a numbered plan before it acts. Every tool the session already permits, including Edit and Write, keeps running normally while the plan is being drafted.

Plan mode blocks writes to files that are tracked by git while leaving untracked and newly created files editable, which is why exploration commands run and why scratch files can still be created during the planning phase.

items.explanation: Plan mode is a permission mode that blocks edits to source, not exploration. Claude still reads files and runs shell commands so it can investigate before proposing an approach, and edits remain blocked until a plan is approved. Approving a plan exits plan mode into whichever permission mode the chosen approve option names; pressing Shift+Tab again leaves plan mode without approving anything.

rationales.A: Plan mode is not Read-only, and it does not silently disengage. Shell commands are part of the documented exploration that plan mode permits, and the block on edits stays in force for the whole time the session is in plan mode.
rationales.C: Plan mode is a permission mode, not an output style. It genuinely blocks the edit tools; a session that let Edit and Write run while a plan was being written would not be in plan mode at all.
rationales.D: There is no git-tracking distinction in plan mode. The block covers changes to source regardless of whether the file is tracked, and it is lifted by approving a plan rather than by the file's git status.

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem: A pipeline stage runs Claude Code non-interactively to write unit tests for every source file a pull request touches, then opens the result as a patch. Reviewers report that the tests are competent but redundant: for cart/discount.ts the stage proposed cases for an empty cart, a single zero-price line and an expired promotion code, all three of which cart/discount.spec.ts already asserts, and the same overlap appears on every file that has an existing spec. The stage passes the changed source files to the run and nothing else. Which change BEST stops the redundant proposals?

options.text: State in the prompt that Claude must not propose any case the existing suite already covers, and give it the repository's naming convention for tests, so that it knows a spec file sits next to every source file it has been asked to write tests for.
Document the team's testing standards, the fixture factories and the criteria for a valuable test in the project CLAUDE.md, so that every CI run starts from the same guidance.
Have the stage delete each module's spec file and regenerate the whole suite from the source on every run, so there is one generated suite per module and nothing can overlap.
Pass the spec file that already sits beside each changed source file into the run along with the source itself, so the generator can see which cases the suite asserts before it proposes anything new.

items.explanation: Test generation can only avoid re-proposing what the suite already covers if the run can see the suite. The documented practice is to put the existing test files into the run's context alongside the changed source, so proposals are made against the cases already asserted rather than against the source file alone. Recording standards and fixtures in CLAUDE.md is the complementary practice for test quality, but nothing in it tells the run which scenarios exist today.

rationales.A: An instruction and a naming convention tell the run that tests exist somewhere; they do not put the contents of those tests in front of it. The run still has no way to know that cart/discount.spec.ts already asserts the empty-cart case, so it keeps proposing it.
rationales.B: This is the documented remedy for low-value or convention-breaking tests, and it is worth doing, but it addresses what a good test looks like rather than what is already covered. None of that guidance tells the run which scenarios the suite asserts today.
rationales.C: Regenerating the whole suite discards hand-written tests along with the redundancy, and it turns every pull request diff into the entire test file rather than the additions, which makes the review problem worse rather than better.

items.objective: 3.4 Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
items.stem: An engineer is mapping a 400,000-line legacy fulfilment service in order to write onboarding notes. Over the first hour the main session fills with Grep output, directory listings and whole-file dumps. Auto-compaction fires twice, and Claude begins answering questions about classes it read earlier with generic descriptions of 'typical patterns' instead of the actual class names it found. Which change best preserves the main conversation for the high-level work?

options.text: Have the discovery run in the Explore subagent, a read-only agent that searches and reads in its own isolated context and returns a summary, so raw search output never lands in the main conversation.

Raise the effort level for the session so that Claude reasons more carefully over the exploration output it has already accumulated and stops falling back on generic descriptions of code it has read once.

Add a directory tree listing and a one-paragraph summary of every module to the project CLAUDE.md, so that the structural information is re-injected from disk after each compaction instead of being rediscovered by searching.
Run /compact with focused instructions after each file is read, so exploration output is condensed continuously and the session never reaches the automatic compaction threshold in the first place.

items.explanation: Verbose discovery is exactly what the Explore subagent exists to isolate. It is a fast read-only agent for file discovery and code search with Write and Edit denied; it works in its own context window and returns a summary, so the grep output and file dumps never consume the main conversation. That directly addresses the described symptom, which is context degradation caused by discovery volume.

rationales.B: Effort changes how much reasoning is spent, not how much context the discovery consumes. The information the engineer needs has already been compacted away, so no amount of extra reasoning over what remains will bring back the class names.
rationales.C: This makes the problem worse in the general case: a large structural dump in CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session and costs tokens on every request, and a bloated memory file measurably reduces adherence. It also has to be maintained by hand as the service changes.
rationales.D: Compacting after every file read is expensive and lossy, and it condenses precisely the findings the engineer wants to keep. Compaction is a recovery lever, not a substitute for keeping the verbose work out of the main window.

items.objective: 3.4 Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
items.stem: A team is starting a large multi-package change and follows a habit of delegating the whole investigation phase to the Explore subagent before approving anything in the main session. The repository's root CLAUDE.md is 90 lines, loads correctly in the main session, and states that all outbound HTTP must go through the internal svc-http client and that no new dependency may be added without an ADR. Explore's returned summaries repeatedly recommend adding axios and describe the repository as 'having no standard HTTP wrapper', even though svc-http is imported in eleven packages, and the plan the team then approves inherits that recommendation. What explains this, and where should the investigation phase run?

options.text: Explore inherits the parent session's loaded context, but its summaries are produced after the parent has compacted, which drops the memory content; re-injecting the file with an @import inside the delegation prompt restores the conventions for each delegation.

The conventions are loading but rank below Explore's own system prompt, which is why the recommendations contradict them; moving the HTTP rule into a .claude/rules/ file with a paths glob for '**/*.ts' raises its priority for every agent the session spawns.

Explore and Plan are the two built-in subagents that skip loading the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and the parent session's git status in order to keep research fast and inexpensive. Investigation that must honor project conventions belongs in the main session under plan mode, where the hierarchy is loaded, or in a custom subagent under .claude/agents/, which loads both.

Explore is read-only, so it never opens package.json or the svc-http package directory and therefore cannot see that an internal client already exists in the tree; granting it read access to the whole workspace root through permissions.additionalDirectories, and adding the package paths with --add-dir on the session that spawns it, lets it discover the wrapper and stop recommending a new dependency.

items.explanation: Explore and Plan are documented as the two built-in subagents that deliberately skip loading CLAUDE.md files and the parent session's git status, precisely so that research stays fast and inexpensive. That makes Explore the wrong place to run an investigation whose conclusions have to honor project conventions. Planning in the main session keeps the CLAUDE.md hierarchy loaded, and a custom subagent defined in .claude/agents/ also starts with that hierarchy in its context. Explore still earns its place for high-volume discovery whose output would otherwise flood the main conversation.

rationales.A: A non-fork subagent does not inherit the parent's conversation history at all, so there is no inherited copy of the memory content for compaction to drop. The behaviour is by design in Explore rather than a compaction artefact.
rationales.B: There is no priority ranking that would let a loaded convention lose to the agent's system prompt in this way, and the conventions are not being loaded in the first place. Changing where the rule is stored does not change which agents load instruction files, and it does not move the investigation anywhere.
rationales.D: Explore being read-only restricts editing, not reading; Read, Grep and Glob are exactly what it uses. The evidence that it can read the repository is that it produced a summary of it at all.

items.objective: 3.4 Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
items.stem: A cross-package rename touching six packages runs for several hours. The developer and Claude agreed an order in conversation: shared types first, then the two server packages, then the two clients, then a codemod for the tests. After the second auto-compaction, Claude starts editing the client packages while the server packages are still half done, and when asked it re-derives a different order. The developer wants the agreed sequence to survive compaction without being retyped each time. What should they do?

options.text: Run the work under an approved plan: plan mode writes the plan to a file, and Claude Code re-injects that plan file after each compaction, so the sequence survives a boundary that ordinary conversation history does not.

Paste the agreed sequence back into the conversation immediately after each compaction, since the most recent messages are the part of the context least likely to be condensed away on the following pass.
Add the sequence to the root CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code re-reads from disk and re-injects after compaction, then delete those lines from the file once the migration has been completed.
Split the work into six sessions, one per package, resuming each by name with --resume, so that no individual session ever accumulates enough context to reach the compaction threshold.

items.explanation: For a long cross-package change, plan mode writes the plan to a file and Claude Code re-injects that plan file after each compaction. That is the documented mechanism for carrying an agreed sequence across a compaction boundary, and it needs no manual intervention from the developer once the plan is approved.

rationales.B: This works only for as long as the developer keeps noticing each compaction and retyping, which is the manual effort the requirement rules out. It also reintroduces the sequence as ordinary conversation, which the next compaction can condense again.
rationales.C: Root CLAUDE.md is indeed re-injected after compaction, so the mechanism is real, but the layer is wrong: CLAUDE.md holds standing project conventions loaded for every teammate in every session and every request, and this is one task's ephemeral ordering that must be added and removed by hand.
rationales.D: Six sessions fragment a change whose whole difficulty is cross-package ordering, and each session still has to be told where the previous one stopped. Session splitting manages context volume; it does not preserve an agreed sequence.

items.objective: 3.4 Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
items.stem: A developer productivity team keeps a weekly queue of Claude Code tasks against their internal tooling repository. The tech lead wants plan mode used where it earns its cost and skipped where it does not. Which TWO of the queued tasks warrant plan mode? (Select TWO)

options.text: Introducing a feature-flag layer ahead of a phased rollout of the new pricing engine, where flagging at the request boundary and flagging inside the pricing service have different rollback profiles and different blast radii if a flag is left switched on.

Consolidating four bespoke retry helpers into one shared policy, where the investigation has to establish which call sites depend on the current backoff behaviour before the shape of the shared policy can be chosen, after which the edits themselves are mechanical.
Bumping a transitive dependency from 4.2.1 to 4.2.2 to clear an advisory, where the lockfile update comes from one documented command and the existing suite already covers the affected code path.

Adding a --json flag to an existing CLI subcommand whose output already passes through one shared serializer function, following the same shape as three similar flags added to neighbouring subcommands last quarter.
Renaming a private helper function and its three call sites inside one module, where the compiler flags any call site that is missed and the module already has coverage.

items.explanation: Plan mode earns its cost when several valid approaches exist, when the decision has architectural implications, and when the change spans many files. Choosing where a feature flag lives ahead of a phased rollout is an architectural decision whose two candidates differ in rollback profile and blast radius. The retry consolidation is the documented case for combining plan mode with direct execution: the investigation has to settle which call sites depend on the current backoff before the shared policy can be shaped, and once that is settled the edits can be executed directly.

rationales.C: A single-command lockfile update with existing test coverage is a well-scoped change with one obvious approach. The diff can be described in a sentence, which is the documented signal to skip the plan.
rationales.D: The approach is already settled by three precedents in the same repository and the change funnels through one shared function. There is no design choice for a plan to resolve.
rationales.E: A rename inside a single module with the compiler enforcing every call site is well-scoped with one obvious approach and an automatic check. Nothing about it is uncertain enough for planning to pay for itself.

items.objective: 3.4 Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
items.stem:
A platform team runs an unattended nightly job that reviews the diffs merged that day and applies the fixes it recommends. Wanting the job to be 'safer', they add a permission mode to the invocation:

    claude -p "review the diffs merged today and apply the fixes you recommend" \
      --permission-mode plan --output-format json

The job exits 0 every night, the JSON result contains a well-formed plan, and not a single file is ever modified. What is the correct diagnosis?

options.text: The run is stopping before it reaches the implementation phase because it exhausts its agentic turns while drafting; raising --max-turns gives the job room to move past the plan and start applying the fixes.

Plan mode is workable unattended, but the run also needs --permission-prompts none so that the pending plan approval resolves itself automatically instead of leaving the edit tools blocked for the whole run.

The plan was written to a plan file rather than applied to the working tree, which is why the JSON result looks complete while nothing changed on disk; adding a second invocation with --continue, still in plan mode so the approved sequence is preserved, picks up that plan file and executes each of its steps in order.

Plan mode is interactive by design: edits stay blocked until a person approves the plan, and an unattended run has no approver, so it correctly produces a plan and exits cleanly rather than failing. Plan mode belongs in the interactive design phase, not in a job with nobody to read the plan.

items.explanation: In plan mode edits remain blocked until a plan is approved, and approval is a human action taken in an interactive session. An unattended print-mode job has nobody to approve, so it does exactly what it was told: it produces a plan and exits successfully without touching the tree. That is not a failure to diagnose in the run itself but a mismatch between the mode and the setting. Plan mode's value is the interactive design phase, where a person reads the plan before implementation begins.

rationales.A: The run is not exhausting turns; it exits successfully with a complete plan. Reaching the --max-turns limit exits with an error rather than a clean result, so the symptom does not match this cause at all.
rationales.B: --permission-prompts none does the opposite of auto-approving: it tells the run not to consult or wait on a permission host and to deny anything unresolved. It creates no approver, so the edits stay blocked and the denials are recorded.
rationales.C: --continue does not lift the block, because plan mode is still in force in the second run, so the second invocation would produce another plan. It also skips sessions created by claude -p unless it is itself invoked as claude -p --continue.

items.objective: 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
items.stem: An engineer working through an unfamiliar legacy codebase uses Claude to convert its old service modules to the team's new handler shape. The prompt reads: 'convert these legacy service modules to the new handler format, cleaning up the signatures and the error handling.' Across three runs on the same module, Claude emits a named export once and a default export once, wraps failures in the team's ServiceError in one run and rethrows them raw in another, and the generated function signatures differ every time. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Restate the instruction more emphatically, adding 'be consistent across every module' and 'always use exactly the same export style and signature shape from run to run' so that the requirement for stability is stated outright rather than left to be assumed.

Add a persona line establishing Claude as a meticulous platform engineer who values deterministic output, and ask for the conversion to be applied methodically, one module at a time, in the order given.

Give Claude concrete before and after code pairs showing one legacy module and exactly the handler it should become, including a function whose signature has to change and a failure path that has to be wrapped.

Move the prose description into the project CLAUDE.md under a 'Handler conversion' heading so that it is loaded at the start of every session, putting the same wording in front of every run in the repository without anyone retyping it per module.

items.explanation: When a prose description of a transformation is being interpreted inconsistently, concrete input/output examples are the documented remedy: they pin down the export style, the signature shape and the error wrapping that the prose leaves open. Showing a module that exercises the awkward cases (a signature that must change, a failure that must be wrapped) communicates the contract far more reliably than any restatement of the requirement.

rationales.A: Emphasis does not add information. The prompt is ambiguous about what a converted module should look like, and repeating the demand for consistency without saying what to be consistent with leaves every one of the open decisions open.
rationales.B: A persona changes tone rather than the specification. The model still has no evidence of which export style or error wrapper is wanted, so it will keep choosing plausibly and differently each run.
rationales.D: This relocates the same ambiguous prose to a file loaded in every session, so it makes an unclear instruction permanent and pays tokens for it on every request without resolving a single one of the inconsistencies.
