items.objective: 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
items.stem: During a feature build, Claude ends most turns by reporting 'implemented and working'. Reviewing the branch the next morning, the team finds that roughly a third of those turns left the code broken: an import was never added, or a signature changed at one call site but not the other three. Nothing in the workflow runs the test suite between turns. Which change most directly addresses this?

options.text: Give Claude a check it can run: name the test command in the prompt and require it to run the suite and report the outcome before it says the work is done.

Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md stating that Claude must never describe a change as complete unless it has verified the change first, so the requirement applies automatically in every session the team runs.
Ask Claude to re-read its own diff at the end of each turn and explain, hunk by hunk, how each change satisfies the stated requirement before it reports the work as complete.
Select a higher effort level for the session so that more reasoning is spent on each turn, which should mean fewer half-finished edits reach the working tree before completion is reported.

items.explanation: This is the documented trust-then-verify gap: a completion claim with nothing that could have falsified it. The remedy is to always provide a check Claude can run, such as tests, a script, or a screenshot, and to require it to run that check as part of the turn. If the check must run without exception, the enforcement ladder continues to a /goal condition re-checked every turn, then to a Stop hook that blocks the turn ending until the check passes.

rationales.B: CLAUDE.md is context Claude may follow, not enforced configuration, and this particular line supplies no way to verify anything. An instruction to verify without a named check leaves the model to decide what verification means.
rationales.C: Self-inspection of the diff shares the reasoning that produced it, so it tends to confirm rather than falsify. A missing import in a file the diff never touched is exactly the kind of defect reading the diff will not reveal.
rationales.D: Effort buys reasoning depth, not execution. A missing import is a fact about the repository that only running something can surface, and higher effort makes the run more expensive without adding that signal.

items.objective: 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
items.stem: An engineer has to add a caching layer to a billing service they have never worked on. They know which endpoint to cache and the latency target, but not the invalidation rules, the tenancy boundaries, or how the service should behave when the cache is cold immediately after a deploy. They want those decisions surfaced before any code is written. Which approach matches the documented pattern?

options.text: Write the longest and most detailed prompt they can manage up front, enumerating every consideration they are able to think of themselves along with the latency target and the endpoint to be cached, then have Claude implement the whole caching layer in a single pass against that prompt and review the result afterwards.

Start with a minimal prompt asking Claude to interview them about the implementation, the edge cases and the tradeoffs, write the agreed decisions to a spec file that names the files and interfaces involved and what is out of scope, then execute that spec in a fresh session.

Ask Claude to produce three candidate implementations of the caching layer in parallel forks from the same baseline, then read the three diffs side by side and keep whichever of them handles invalidation most convincingly.
Ask Claude to implement the straightforward version first and then list the assumptions it made along the way, iterating on whichever of those assumptions turn out on inspection to have been wrong.

items.explanation: The documented interview pattern for larger features is to start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you, surfacing considerations you had not anticipated, then capture the agreed decisions in a spec. A useful spec names the files and interfaces involved, states what is out of scope, and ends with an end-to-end verification step. Executing it in a fresh session means implementation begins with clean context rather than the whole interview transcript.

rationales.A: The premise of the situation is that the engineer does not know what the considerations are. A long prompt written from that position can only be detailed about the things they already thought of, which is precisely the set the interview exists to extend.
rationales.C: Building three implementations spends the cost of implementation to discover a design question, and comparing diffs surfaces the differences the candidates happen to embody rather than the questions the engineer needed answered.
rationales.D: Assumptions reported after the fact arrive once the code has already been written around them, so the cheap decisions have become expensive to revisit and the failure modes that matter may never appear in the list at all.

items.objective: 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
items.stem: Review of a generated pagination module turns up four problems. Three of them interact: the cursor is encoded as an opaque base64 blob, the cache key is derived from that encoded cursor, and the retry path re-issues the original cursor after a partial page. The fourth is independent: a log line says 'fetching page' where it is actually fetching a cursor window. How should the engineer BEST group this feedback when sending it back to Claude?

options.text: Send all four in one message ordered by severity, since a single message gives Claude the most complete picture of the module's problems and avoids paying for the same context to be reloaded four separate times.

Send them one at a time in severity order, verifying each fix before the next problem is raised, so that every change is reviewed on its own and no fix is confounded by another fix arriving in the same message.
Run /clear and restart with one prompt describing the module's correct behaviour from scratch, since four defects in one generated module indicate the original prompt was inadequate.

Send the three interacting problems together in one detailed message so that the fix is designed once against all three constraints at the same time, and raise the independent logging issue separately.

items.explanation: The documented distinction is between interacting and independent problems. The cursor encoding, the cache key derived from it and the retry that replays it are one coupled design: fixing any one in isolation forces a decision the other two constrain, and a fix chosen without them will be undone by the next round. Those belong in a single detailed message. The log wording touches none of that and can be handled on its own.

rationales.A: Bundling the independent issue in is not harmful in itself, but ordering everything by severity misses the point: what governs the grouping is whether the fixes interact, not how bad each problem is on its own.
rationales.B: Strict sequencing is right for independent problems and wrong here. Fixing the cursor encoding first commits to a representation the cache key and the retry path both depend on, so the next two rounds spend their effort revisiting a decision already taken.
rationales.C: A clean restart is the documented remedy after repeated failed corrections on the same issue, not on the first pass of a review. Discarding a module that is mostly correct also discards the three-way constraint the engineer has just worked out.

items.objective: 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
items.stem: An engineer is about 40 turns into one session chasing an off-by-one in a pagination helper. Three times now they have described the wrong behaviour and Claude has produced a fix that resolves the reported case while reintroducing one it had fixed earlier. The engineer now has a precise reproduction: page size 20, 41 total rows, third page returns one row but reports hasMore as true. The helper is a single 40-line file and the exploration that preceded the three attempts amounted to reading it once, so nothing expensive would have to be redone. What is the documented next move?

options.text: Run /compact with instructions to focus on the pagination helper and continue correcting in the same session, so that the understanding built up across the three earlier attempts is condensed rather than discarded.

Run /clear and start again with a specific prompt built from what has been learned, including the precise reproduction, because a clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session carrying accumulated corrections.

Rewind to the checkpoint immediately before the first correction and re-explain the requirement in the same session, so that all three failed attempts leave the transcript while the exploration of the pagination helper that preceded them is kept intact and does not have to be repeated.
Raise the effort level and ask Claude to re-derive the boundary arithmetic from first principles before it touches the helper again, keeping the session and its full history in place for continuity.

items.explanation: The documented rule is that after two failed corrections on the same issue you run /clear and restart with a more specific prompt that incorporates what you learned: a clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections. The engineer now has exactly the material that makes the new prompt better, namely a precise failing case they did not have at the start.

rationales.A: Compaction condenses the transcript but keeps the session, so the three contradictory correction rounds remain in play in summarized form. The problem is not context volume; it is that the accumulated corrections are steering the model.
rationales.C: Rewinding restores conversation or code state but leaves the framing that produced the loop unchanged, and the engineer would be re-entering the same conversation with the same starting prompt rather than a better one.
rationales.D: Effort and a request to reason from first principles do not remove the three prior wrong descriptions from context, and those are what keep pulling each new fix back toward the case discussed most recently.

items.objective: 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
items.stem: A team asks Claude to implement a currency rounding module for invoice totals. Every round of feedback is prose ('it is still wrong for three-way splits', 'the VAT line is a cent out'), and after five rounds the module handles the cases discussed most recently while breaking ones that were fixed earlier. The team wants the iteration to converge. Which workflow should they adopt?

options.text: Have Claude implement the module first and then generate a test suite from the finished implementation, iterating on any test in that generated suite which fails when the module is run against it.
Keep the prose feedback but make each round more detailed, describing the expected behaviour of every rounding case in the message rather than only the case that happened to fail on that round.
Write the test suite first, covering expected behaviour, the edge cases and the performance requirements, then iterate by handing Claude the failing test output on each round.
Ask Claude to self-review each implementation against the stated requirements before returning it, and send feedback only on the issues that its own self-review failed to catch on that pass.

items.explanation: Test-driven iteration is the documented workflow: write the test suite first so that expected behaviour, edge cases and performance requirements are pinned down before any code exists, then drive each round of refinement with the failing test output. The regression symptom described here is exactly what a suite prevents, because a fix that breaks an earlier case now fails visibly instead of quietly.

rationales.A: Tests generated from a finished implementation encode the behaviour that implementation already has, bugs included. They will pass on the rounding cases that are wrong and cannot drive the module toward correctness.
rationales.B: Longer prose is still prose: it is re-interpreted from scratch on every round and nothing checks the earlier cases, so the same regression pattern continues while each message costs more to write.
rationales.D: Self-review from the session that just wrote the code inherits its reasoning and is poor at questioning its own decisions, and it still produces no executable check that the earlier cases still pass.

items.objective: 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
items.stem: An engineer has spent the afternoon in a single Claude Code session that drifted across three unrelated tasks: a flaky test, a new CLI flag, and a dependency upgrade. Progress has slowed, the same corrections are being repeated, and a bash script Claude ran rewrote several generated files. Which THREE actions follow documented iterative refinement practice? (Select THREE)

options.text: Add every correction made this afternoon as a new rule in the project CLAUDE.md, so the same mistakes are prevented in advance in every future session anyone on the team runs.
Run /clear between the unrelated tasks so that each one starts with a context holding only what that task needs, instead of continuing a single session carrying all three.
Replace prose restatements of the requirement with the failing test output, so that each round of feedback carries a check Claude can run and re-run for itself.
Write the agreed design for the CLI flag to a spec file and execute that spec in a fresh session, so implementation starts from clean context.
Rely on /rewind to undo the files the bash script rewrote, since checkpoints capture the state of the working tree at every turn boundary in the session.
Keep iterating in the current session, on the grounds that the accumulated transcript makes each successive correction better informed than a restart would leave it.

items.explanation: Three documented practices apply here. The kitchen-sink session is fixed with /clear between unrelated tasks. Feedback converges faster when it carries a check Claude can run, so failing test output replaces prose restatement. And a spec written down and executed in a fresh session gives implementation clean context rather than the whole design discussion.

rationales.A: This is the over-specified CLAUDE.md failure pattern. The documented fix is to prune ruthlessly, or to convert a rule that must always hold into a hook; accreting every incident as a new line makes the file longer and measurably reduces adherence to all of it.
rationales.E: Checkpoints only track changes made through Claude's file editing tools. Changes made by Bash commands or external processes are not captured, so /rewind will not restore the generated files the script rewrote and is not a substitute for git.
rationales.F: This is the named anti-pattern: after repeated failed corrections a clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session carrying the accumulated corrections that produced the loop.

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem: A CI job has to run Claude Code over a pull request diff and hand the pipeline a findings object that a Node wrapper can parse and validate before it posts comments. The workflow passes the finding schema to the invocation and the wrapper validates against the same schema, and nothing in the job can respond to a prompt. Which invocation matches the documented approach?

options.text: claude -p "review the staged diff against the review criteria" --output-format json --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"findings":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"object"}}},"required":["findings"]}'
claude -p "review the staged diff against the review criteria" --output-format stream-json --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"findings":{"type":"array"}}}'
claude -p "review the staged diff and reply with JSON matching this schema: {...}" --output-format text, then have the wrapper extract the JSON block from stdout
claude "review the staged diff against the review criteria" --json-schema '{"type":"object"}' --interactive false --quiet

items.explanation: The documented CI toolkit is -p (or --print) for non-interactive execution, --output-format json for a parseable envelope, and --json-schema to constrain the payload to a schema the pipeline already knows. --json-schema takes the schema itself as an inline JSON Schema string rather than a path to a schema file, and it is documented as being used together with --output-format json.

rationales.B: --json-schema is documented as being used together with --output-format json. stream-json is a valid output format for streaming consumers, but it is not the format the schema flag pairs with.
rationales.C: Pasting a schema into the prompt and scraping the text output puts the pipeline back in the business of tolerating stray prose, truncated braces and code fences. The schema flag exists so the runtime rather than the wrapper enforces the shape.
rationales.D: There is no --interactive or --quiet flag on the CLI, and without -p or --print the command is an interactive session, which is what a pipeline must avoid.

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem:
A pipeline step runs:

    claude -p "$REVIEW_PROMPT" --output-format json --json-schema "$(cat ./finding.schema.json)"

The wrapper reads the result field of the JSON envelope and calls JSON.parse on it, which throws because that field holds a prose summary of the review rather than an object. The process exited 0 and no schema error was printed. Where is the schema-conforming payload?

options.text: Nowhere in this run: --json-schema only validates the model output, and when validation passes it leaves the text in result untouched, so the wrapper has to parse the prose itself.
In a sidecar file written next to the schema and named after the session id, which the wrapper is expected to read from disk once the process has exited.
In result, but only after --include-partial-messages is added, which causes the final assistant message to be emitted as a discrete JSON object rather than as text.
In the structured_output field of the same JSON envelope; result continues to hold the text result alongside the usual run metadata.

items.explanation: With --json-schema, the schema-conforming payload arrives in the structured_output field of the JSON envelope. The result field still carries the text result, alongside metadata such as total_cost_usd. A wrapper that parses result is reading the wrong field, which is why it sees prose.

rationales.A: The flag does more than validate: it produces a separate schema-conforming object. Treating result as the payload puts the burden of parsing free text back on the pipeline, which is the problem the flag removes.
rationales.B: No sidecar file is written. Everything the run produces, including the structured payload and the cost metadata, comes back on stdout in the single JSON envelope.
rationales.C: --include-partial-messages requires --print with --output-format stream-json and concerns incremental streaming of partial content; it does not change which field carries the structured payload.

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem: A pipeline generates a database migration script and then, inside the same non-interactive Claude Code invocation, appends a second instruction: 'now review the code you just wrote for correctness and report any issues'. The review reports 'no issues found' on changes where a human reviewer later finds real defects, including one migration that drops a column still read by a running service. What should change?

options.text: Add an instruction to the same prompt telling Claude to assume it has made mistakes and to review its own work adversarially, listing three candidate problems first.
Run the review as a separate Claude Code invocation whose context holds only the diff and the review criteria, so the reviewing instance does not carry the reasoning that produced the code.
Raise the effort level for the combined invocation so that noticeably more reasoning is spent on the review portion of the run than on the generation portion.
Split the prompt into two turns inside the same session, so that generation and review are separated by a turn boundary rather than run as one instruction.

items.explanation: This is session context isolation. A session that has just generated code retains the reasoning that produced it and is therefore less likely to question its own decisions than an instance that sees only the diff and the criteria. The documented remedy is an independent review invocation, which is also why the pipeline should run generation and review as two separate steps.

rationales.A: Instructing a session to be adversarial about its own output does not remove the reasoning it is being adversarial about. Self-review instructions are documented as less effective than an independent instance for catching subtle issues.
rationales.C: Effort changes how much reasoning is spent, not what is in context. The generation reasoning is still present and still shaping the review, so the same blind spots persist at greater cost.
rationales.D: A turn boundary does not clear context. The full generation transcript remains in the session, so the second turn is still the instance that wrote the code, reviewing itself.

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem: A nightly job runs claude -p "generate tests for the files changed in the last 24 hours" and opens a pull request with the result. Reviewers reject most of it: the generated tests assert that getters return what was set, they build customer objects by hand although the repository ships a fixtures/customers.ts factory, and they use a mocking style the team abandoned a year ago. The prompt string in the workflow is one sentence, and the job invokes claude -p directly, without --bare, so the run loads the project's normal context. What is the documented fix?

options.text: Add --bare to the invocation so that the nightly job produces the same tests on the runner as it would on a developer laptop, and is not influenced by whatever plugins, hooks or local settings happen to be present on the CI runner when the job starts.

Expand the prompt string in the workflow file to spell out the testing standards, the fixture factories that already exist and the current mocking style, keeping that guidance next to the job that actually consumes it.
Document the testing standards, what the team counts as a valuable test, and the available fixtures in the project CLAUDE.md, which is the mechanism for giving a CI-invoked run its project context.
Raise --max-turns so the run has enough turns to explore the repository and discover the fixture factories and the prevailing mocking conventions for itself before it writes anything.

items.explanation: CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for supplying project context (testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria) to a CI-invoked Claude Code run. Recording what the team counts as a valuable test, which fixtures exist and how mocks are written raises test generation quality and cuts the low-value output reviewers are rejecting, and it is versioned with the code it describes so interactive sessions benefit too.

rationales.A: --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md. It would strip away exactly the project context this job is missing, making the output worse rather than better.
rationales.B: This can work, but the guidance then lives in a workflow file: it is duplicated in every job that invokes Claude, drifts from the conventions it describes, and is invisible to engineers working interactively in the same repository.
rationales.D: More turns buy more exploration, not the team's judgement about which tests are worth writing. Nothing in the repository tells Claude that asserting a getter is low value or that the old mocking style has been retired.

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem: A review job runs on every push to an open pull request. On the third push, contributors complain that Claude has posted the same six comments for a third time, including two on lines nobody has touched since the first run and one the author fixed two commits ago. The job re-runs an identical prompt against the full pull request diff each time, and diffing the three runs shows that the wording of each finding is regenerated from scratch every time, so the same underlying issue is phrased differently on every push. Which change MOST effectively suppresses duplicate comments while still reporting issues the author has not fixed?

options.text: A deduplication step in the wrapper that hashes the text of each finding and refuses to post any hash already posted on this pull request, so that the job comments only on issues that are new or still unaddressed and never repeats one it has raised before.

A narrowing of scope so that each run reviews only the diff introduced by the newest commit rather than the accumulated diff of the whole pull request, with everything in the earlier commits treated as already reviewed.
A --continue on the invocation so that the job resumes the previous review session and the context it accumulated instead of starting a fresh session on every push.
Feed the findings from the earlier runs back into the run's input, and have Claude judge for each one whether the problem is still present in the code as it now stands before it comments again.

items.explanation: When a review is re-run after new commits, the documented practice is to give the run the findings it produced earlier and to have it comment only where a problem is new or has not yet been dealt with. That puts the comparison inside the model, which can see the current code: a finding the author has fixed drops out, and one that is genuinely still open is not silently swallowed.

rationales.A: The stem rules this out directly: the finding text is regenerated on every push, so the hashes never match and all six comments post again. Even with stable wording a hash records only that something was said before, not whether the author has since fixed it.
rationales.B: Reviewing only the newest commit stops the duplicate comments but loses the issues that live in earlier commits and are still unaddressed, and it misses defects that only appear in the interaction between the newest commit and the earlier ones.
rationales.C: --continue skips sessions created by claude -p unless the resuming command is itself claude -p --continue, and even then it resumes stale tool results captured against an older diff rather than comparing findings against the code as it now stands.

tags: scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem:
A team wires the Claude Code GitHub Action into pull request review:

    - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
      with:
        prompt: "/code-review"
        claude_args: "--max-turns 15"

The job declares permissions: contents: read, pull-requests: write and id-token: write. Every run succeeds, and the workflow run log contains a complete and accurate review. No comment ever appears on the pull request. What is wrong?

options.text: In automation mode the action's results go to the workflow run log by default. Posting on the pull request needs the review invoked with --comment, and claude_args must also name the inline comment MCP tool in --allowedTools, because the action only starts that server when --allowedTools names it.

The action is running in interactive mode because no trigger phrase has been configured, so it is waiting for a mention that never arrives; adding trigger_phrase: "@claude" puts it into the mode that posts its output back onto the pull request as a comment.

The default GITHUB_TOKEN cannot write comments from within an action run regardless of the permissions block, so the posting step is silently skipped; passing github_token with a custom GitHub App token is what makes the comment appear.

The --max-turns 15 cap is being reached before the posting step, which the action performs as the final turn of the run, so the review completes but is never delivered; raising the cap lets the run get as far as posting the comment.

items.explanation: A prompt input puts anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 into automation mode, where it runs on the event without waiting for a trigger phrase and, by default, sends results to the workflow run log rather than to the pull request. Posting requires the review to be invoked with --comment, and the claude_args --allowedTools entry naming the inline comment MCP tool must be kept, because the action starts that MCP server only when --allowedTools names it.

rationales.B: A prompt input is exactly what selects automation mode, so the action is not waiting for a mention: the run log proves it executed a full review. Adding a trigger phrase would move it toward the interactive mode that does wait for one.
rationales.C: The permissions block already grants pull-requests: write, and the documented GITHUB_TOKEN caveat is different in kind: commits made with it do not trigger further workflow runs. Nothing about it silently suppresses a review comment.
rationales.D: Reaching a turn cap surfaces as a failure rather than a clean success with a complete review in the log, and posting is not an extra agentic turn the cap would consume. The symptom described is a successful run that was never asked to comment.

items.objective: 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
items.stem: An unattended review job drives Claude Code from an Agent SDK wrapper that supplies a canUseTool callback, and the underlying run is configured as claude -p "$PROMPT" --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Bash(git diff *)" --output-format stream-json --verbose. Some runs finish in two minutes; others sit until the ten-minute job timeout, and some end with unexplained tool denials and no findings. The team wants the run to be deterministic about permissions: it must never wait on a person, and it must never do anything outside the allowed set. Which TWO changes achieve that? (Select TWO)

options.text: Pass an explicit --permission-mode dontAsk, because a print-mode run starts in the manual default on every plan and dontAsk denies anything that is not in permissions.allow or the read-only command set.

Pass --permission-prompts none so the run never consults or waits on a permission host and denies anything unresolved, with the denials surfaced as permission_denied messages and in the result's permission_denials list.
Pass --permission-mode bypassPermissions so that no permission check can block or stall the run, relying on the --allowedTools list already in the command to bound what Claude actually does.

Add 'do not request permission for any tool; if a tool is not allowed, skip it and carry on' to the prompt text, so that Claude resolves the situation itself rather than stalling on a call it cannot make.
Raise --max-turns substantially so that the run has enough turns to work around any tool call it is unable to make instead of stalling on the blocked call until the job times out.

items.explanation: Two things are missing. First, a print-mode run starts in the manual default permission mode on every plan, so the job has to state the mode it wants; dontAsk is the documented choice for a locked-down CI run because it denies whatever is not in permissions.allow or the read-only command set. Second, this run has a permission host in the canUseTool callback, and without --permission-prompts none the run waits for that host to answer every permission request, which is where the intermittent stall comes from. With the flag the run neither consults nor waits on the host, denies anything the permission rules, PermissionRequest hooks and the permission mode have not already resolved, and tells Claude not to retry; because the run emits stream-json, those denials arrive as permission_denied system messages and are listed in the final result's permission_denials field.

rationales.C: bypassPermissions removes the checks rather than making them deterministic, which is the opposite of the stated requirement. --allowedTools is an allow list consulted by those checks, not an independent boundary, so switching the checks off leaves nothing enforcing the allowed set.
rationales.D: Prompt text is advisory context with a non-zero failure rate, and it cannot change how the runtime resolves a permission request. The hang happens in the permission layer, below anything the prompt can influence.
rationales.E: More turns give a stalled run more opportunities to stall. The intermittent hang is a run waiting on a permission decision that nobody is there to make, and no number of turns resolves that.

items.objective: 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
items.stem: A Claude Code review job runs in CI on every pull request, invoking /code-review over the branch. Its appended system prompt ends with: 'Be conservative. Only report issues you are highly confident about.' The wording has been strengthened twice over two sprints and the false-positive rate is still about 45 percent. What change is most likely to actually raise precision?

options.text: Have the model attach a numeric confidence score between 0.0 and 1.0 to each finding, post only findings above 0.85, and retune that threshold each sprint from the dismissal data.

Replace the general instruction with specific categorical criteria naming the reportable conditions, such as reporting a comment only when the claimed behavior contradicts what the code does, and naming the classes to skip.
Move the conservative wording out of the appended system prompt into CLAUDE.md at the repository root so every invocation in the repository inherits it.
Raise the effort level on the /code-review invocation the job runs from medium to max, so the reviewer examines the diff more thoroughly before it decides.

items.explanation: General hedging language such as 'be conservative' or 'only report high-confidence findings' does not improve precision. What does is a specific categorical definition of the conditions that qualify as reportable, together with an explicit list of what to skip, so the model has a testable boundary instead of a mood.

rationales.A: The 45 percent false-positive rate comes from the reviewer believing a wrong finding qualifies, so it scores those findings high and the threshold suppresses borderline true findings instead; confidence-based filtering leaves the reportable boundary exactly as undefined as the wording did.
rationales.C: Relocating a vague instruction does not make it specific; the same undefined boundary simply applies in more places than before.
rationales.D: Higher effort levels broaden coverage and are documented to include findings the review is less sure about, which raises the false-positive rate rather than lowering it.

items.objective: 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
items.stem: A repository reviewed by Claude Code's Anthropic-managed Code Review already carries a REVIEW.md at its root that redefines severity and caps nits. The remaining complaint is a class of finding that asserts what a function does from its name -- 'validate_token checks expiry, so this call is safe' -- where the function does no such thing. Authors spend a round trip refuting each one. Which addition to the repository's review instructions best removes this class?

options.text: Add a line to REVIEW.md telling the review to double-check each candidate finding and to post only the ones it has carefully verified before it writes the comment.
Put the requirement in .claude/rules/review.md with a YAML frontmatter paths field scoping the rule to the file globs the pull request touches.
Require in REVIEW.md that a finding claiming what code does cite a file and line in the source, and that a claim resting only on a symbol name is not posted.

Move the requirement into CLAUDE.md at the repository root so that one evidence standard governs every Claude Code task run against the repository, including this review job and every interactive session.

items.explanation: The documented REVIEW.md pattern for this failure is a verification bar: require evidence before a class of finding is posted, for example that a behavior claim carry a file and line citation in the source rather than an inference from naming. That rule reaches the finding and verification agents directly, which is where an unfounded claim would otherwise survive.

rationales.A: This is the general hedge that documented guidance says does not improve precision; a review that is already wrong about what a function does believes it has verified the claim.
rationales.B: .claude/rules/ carries coding conventions for interactive Claude Code sessions, scoped by frontmatter globs; it is not the instruction surface the managed review's agents are given.
rationales.D: CLAUDE.md is general project context, and the managed review treats newly introduced violations of it as nit-level findings, so a rule placed there does not bind the agents that decide whether a finding is posted; review-specific rules land more reliably in REVIEW.md.

items.objective: 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
items.stem: The CI reviewer's criteria live in an appended system prompt that the pipeline builds on every run. The repository's scripts/ directory holds one-off operational scripts; reviews of pull requests touching it are dominated by naming and error-handling nits the team never acts on, but twice this year a review there caught a script that would have deleted production data. Someone proposes a criteria rule that stops reviewing scripts/ altogether. Which instruction BEST fits this path?

options.text: Stop reviewing scripts/ entirely, since the findings that path produces are overwhelmingly of a class the team has already decided it never wants to see.
Stop reviewing scripts/ on pull requests and add a weekly scheduled audit that searches the whole repository for destructive operations.
Leave the criteria unchanged everywhere and cap the review at five nits per pull request, which absorbs most of the volume that directory produces.
Keep scripts/ in scope and write a path-scoped bar into the criteria: report there only when a finding is both severe and near-certain.

items.explanation: A path that produces mostly noise but occasionally a severe catch is the case for a stricter reporting bar scoped to that path, not a blanket skip. Skip instructions belong to paths where no finding is wanted at all -- generated code, lockfiles, vendored dependencies -- while a graduated bar keeps the rare severe catch and drops the nits, and it stays in the criteria prompt where the report-versus-skip boundary is defined.

rationales.A: A blanket skip removes the two catches the team values along with the nits, because nothing in the directory is reviewed at all after it.
rationales.B: A weekly audit finds the destructive script after it has merged, which is precisely what the pull-request review it no longer gets was providing.
rationales.C: A nit cap is a volume control applied across the whole review, so the directory's nits crowd out nits in code the team does want reviewed, and the bar inside the directory is unchanged.

items.objective: 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
items.stem: Review findings are grouped into four categories, each defined by its own block of criteria in the reviewer's prompt. The comment-accuracy category runs at roughly 60 percent false positives; the other three run under 10 percent. Developers have begun dismissing the whole findings list unread, including SQL-injection findings that have all been genuine. Rewriting the comment-accuracy criteria will take about two weeks, and the team's goal is to get the security findings read again this sprint. What is the MOST effective action to take now, before the rewrite lands?

options.text: Remove the comment-accuracy criteria from the reviewer's prompt while they are rewritten, leaving the three accurate categories reporting exactly as they are.
Raise the evidence bar across every category so that any finding must cite a file and line proving the claimed behavior, which suppresses the weakest findings wherever they occur.
Keep posting comment-accuracy findings but at the lowest severity rather than the highest, so they stay visible for tuning without competing with the security findings.
Keep producing comment-accuracy findings but write them to a separate CI summary artifact instead of posting them as inline comments on the diff.

items.explanation: A category with a 60 percent false-positive rate is destroying trust in the three categories that are accurate. The documented remedy is to disable the offending category temporarily -- here, by lifting its criteria block out of the prompt -- while those criteria are improved, so that the trustworthy findings are read again this sprint.

rationales.B: A global evidence bar penalizes the three healthy categories as well and still leaves the broken category posting whatever it can cite; the graduated form of this lever is scoped per category or per path, not applied everywhere.
rationales.C: The noise is still produced, and the volume of wrong findings is what trained developers to dismiss the list; a long tail of wrong low-severity findings sustains that habit through the sprint in which the security findings need reading.
rationales.D: The summary artifact is the one place the team reads for a tally of what the review found, so the wrong findings still fill it and its counts stay inflated by the broken category.

items.objective: 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
items.stem: A support resolution agent decides refunds, and a second Claude pass checks each decision against the ticket and the order record and files whatever it finds to a human reviewer queue. Every class it reports is precisely defined, and it files them all at the same weight: refunds approved where the order record does not support the stated reason, and refunds issued above the order total, arrive alongside a customer name capitalized differently from the account record, trailing whitespace in the free-text justification, and dates rendered as 03/04/2026 rather than 2026-03-04. Reviewers have started scrolling past the queue. Which change gives the largest precision improvement?

options.text: Rank the queue so that the classes the pass judges more serious appear at the top of it, leaving every class it currently files still filed as it is today.
Give the pass an explicit report-versus-skip list: name the classes that reach the queue, and name the classes -- whitespace, capitalization, date rendering -- that are never filed.
Instruct the pass to file only the findings a reviewer would consider worth their time, and to use its own judgement about which of them clear that bar.
Split the pass into two runs, one over the refund-decision classes and one over the presentation classes, and file each run into a separate queue that reviewers work through in turn.

items.explanation: Precision here is a scoping problem rather than a vagueness problem: every class is already defined, but nothing tells the pass which classes are worth a reviewer's attention. Criteria that name the classes to report and, explicitly, the classes to skip are what clear the cosmetic variance out of the queue while leaving the refund errors in it.

rationales.A: Ordering changes what a reviewer sees first rather than how much of the queue is noise; the cosmetic findings are still filed and still have to be scrolled past.
rationales.C: This substitutes one open judgement for another and gives the pass no testable boundary, which is the pattern documented guidance says does not raise precision.
rationales.D: Both classes are still reported, now across two surfaces; splitting the queue divides the noise rather than removing it, and the reviewers working both queues are the same people.

items.objective: 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
items.stem: The same class of defect is labelled Important on one pull request and Nit on the next, and two engineers disagree about which label was right. The team wants severity classification that is reproducible across pull requests. Which TWO changes address the cause? (Select TWO)

options.text: Instruct the reviewer to stay consistent with previous reviews and give it read access to the last twenty review comments posted on the repository.
Move the severity definitions into CLAUDE.md at the repository root so that one statement of standards governs every Claude Code task in the repository.
Define in REVIEW.md what Important means for this repository in concrete terms, for example a defect that can write incorrect data on the payments path.
Attach a short worked code example to each severity level so the reviewer has a concrete anchor for the boundary between one level and the next.
Have the reviewer emit a severity confidence value with each finding and downgrade any finding whose confidence falls below an agreed team threshold.

items.explanation: Inconsistent classification comes from an undefined boundary. Redefining what Important means for this repository in concrete terms, and anchoring each level with a worked code example, gives the model a stable reference that produces the same label for the same defect shape on every pull request.

rationales.A: Prior comments are themselves inconsistent, so they teach the inconsistency; and 'be consistent' is precisely the general wording that fails to produce reproducible classification.
rationales.B: The managed review treats newly introduced CLAUDE.md violations as nit-level findings, so severity definitions placed there do not bind the agents that rank findings; review-specific severity belongs in REVIEW.md.
rationales.E: Confidence and severity are different quantities. The defect in dispute is one both engineers are certain about and disagree over the impact of, so a certainty threshold cannot arbitrate it, and downgrading on low confidence would reclassify an uncertain but serious defect as a nit.

items.objective: 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
items.stem: Comments produced by the CI reviewer are frequently unactionable ('this could be improved', 'consider refactoring'). The prompt currently reads: 'Do not be vague. Do not nitpick. Do not repeat yourself.' Which revision follows documented prompting guidance?

options.text: Keep the prohibitions but move them to the very end of the prompt and mark them IMPORTANT in capitals so they are the last thing the model reads before it answers.
State positively what every comment must contain: the file and line, the specific behavior that is wrong, why it matters, and a concrete suggested fix.
Add a posting-script rule that rejects any comment shorter than forty words and regenerates it until the comment clears the length check.
Lower the max_tokens ceiling so the reviewer spends its budget on a few dense comments instead of a long list of shallow ones.

items.explanation: Documented guidance is to tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do. Naming the required elements of a comment gives the model a target shape; a list of prohibitions leaves it to infer one.

rationales.A: Emphasis and placement do not convert a prohibition into a specification; the model still has to guess what an actionable comment looks like.
rationales.C: A word-count gate rewards padding rather than specificity, and regenerating against a length check adds cost without defining content.
rationales.D: A tighter output ceiling truncates the list of comments; it says nothing about what belongs inside each one.

items.objective: 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
items.stem: The CI reviewer's markdown comments vary from run to run: some open with a file and line, others bury it in prose; severity appears as a word, as an emoji, or not at all; and the suggested fixes range from a one-line patch to 'consider refactoring'. The prompt already contains a nine-bullet description of the required comment format. The comment posted to the pull request must remain markdown prose written by the model; the team has ruled out rendering comments from structured fields. What is the MOST effective next step?

options.text: Convert the nine bullets into a numbered procedure and repeat the format requirement at both the top and the bottom of the system prompt so it cannot be missed.
Define a submit_comment tool with strict set to true whose input schema carries location, issue, severity and fix, and emit every comment through that tool.
Raise the effort level on the review invocation, on the basis that a more thorough pass produces more complete comments with fewer omitted fields.
Add a small set of worked examples showing complete comments in the exact target shape, including one example for each severity level.

items.explanation: When detailed instructions alone still produce inconsistent output, worked examples are the documented remedy. Examples fix both halves of this failure at once: the shape of the comment, and the substance of what a real suggested fix contains.

rationales.A: Restating and reordering a specification that has already failed twice does not change what the model infers a good comment contains; the shape problem persists alongside the substance problem.
rationales.B: A schema guarantees that a fix field exists but not that its contents are a concrete patch rather than 'consider refactoring', and the team has ruled out rendering the posted comment from fields, so this cannot produce the artifact the workflow requires.
rationales.C: Effort governs how hard the reviewer looks for candidate findings, not how it presents one; all three symptoms here are the presentation and specificity of findings it has already made.

items.objective: 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
items.stem: Invoice extraction uses four few-shot examples, all taken from one vendor's PDF layout because that vendor supplied the cleanest test files. Accuracy on that vendor is 97 percent; across the other eleven vendors it sits near 71 percent, with header fields most often wrong. Which change best matches documented few-shot guidance?

options.text: Replace two of the four examples with invoices from structurally different vendors so that the example set spans the layouts the pipeline actually receives.
Keep the four examples and add twelve more from the same vendor so the model has a much larger sample of correctly extracted header fields to imitate.
Maintain a separate prompt and example set per vendor, routing each document by a vendor identifier detected in a cheap classification pass beforehand.
Drop the examples and replace them with a written specification of every header field and of where it appears in each vendor layout.

items.explanation: Examples must be diverse as well as relevant: they should cover the edge cases and vary enough that the model does not learn an unintended pattern. Four samples of one layout taught layout-specific positions, so replacing some with structurally different invoices is the documented correction.

rationales.B: More of the same layout deepens the unintended pattern already learned and adds nothing about the eleven layouts that are failing.
rationales.C: Twelve maintained prompts is a heavy surface that still fails on the first vendor onboarded after it was built, whereas a diverse example set generalizes to unseen layouts.
rationales.D: A prose specification is what the pipeline already relies on between examples; specifications convey the mapping less reliably than worked examples, which is why the examples exist.

items.objective: 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
items.stem: Clinical study extraction must populate enrollment_date. Papers routinely carry several dates: submission, acceptance, first patient enrolled, and a date inside a figure caption. Four input and output example pairs were added showing the right answer for four papers; accuracy improved only slightly, and the model still picks the wrong date on papers whose layout resembles none of the four. What is the most effective refinement?

options.text: Grow the example set to twenty input and output pairs so that the range of paper layouts present in the corpus is represented directly in the prompt.
Put a numbered list of twelve date-selection heuristics ahead of the examples and instruct the model to evaluate them in order for every candidate date.
Add thinking blocks inside the existing examples that show why the chosen date was correct and why the closest competing date was rejected.
Enable extended thinking on the request so the model reasons for longer over each candidate date before it commits to a value for the field.

items.explanation: Examples that show only the chosen answer let the model imitate surface layout. Putting the reasoning inside the examples, in thinking tags, demonstrates why one candidate was preferred over a plausible alternative, and the model generalizes that reasoning pattern to layouts it has never seen.

rationales.A: More pairs still show what was chosen and not why, so the model keeps matching on layout; the corpus will always contain a shape that is not in the prompt.
rationales.B: An ordered heuristic list is brittle and grows a rule for every new paper shape; it is the enumerated-rules approach that demonstrated reasoning is meant to replace.
rationales.D: Longer reasoning supplies no criterion for choosing among four plausible dates, so the model still lacks a basis for preferring first-patient-enrolled over acceptance date and reasons at greater length toward the same wrong pick.

items.objective: 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
items.stem: A support resolution agent reaches backend systems through MCP tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. On clear-cut tickets it behaves well. On ambiguous ones -- 'the jacket showed up damaged and nobody has answered my emails, just sort it out' -- it sometimes issues a refund immediately and sometimes escalates, and two near-identical tickets an hour apart were handled differently. The tool descriptions already state in detail what each tool does and when it applies. What is the MOST effective change?

options.text: Add two to four worked examples covering the ambiguous ticket shapes, each showing the reasoning for why the chosen tool was preferred over the plausible alternative.
Put a decision tree in the system prompt that enumerates the ticket categories and maps each category to the one tool the agent must call for it.
Set tool_choice to "any" so the agent is obliged to call one of the four tools on every turn rather than answering the customer in prose.
Have the agent emit a resolution-confidence value with each decision and route anything below the agreed threshold to escalate_to_human.

items.explanation: Detailed tool descriptions define what each tool does; they do not resolve which of two defensible tools a genuinely ambiguous request calls for. The technique for ambiguous-case handling is a small set of targeted examples that show not only the action chosen but the reasoning for choosing it over the plausible alternative, which the model then generalizes to ambiguous tickets nobody wrote an example for. The two-to-four figure is the exam guide's own, and the item keys to the guide; the live prompting best-practices page instead advises three to five examples, so the two ranges overlap without matching and nothing in this item turns on the count.

rationales.B: A category-to-tool mapping needs a category for every ticket, and the tickets that are failing are exactly the ones that sit between categories; the next unmapped shape gets an arbitrary answer again.
rationales.C: Requiring that some tool be called says nothing about which one, so the agent still chooses between process_refund and escalate_to_human on the same unstable judgement, and it loses the ability to simply answer a question.
rationales.D: The threshold has never been calibrated against resolved tickets, so it stacks a second unvalidated judgement on the first; and the failure here is not hesitancy, since the agent is confident on both runs and confidently disagrees with itself.

items.objective: 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
items.stem: A veterinary records extractor fills dose_volume_ml. Transcribed notes read 'about two and a half mils', 'approx 2.5cc', or '2 1/2 ml'. The field comes back null on 22 percent of records even though a value is plainly present in the text. The schema already declares dose_volume_ml as a nullable number. What should be added?

options.text: Few-shot examples pairing several of the informal phrasings with the normalized numeric value, so the model learns the mapping instead of only the clean printed case.
A pattern keyword on the field constraining it to a decimal number, so that the model is forced to emit a value the downstream parser can read.
A retry loop that resends the same document with the message 'dose_volume_ml was null, extract it' whenever the field comes back empty on the first attempt.
An instruction stating that the field is mandatory and that returning null counts as a failure, together with marking the field required in the schema.

items.explanation: The nulls come from unrecognized informal phrasing, not from output formatting. Examples that show varied informal measurements mapped to the normalized number teach the recognition and normalization the model is missing, which is the documented use of few-shot for varied document structures.

rationales.B: A pattern constrains the shape of an emitted string and cannot be applied to a numeric field at all; more importantly, no output constraint teaches the model that 'two and a half mils' is 2.5, because the failure is in reading the source rather than in formatting the answer.
rationales.C: Resending an identical request over text the model did not parse repeats the same failure at twice the cost; retry with feedback addresses format and structural errors, not comprehension gaps.
rationales.D: Making the field required pressures the model to invent a number when it cannot parse the phrasing, trading a detectable null for an undetectable wrong value.

items.objective: 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
items.stem: A prompt extracts funding-source statements from 40-page research papers. Some papers declare funding inline in the acknowledgements; others carry only a structured block at the end of the paper. The prompt currently opens with the instructions, then three examples, then the full paper text. Which THREE changes follow documented guidance? (Select THREE)

options.text: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so that the model is forced to begin its answer with a JSON object rather than a preamble.
Replace the examples with a longer natural-language specification covering every funding-statement shape observed in the corpus so far.
Move the paper text to the top of the prompt, above the query, the instructions and the examples.
Wrap each example in example tags and enclose the whole set in a single examples block so they are distinguishable from the instructions.
Make the examples span the structural variants, so that at least one shows an inline acknowledgement and at least one shows an end-of-paper block.
Attach the three examples as input_examples on the built-in web search tool so that they also steer any lookups performed during extraction.

items.explanation: Documented long-context guidance places longform data near the top of the prompt, above the query, instructions and examples, and reports that this improves performance across all models. Examples should be structured in tags so they are separable from instructions, and diverse enough to cover the structural variants the pipeline meets.

rationales.A: A prefilled assistant message on the last turn returns a 400 error on current models; the documented replacement for forcing JSON is structured outputs or a schema-constrained tool.
rationales.B: A longer prose specification is what worked examples exist to replace, and it still does not demonstrate how to handle the ambiguous structural variants.
rationales.F: input_examples is not supported on server tools such as web search, and steering a search tool would not change extraction from the paper text already supplied.

items.objective: 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
items.stem: The repository deliberately uses a broad 'except Exception:' inside its retry decorator, plus several similar sanctioned patterns. The reviewer flags every one of them. The team added six allowlist rules naming the exact functions to ignore, yet new variants of the same sanctioned pattern in new files keep being flagged, while a genuinely unsafe swallowed exception in a payment handler went unreported. What is the best remedy?

options.text: Extend the allowlist until it enumerates every function in the repository permitted to catch a broad exception, regenerating that list in CI whenever a new one is merged.
Add a REVIEW.md skip rule suppressing the broad-exception finding category outright, since the repository has an established and documented convention for it.
Instruct the reviewer to flag broad exception handling only when it is confident the pattern was not intentional, noting that the repository has sanctioned uses of it.
Add contrasting examples that place a sanctioned use and a genuine defect of the same class side by side, with the reasoning that distinguishes one from the other.

items.explanation: Examples that contrast an acceptable pattern with a genuine issue of the same class, and show the distinguishing reasoning, let the model generalize the judgement to variants nobody enumerated, which is exactly what an allowlist of named functions cannot do.

rationales.A: An enumerated allowlist cannot cover patterns that do not exist yet, which is the failing case here, and it does nothing about the real defect the reviewer missed.
rationales.B: Suppressing the category also suppresses the payment-handler defect the team wants found; the problem is discrimination within the category, not the category itself.
rationales.C: A confidence hedge is the general wording that does not improve precision, and it gives the model no basis for telling a sanctioned use from an unsafe one.

items.objective: 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
items.stem: The document-analysis subagent in a multi-agent research system handles four source types and defines four extraction tools: extract_journal_article, extract_preprint, extract_dataset_card and extract_standard. The type is not known until the subagent has read the source. With tool_choice left at its default, about 7 percent of calls come back as a prose summary with no tool call, and the coordinator's aggregation step drops those sources silently. Which setting resolves this?

options.text: tool_choice set to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_journal_article"}, with a follow-up routing step that corrects the record type when the source turns out to be something else.
tool_choice set to "none", which stops the subagent returning an unstructured tool-free answer and pushes it onto the schema-constrained extraction path instead.
tool_choice set to "any", which requires a tool call on every request while leaving the subagent free to pick whichever of the four extraction tools fits the source.
tool_choice left at "auto" with an added instruction stating that the subagent must always call exactly one extraction tool and must never answer in prose.

items.explanation: With several extraction schemas and an unknown source type, 'any' is the documented setting: it guarantees that some tool is called on every request while letting the model choose which schema matches the source it just read.

rationales.A: Forcing a named tool pins the journal-article schema onto sources of three other types and creates a repair step that a type-aware choice makes unnecessary.
rationales.B: 'none' prevents tool use altogether, which is the opposite of the requirement; it is the default only when no tools are supplied at all.
rationales.D: 'auto' is already the default whenever tools are provided, and an instruction is not a mechanism; the 7 percent of prose responses is the measurement showing that instruction alone does not bind.

items.objective: 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
items.stem: The document-analysis subagent extracts a citation record from each source through a tool whose input_schema lists doi, publication_year and funding_statement in its required array. Roughly one source in six is a working paper carrying neither a DOI nor a funding statement; for those the subagent emits a well-formed DOI that resolves to nothing and a funding sentence that appears nowhere in the source, and the report generator then cites both. Which schema change BEST stops the fabrication?

options.text: Take doi and funding_statement out of the required array and make them nullable, so that an absent value has a correct representation the subagent can emit.
Keep both fields required and add a prompt instruction telling the subagent never to guess a DOI or a funding statement it cannot find in the source.
Keep both fields required and add a validation pass that resends the source together with the failed extraction and the specific errors so the subagent can correct itself.
Keep both fields required and set strict to true on the extraction tool, so grammar-constrained sampling rejects a non-conforming value before it is emitted.

items.explanation: A required field with no permitted empty value leaves the model no correct answer when the source genuinely lacks the information, so it fills the field to satisfy the schema. Documented schema design is to make a field optional or nullable wherever the source may not contain it: absence then has a representation, and a null is a signal the coordinator can act on rather than a plausible fabrication.

rationales.B: The instruction competes with a schema that still forbids the honest answer. Something has to occupy a required field, and 'do not guess' does not tell the subagent what to put there instead.
rationales.C: Retry with error feedback corrects format and structural errors. It cannot recover information that is not in the source, so each retry re-runs the same impossible request at additional cost.
rationales.D: strict guarantees the emitted value is a well-formed string in the required field, which is exactly what the fabricated DOI already is; grammar constraints govern shape, never whether a value is true of the source.

items.objective: 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
items.stem: An intake service defines extract_invoice and extract_receipt and must record one of them for every document it processes. Over 2,000 runs, 4 percent returned a prose summary and called neither tool; among the calls that did happen, some carried amount_due as a string and some omitted issued_on, which the schema marks required. The model in use supports forced tool use. Which configuration closes both gaps?

options.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} and leave the two tool definitions as they are, since requiring a tool call puts every document onto a schema.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} and strict to true on both tool definitions, since one guarantees that a tool is called and the other that its input conforms to the schema.
Set strict to true on both tool definitions and leave tool_choice at its default, since grammar-constrained sampling makes the schema the only well-formed way for the model to answer.
Leave tool_choice at its default, add input_examples showing a correctly typed call to each tool, and state in the system prompt that one of the two tools must always be called.

items.explanation: The two guarantees are separate. Forcing a tool call says nothing about the shape of the input that call carries, and grammar-constrained sampling says nothing about whether a tool is called at all. On models that support forced tool use, documented guidance is to combine the forced choice with strict tool definitions so that both hold.

rationales.A: This removes the prose responses but leaves plain tool use in place, where a type can come back as a string and a required field can be omitted.
rationales.C: Strict tool use constrains the input of a call that happens; at the default setting the model may still answer in prose and call nothing, which is the larger of the two failures here.
rationales.D: Examples and instructions are guidance rather than enforcement: they raise the odds of a well-formed call without guaranteeing either that a call occurs or that its input validates.

items.objective: 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
items.stem: claim_category is declared as an enum of six values. Auditors report two problems: claims that fit none of the six are assigned the nearest value, and genuinely ambiguous claims get an arbitrary pick with no signal that the model was unsure. Downstream reporting groups by this field and must stay stable. Which schema change addresses both problems?

options.text: Drop the enum, let claim_category be free text, and cluster the observed values each week so that they can be mapped back onto the six existing reporting groups.
Keep the six values and add a separate boolean field, needs_human_review, that the model sets whenever it is not certain about the category it selected.
Expand the enum to roughly forty values derived from a year of claim descriptions, so that nearly every incoming claim has an exact match available.
Add an "other" value paired with a free-text detail field, plus an "unclear" value for ambiguous claims, keeping the six existing values intact.

items.explanation: The documented schema pattern for extensible categorization is an enum with escape hatches: 'other' with a detail string for claims outside the known set, and 'unclear' for ambiguous ones. Both stop the model forcing a wrong value into a fixed enum, and the six reporting groups stay intact.

rationales.A: Free text destroys the stable grouping the reporting layer depends on and pushes the categorization problem into a recurring manual mapping exercise.
rationales.B: A needs_human_review flag still leaves a claim outside the six categories with no correct value to carry, so the enum is filled wrongly and the flag only records that it might have been; the escape hatch has to exist inside the enum itself.
rationales.C: A forty-value enum is harder to choose from, still cannot cover a claim type that has not appeared yet, and fragments the reporting groups it was meant to stabilize.

items.objective: 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
items.stem: A codebase-exploration agent builds a dependency inventory for a legacy monorepo through a strict extraction tool whose input_schema declares version as a string. Every call validates and no request has failed. The emitted values are 1.2.3, v1.2.3, ^1.2.3, 1.2 and 1.2.3-rc1 depending on which manifest the version was read from, and the downstream step that flags outdated packages cannot order them. What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Replace the string type on version with an enum listing the roughly forty distinct version strings the last inventory run produced, so the schema itself rejects anything outside that set.
Keep the strict schema and add format-normalization rules to the prompt: emit major.minor.patch, drop a leading v and any range operator, and zero-pad a missing patch component.
Drop strict from the tool and have the agent return the raw manifest line for each dependency, then parse the version out of it in the comparison step.
Split the run in two: one call extracting the version text as it appears, and a second call that normalizes the collected values into a consistent form.

items.explanation: A schema constrains the shape and the type of a value; it does not constrain which convention a string follows, which is why every one of these inconsistent versions validates. The documented pairing for inconsistent source formatting is a strict output schema plus explicit format-normalization rules in the prompt, so the model normalizes while the source is still in front of it and the schema keeps the result typed.

rationales.A: An enum of previously observed values cannot admit the next release, and the inventory exists precisely to surface versions that have not been seen before.
rationales.C: Dropping strict trades a guaranteed string field for free text, and a parser over raw manifest lines has to re-implement version extraction for every manifest format in the monorepo.
rationales.D: A second call pays for the whole inventory twice and normalizes with the source out of view, so a value such as 1.2 cannot be resolved against the manifest that produced it.

items.objective: 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
items.stem: A CI job files findings through a submit_findings tool whose input_schema types line as integer and lists severity as required. Occasionally the recorded input carries line as the string "418" and omits severity entirely, and the pipeline writes a malformed row. Which change guarantees that the tool input conforms to the schema?

options.text: Add a sentence to the tool description stating that line must be a JSON number and that severity must be present on every finding submitted.
Set tool_choice to "any" so the model is obliged to call a tool on every turn and cannot return an unconstrained free-text response instead.
Set strict to true on the tool definition and set additionalProperties to false in its input_schema, which grammar-constrains the generated tool input.
Add input_examples to the tool definition showing several correctly typed findings so the model has a typed template it can copy on each call.

items.explanation: Plain tool use does not guarantee schema conformance; documented behavior is that a type may come back as a string instead of a number, or a required field may be omitted. strict: true enables grammar-constrained sampling and requires additionalProperties: false in the schema.

rationales.A: Descriptions are guidance and carry no enforcement, which is precisely why the documented failure modes include incompatible types and missing required fields.
rationales.B: Forcing a tool call guarantees that a call happens, not that its input matches the schema; the type drift occurs inside a call that already took place.
rationales.D: Examples raise the odds of correct typing without guaranteeing it, and they add prompt tokens to every request while leaving the failure open.

items.objective: 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
items.stem: An extraction service returns a JSON object as its answer and also calls a lookup_customer tool during the run. The team wants both the answer and the tool input to be schema-guaranteed. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.text: Both are enforced by one grammar pipeline: the first request on a new schema pays a compile cost, and compiled grammars are then cached for 24 hours from last use.
The schema guarantee extends to the correctness of the extracted values, so a downstream semantic validation pass is no longer necessary.
Prefilling the assistant turn with an opening brace remains the supported way to guarantee that the answer begins as a JSON object.
Structured outputs requires the structured-outputs beta header on every request, because the feature has not yet reached general availability.
output_config.format with {"type": "json_schema", "schema": {...}} constrains the model's own response, while strict on the tool constrains that tool's input parameters.
Setting strict to true on the tool also constrains the model's final text answer, which makes a response-level format setting redundant here.

items.explanation: Two separate points earn credit here. The first is which layer each mechanism governs: output_config.format constrains Claude's own response to a schema, strict tool use constrains a tool's input parameters, and the two are complementary settings that can be sent independently or together in one request. The second is how both are enforced -- each schema is compiled into a grammar, the first request on a schema the service has not seen carries the compilation latency, and compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use, so editing a schema pays that cost again while renaming a field description does not. Note also which layer each name belongs to: on the Messages API the earlier output_format request field has moved to output_config.format and no beta header is required, while the Agent SDK keeps a separately named outputFormat option of its own.

rationales.B: The guarantee covers shape and types, never semantics, which is why values that fail to reconcile still need application-level validation.
rationales.C: A prefilled assistant message on the last turn returns a 400 error on current models; structured outputs or a schema-constrained tool is the documented replacement.
rationales.D: Structured outputs is generally available on the Messages API; the older beta header and request field are accepted only during a transition period.
rationales.F: strict constrains tool input only, and leaves the model's own response text unconstrained unless a response format is set as well.
