items.objective: 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
items.stem: The document-analysis subagent in your research system extracts a structured study record from each paper and validates it against a JSON Schema, retrying on failure. The retry appends one message to the same conversation: "That output was invalid. Please try again." Across 4,000 papers the second attempt succeeds only 11 percent of the time. Which change to the retry request MOST directly raises the correction rate?

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature on the retry so the model produces a structurally different record instead of reproducing the shape that already failed, and leave the retry message as it is.
Send a follow-up request carrying the original paper, the exact record that failed, and the specific validation errors that were raised, naming the offending fields and what was expected.

Raise the retry ceiling from two attempts to six so the pipeline keeps resampling the same request until one of the attempts happens to satisfy the validator, and log the attempt count for later tuning.
Replace the retry message with the full JSON Schema restated inline and an instruction to follow every declared type exactly, without referring to what the previous attempt actually produced.

items.explanation: A retry only helps if it tells the model what went wrong. The documented shape of a correction request is the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors, so the model can locate and repair the offending fields rather than re-deriving the whole record from scratch. Anthropic's tool-handling guidance makes the same point about feedback generally: an error should say what went wrong and what to try next, not just that something failed.

rationales.A: Resampling at a higher temperature changes what is generated but not what the model knows about the failure. It is a lottery over the same uninformative prompt, and higher temperature on a schema-constrained extraction task tends to reduce fidelity to the paper rather than improve it.
rationales.C: More attempts at an uninformative prompt multiply cost without raising the per-attempt success probability. The 11 percent figure is a property of the retry message, and repeating a message that carries no diagnostic information six times leaves that property unchanged.
rationales.D: Restating the schema tells the model the target but not the miss. The model already had the schema on the first attempt; without the failed record and the validation errors it cannot tell which field it got wrong, so the same error class recurs.

items.objective: 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
items.stem: Freight invoice extraction fills a required broker_reference string. For the 9 percent of invoices issued directly by a carrier, that reference is printed only on a separate broker statement that is never part of the submitted PDF. Those documents consume all three retry attempts, and the values that eventually pass validation turn out to be the carrier account number reformatted to look like a broker reference. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Raise the retry ceiling from three attempts to eight and append the validator message "broker_reference did not match ^BRK-[0-9]{8}$" to each attempt, so the model narrows in on a value that satisfies the pattern.

Set strict: true on the extraction tool with additionalProperties: false, so that grammar-constrained sampling refuses to emit a broker_reference that is not a well-formed reference for this document.
Add two few-shot examples showing a correctly extracted broker_reference, so the model learns where on a freight invoice the reference is normally printed and stops looking in the wrong place.
Make broker_reference optional and nullable so a carrier-direct invoice can legitimately return no value, and route those records to the broker-statement lookup instead of retrying the extraction.

items.explanation: Retry-with-error-feedback repairs format and structural failures. It cannot conjure information that is absent from the source, and a required field on a document that does not contain it is direct pressure to fabricate, which is exactly what the reformatted account numbers are. The documented move is to match the schema to the task: make fields optional when the source may not carry them, and handle the gap outside the extraction call.

rationales.A: More attempts against absent information increase the fabrication rate rather than the accuracy rate. Naming the pattern makes matters worse: a fabricated value satisfies ^BRK-[0-9]{8}$ just as easily as a real one, so the pipeline converges on plausible-looking wrong answers faster.
rationales.B: Strict tool use guarantees that the emitted input conforms to the schema; it says nothing about whether the value is true. A grammar-constrained string field will happily accept a fabricated reference, and keeping the field required is what forces the fabrication in the first place.
rationales.C: Few-shot examples teach where to look on documents that contain the field. On carrier-direct invoices there is nothing to find, so better location guidance cannot help, and examples that always show a populated value reinforce the expectation that one exists.

items.objective: 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
items.stem: Every extracted invoice parses cleanly and conforms to the schema: line_items is an array of objects with numeric amounts, and total_amount is a number. Finance reports that on roughly one invoice in thirty the line items add up to a different figure from total_amount, and the record was written to the ledger anyway. Which change catches this class of defect?

options.text: Have the model emit a calculated_total alongside the transcribed stated_total, and compare the two in pipeline code before the record is written, holding any discrepancy for review.
Add strict: true to the extraction tool so grammar-constrained sampling guarantees the numeric fields conform to the declared types and the arithmetic is settled during generation.
Add "minimum": 0 and a multipleOf constraint to the monetary fields in the schema so amounts that cannot combine into the stated total are rejected by the API before they return.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to check its own arithmetic before responding and to re-read the invoice whenever the line items and the stated total do not agree.

items.explanation: Schema enforcement guarantees shape and type, never that the values are right; the exam guide and the structured output documentation both draw that line explicitly. Line items that fail to reconcile with a stated total are a semantic error, and the documented self-correction pattern is to extract a calculated_total next to the stated_total so deterministic pipeline code can detect the discrepancy and hold the record.

rationales.B: Strict tool use constrains the generated tool input to the schema. It makes no arithmetic claim at all, so a set of line items that does not sum to total_amount is still perfectly schema-valid and still passes straight through to the ledger.
rationales.C: Numeric constraints such as minimum and multipleOf are not supported in the grammar-constrained schema subset and return a 400 naming the unsupported keyword. Even if they were accepted, a range constraint cannot express a relationship between an array of values and another field.
rationales.D: A prompt instruction to self-check produces no signal the pipeline can act on. There is no place for the check to fail, so a record whose arithmetic is wrong is still returned and still written; a deterministic comparison is what turns the problem into a detectable event.

items.objective: 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
items.stem: A CI step runs the Claude Agent SDK with output_format set to {"type": "json_schema", "schema": REVIEW_SCHEMA} and posts the findings it receives. Which check should the calling code apply to the result message before it treats the run as usable?

options.text: Check that the result subtype is success, because the SDK only reports that subtype once the output has been validated against the supplied schema.
Check that the result subtype is not error_max_structured_output_retries, then parse the result text field, which carries the schema-conforming object for successful runs.
Check both that the result subtype is success and that a structured_output value is present, treating a success that carries no structured_output as a failed run.
Check that structured_output parses as JSON, and if it does not, re-run the job with the schema converted to draft-07 before reporting a failure to the pipeline.

items.explanation: The SDK validates structured output and re-prompts on mismatch, and it signals exhaustion with the subtype error_max_structured_output_retries. The documentation also warns that a result can come back with subtype success and no structured_output value, and says to treat that as a failure too, so correct handling tests both conditions. Note the layer: the Agent SDK's option is outputFormat in TypeScript and output_format in Python, whereas at the Claude API level the old output_format parameter has been superseded by output_config.format, so the two names are two layers rather than two spellings of one parameter.

rationales.A: Subtype success alone is not sufficient. The documentation explicitly describes a success result that carries no structured_output, and code that trusts the subtype on its own will post an empty or missing findings object as though the review had passed.
rationales.B: The validated object arrives in structured_output, not in result, which holds the model's text answer. Reading result and parsing it as the findings object misses the field that the schema actually governs.
rationales.D: Draft version is a startup concern, not a per-result recovery step: an invalid or wrong-draft schema fails the run at startup with an error naming the problem, so converting the schema after a bad result is both too late and the wrong layer.

items.objective: 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
items.stem: Developers dismiss about 40 percent of the findings your review agent posts in the possible_null_dereference category. Findings are stored as structured records carrying file, line, severity and message, and dismissals are recorded by the review tool. Before rewriting the prompt you want to know which code shapes are producing the dismissed findings. Which change to the finding schema enables that analysis?

options.text: Add a confidence value the model assigns to each finding and set a cut-off from the confidence distribution of dismissed versus accepted findings, suppressing everything below it.
Add a detected_pattern field naming the code construct that triggered the finding, so dismissals can be grouped by construct and the recurring false-positive shapes identified.
Add a reviewer_reasoning free-text field holding the model's full explanation for each finding, then read the explanations attached to the findings developers dismissed.
Add a run_id and archive the full prompt used for every run, so each dismissed finding can be traced back to the prompt version that was live when it was produced.

items.explanation: Systematic analysis of dismissals needs a categorical key to aggregate on. A detected_pattern field naming the construct that triggered the finding turns a pile of individual dismissals into counts per construct, which is what identifies the false-positive shapes worth rewriting the prompt against.

rationales.A: Confidence routing is a real verification technique, but it answers a different question here. A score ranks findings by how sure the model was and lets you suppress the low end; it never names the code shape that produced them. The team asked which constructs are driving the dismissals, and no threshold on a score can group findings by construct.
rationales.C: Free-text reasoning cannot be grouped without a second analysis pass to categorise it, which is the work the detected_pattern field does at write time. Reading explanations one by one does not scale past a few dozen dismissals.
rationales.D: Prompt versioning is useful for measuring whether a rewrite helped, but it partitions findings by run rather than by the construct that triggered them, so it never surfaces the recurring code shapes behind the dismissals.

items.objective: 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
items.stem: An extraction pipeline logs the reason each record failed validation. Which TWO of these failures are the kind that a retry carrying the specific validation error is likely to correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: invoice_date came back as "03/07/2026" where the downstream loader requires the ISO form 2026-07-03, so the record was rejected by the date check.
The parties field was returned as one concatenated string instead of the array of objects the schema declares, so structural validation failed.
The vendor_address string was extracted from the shipping block instead of the remit-to block, so a valid but wrong address reached the loader and was caught only by a downstream address check.
policy_number is absent because the submitted document is a renewal notice, and this insurer never prints the policy number on renewal notices.
The extracted customer_name differs from the name held for that account in the CRM, which the reconciliation job treats as a mismatch.

items.explanation: Retry-with-error-feedback works on format and structural output errors: the information is present and correctly read, but rendered in the wrong shape. A date written in the wrong notation and a nested structure flattened into a string are both repairable once the retry names the expected form, so the model can restate what it already extracted.

rationales.C: A value read from the wrong region of the document is schema-valid and parser-clean, so the validator raises nothing that could be fed back to the model. The fix is a field-scoped instruction naming the remit-to block, or a per-section pass, not a retry.
rationales.D: The information is simply not in the source. Retrying pushes the model to invent a policy number that satisfies the validator, which is the failure mode the retry was meant to prevent; the right answer is an optional field and a lookup elsewhere.
rationales.E: A disagreement with an external system of record is a data question, not an output-format question. The extraction may be a faithful reading of a document that genuinely differs from the CRM, and no restatement of format resolves it.

items.objective: 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
items.stem: A codebase-exploration agent walks a legacy repository and asks Claude to emit a JSON inventory of every exported symbol in each file. On about one file in six -- always the largest modules -- the response is cut off mid-object, the pipeline records stop_reason "max_tokens", and the retry loop resends the file with the message that the returned JSON was malformed. The retry fails identically and the file lands in the dead-letter queue. What should the pipeline do instead?

options.text: Branch on stop_reason before validating: on max_tokens, raise the output budget or continue the response, rather than feeding back a validation error the model did not actually cause.
Add strict: true to the inventory tool, so grammar-constrained sampling guarantees a complete and well-formed object is emitted even when the response runs long against its budget.
Keep the retry loop as it is but include the truncated output and the exact parser error in the follow-up message, which is the documented shape of a retry-with-error-feedback correction request.
Move these files to the Message Batches API, whose longer processing window lets a long response run to completion before the request is cut off and returned.

items.explanation: stop_reason is the signal that separates a bad answer from an incomplete one. A max_tokens stop means the response, and possibly an in-flight tool_use block, was truncated at the output budget; the documented handling is to raise max_tokens or continue the response. Routing truncation into the validation-error path treats a capacity symptom as a formatting mistake, so every retry reproduces it.

rationales.B: Strict tool use constrains what tokens may be generated, not how many. A grammar-constrained response that hits the output budget is cut off in exactly the same place, so the object is still incomplete when it returns.
rationales.C: This is the right technique aimed at the wrong failure class. The model's output was not malformed by a reasoning error; it was cut off, and a better-worded correction request still asks for a response that will not fit inside the same budget.
rationales.D: The batch processing window governs how long a request may sit in the queue, not how many output tokens one response may contain. The same request submitted in a batch truncates at the same point.

items.objective: 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies
items.stem: Your pre-merge review gate blocks the merge button and runs on the Messages API. Each run sends three things: a package dependency graph and an ownership map, which change only when the repository's manifest files change; a per-package summary of open and recent production incidents, which the team requires to be no more than one hour old at review time; and the diff itself. The gate must stay synchronous. Which restructuring earns the 50 percent Message Batches API discount on the largest share of these tokens without breaking either constraint?

options.text: Precompute the dependency graph and the ownership summaries in a batch triggered whenever the manifest files change, cache them against that commit, and leave the incident summary and the diff-scoped review synchronous.
Move the entire context package, incident summary included, into a nightly batch and have the gate read all three parts from the cache that batch writes before developers arrive.
Leave the gate exactly as it is and accept the current cost, since no part of a workflow that blocks a merge can be served from a queue that publishes no latency guarantee at all.
Submit the whole gate to the batch API and poll for the result, falling back to a synchronous call whenever the batch has not returned within 90 seconds of a developer pressing the merge button.

items.explanation: Batch pricing is earned by work that can wait, so the question is which inputs can be computed before anyone is waiting. The dependency graph and the ownership map change only with the manifest files, so they can be built on a batch triggered by those commits and read from cache; that is the largest and most stable part of what the gate sends. The incident summary carries a one-hour freshness requirement that no scheduled precompute can meet, and the diff does not exist until the pull request does, so both stay on the Messages API. The guide's split between latency-tolerant analysis and blocking checks is applied here at the level of the individual input rather than the whole workflow.

rationales.B: This earns the discount on more tokens but breaks the freshness constraint that was given: a nightly job cannot produce an incident summary under an hour old at review time, so the gate would judge a diff against a picture of production up to a day stale.
rationales.C: The constraint given is that the gate stays synchronous, not that every token it consumes must be produced inside it. Two of the three inputs are independent of the diff and can be built before any developer is waiting, so paying full price on all of them concedes more than the constraint requires.
rationales.D: A synchronous fallback pays for the same review twice whenever the batch is slow, and the batch API publishes no latency guarantee, so a 90-second poll on a blocking gate is a bet rather than a design. It also leaves the developer waiting on a queue never intended to serve interactive traffic.

items.objective: 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies
items.stem: Test generation for merged commits runs through the Message Batches API. Once results come back, a downstream job formats and commits the generated tests, and that step is allowed up to 2 hours. The team's SLA is that generated tests must be committed within 36 hours of the merge that triggered them. Which submission schedule guarantees that SLA in the worst case?

options.text: Accumulate merges for 24 hours and submit one batch each night at 02:00, since batches typically complete well inside an hour and the documented ceiling is rarely approached in practice.
Accumulate merges for 12 hours and submit two batches a day, which keeps each batch small enough to process quickly and still leaves several hours of slack against the SLA.
Accumulate merges for at most 8 hours and submit a batch per window, so the oldest commit waits 8 hours before submission, then at most 24 hours of processing, then the 2-hour commit step.
Accumulate merges for at most 16 hours and submit batches at 06:00 and 22:00, which halves the nightly window and still leaves a comfortable margin against the SLA.

items.explanation: Worst-case age is the accumulation window plus the documented 24-hour processing ceiling plus the 2-hour commit step. An 8-hour window gives 34 hours, inside the 36-hour SLA with two hours to spare; any window longer than 10 hours cannot be guaranteed. The arithmetic must run against the ceiling, not against the typical completion time, because the batch API publishes no latency guarantee and batches expire at 24 hours rather than finishing by then.

rationales.A: A 24-hour window plus the 24-hour ceiling plus 2 hours is a 50-hour worst case, far outside the SLA. It also leans on typical completion time, which the API does not guarantee, so the schedule holds only until the first slow night.
rationales.B: A 12-hour window plus the 24-hour ceiling plus 2 hours is a 38-hour worst case, which breaches the SLA by two hours. The apparent slack comes from using average completion rather than the documented ceiling.
rationales.D: A 16-hour window plus the 24-hour ceiling plus 2 hours is a 42-hour worst case, six hours outside the SLA. Splitting the day into two windows narrows the breach but does not close it.

items.objective: 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies
items.stem: A 45,000-document extraction batch reaches processing_status ended with request_counts showing 41,900 succeeded and 3,100 errored. Every errored entry is an oversized contract that exceeded the context window. What is the correct recovery?

options.text: Build a new batch containing only the 3,100 failed custom_id values, with those contracts split into chunks that fit the context window, and keep the 41,900 results already retrieved.

Cancel the ended batch and resubmit all 45,000 documents through a pipeline that now chunks oversized contracts first, so that every record in the ledger is produced by one consistent pipeline version.

Fetch the batch, edit the 3,100 failed requests in place so their params point at the chunked versions of those contracts, and let the batch resume processing the entries it had not completed, keeping one batch_id for the whole job.
Resubmit all 45,000 documents in a new batch with chunking applied, accepting the duplicate spend because errored requests were already billed on the first submission.

items.explanation: Requests inside a batch fail independently, and custom_id exists precisely so failed entries can be identified and reprocessed. The documented recovery is a fresh batch containing only the failures, modified as needed, which here means chunking the oversized contracts; the succeeded results stand and are downloadable for 29 days from the batch's created_at.

rationales.B: A batch whose processing_status is already ended cannot be cancelled, and reprocessing 41,900 documents that succeeded pays for the same work twice for no benefit. Pipeline consistency is a property of the chunking code, not of which batch a record came from.
rationales.C: A submitted batch is immutable. There is no edit-in-place operation on its requests and no resume once processing has ended: the documented path when requests need changing is to submit a new batch containing the corrected requests, which is why custom_id matters.
rationales.D: The premise is wrong: errored, canceled and expired requests are not billed. Only the succeeded requests cost anything, so wholesale resubmission buys duplicate charges on those 41,900 rather than avoiding a sunk cost.

items.objective: 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies
items.stem: Your pipeline submits 8,000 extraction requests as one batch, then reads the .jsonl file at results_url when the batch ends and zips each line with the input list by position. Extracted records are being written against the wrong source documents. What is the underlying mistake?

options.text: The pipeline reads the results file before processing_status reaches ended, so only the requests finished so far are present and every later position is shifted.
Result ordering in a batch is not guaranteed, so results must be matched back to inputs by the custom_id sent on each request and returned on each result.
The results file interleaves succeeded, errored, canceled and expired entries, so positions only line up once the non-succeeded entries have been filtered out first.
Results are retained for only 24 hours after a batch ends, so a late read returns a partial file whose remaining lines no longer align with the submitted request list.

items.explanation: The documentation is explicit that results are not returned in submission order and that meaningful custom_id values are how you match a result to its request. Positional zipping is unsafe by design, and the fix is to key the join on custom_id, which must be unique within the batch and match the documented pattern.

rationales.A: Reading early is not the described situation: the pipeline waits for the batch to end. Even a complete file read after the batch ends carries results in an arbitrary order, so the mismatch persists once the timing question is settled.
rationales.C: Filtering by result type does not restore an order that was never guaranteed in the first place. Removing errored or expired entries would still leave the succeeded ones in an arbitrary sequence relative to the input list.
rationales.D: The retention figure is wrong: results remain downloadable for 29 days from the batch's created_at. Retention also has nothing to do with the order of the lines that are returned.

items.objective: 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies
items.stem: Your support platform re-classifies the previous day's resolved conversations overnight through the Message Batches API so the intent taxonomy stays current. The job submits about 60,000 requests at 01:00. This week the batch returns 54,300 succeeded and 5,700 results whose type is expired. The pipeline currently treats every non-succeeded result as a model failure and sends it into the retry-with-error-feedback path. What is the correct handling for the 5,700?

options.text: Resubmit those custom_id values unchanged in a fresh batch, and submit earlier or split the volume, because an expired request never reached the model and was not billed.
Feed each of them back through the correction path with the validation error attached, so that the model can repair whatever in its own output caused the request to be rejected.
Treat them as billed work already paid for and absorb the cost, then raise max_tokens on the resubmission so the classifications are not cut short a second time.
Cancel the batch and resubmit all 60,000 conversations, since a batch that recorded expired requests may have classified the rest of the day against a taxonomy that was only partially updated.

items.explanation: The four batch result types mean different things and the pipeline is collapsing them. expired means the batch reached its 24-hour ceiling before that request was ever sent to the model: there is no output to correct and, as the documentation states, no charge for it. The remedy is operational rather than prompt-level, which is the shape the guide gives for batch failure handling generally: identify the failures by custom_id, resubmit only those, and change what caused the failure -- here by submitting earlier or breaking a very large dataset into several batches, which the documentation recommends anyway.

rationales.B: There is no output and no validation error to feed back. An expired request produced nothing at all, so a correction request built around the model's previous answer has no previous answer to work from.
rationales.C: Expired requests are explicitly not billed, alongside errored and canceled ones, so there is no sunk cost to absorb. max_tokens is also unrelated: expiry is a queue deadline, not an output budget.
rationales.D: Requests in a batch are processed independently and the 54,300 succeeded results are valid, so reprocessing them pays twice for work already done. A batch that has ended cannot be cancelled in any case.

items.objective: 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies
items.stem: You are about to submit 50,000 loan files to the Message Batches API for the first time, using an extraction prompt written last week. Which TWO practices match Anthropic's documented batch guidance for this first submission? (Select TWO)

options.text: Dry run one request of the same shape against the Messages API first, so validation errors surface before 50,000 copies of the same mistake are submitted.
Set stream: true on the batch requests so partial output can be inspected while the batch is still in progress and a bad run can be spotted early.
Submit the entire dataset as a single batch rather than several, because prompt caching is guaranteed across requests that share the same instruction preamble.
Plan to cancel and resubmit if the early results look poor, since cancellation takes effect immediately and no request that had started is billed.
Refine the prompt against a sample set first, so the first pass succeeds on as many files as possible and fewer documents have to be resubmitted afterwards.

items.explanation: Two pre-flight practices are documented for large batches: dry run a single request shape against the Messages API to catch validation errors, and refine the prompt on a sample before committing the volume, so the first pass succeeds as widely as possible and resubmission costs stay low. Both act before the immutable batch is created.

rationales.B: stream: true is one of exactly three parameters the batch API rejects with a validation error, alongside speed and max_tokens: 0. The submission would fail rather than provide early visibility.
rationales.C: The documentation recommends the opposite for very large datasets: split them into multiple batches for manageability. Cache hits inside a batch are best-effort because requests are processed concurrently and in any order, so nothing about caching is guaranteed by keeping the batch large.
rationales.D: Cancellation is not immediate; a cancelling batch still moves to ended and may carry partial results for requests already processed. It is a damage-control path, not a substitute for prompt refinement before submission.

items.objective: 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies
items.stem: Policy extraction runs synchronously today: for each document Claude calls your lookup_policyholder tool, your service queries the customer database, returns the result as a tool_result, and the model finishes the extraction using it. You now want to run a 200,000-document backfill, split across several batches, through the Message Batches API. What does the move require?

options.text: Nothing beyond the endpoint change: when a batch request produces a tool_use block the batch API invokes the named client tool on your behalf and returns the completed extraction.
Removing the tools array from every request, because tool definitions and tool use of any kind are rejected by the batch API with a validation error at submission.
Resolving the policyholder lookups before submission and passing the data in the prompt, because a batch request cannot pause for your service to execute a tool and return a result.
Setting tool_choice to "none" on every batch request and running a second synchronous pass afterwards to fill in the fields the lookup tool would otherwise have supplied.

items.explanation: The batch API accepts tool use, multi-turn conversations, system messages, extended thinking and vision. What it cannot do is suspend a request mid-flight so your client executes a tool and posts a tool_result back, because there is no interactive turn to return into. A backfill therefore has to pre-resolve the client-side lookups and supply the data in the request itself. Guide-versus-docs note: the guide's TS 4.5 bullet reads "The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request", which on a fast reading sounds like multi-turn conversations cannot be batched at all. Its own parenthetical -- "cannot execute tools mid-request and return results" -- is the precise claim, and it agrees with current documentation, which lists multi-turn conversations and tool use among what can be batched. Both the guide and the docs support the same answer here.

rationales.A: Client-defined tools are executed by your application, not by the API, in batch or otherwise. Nothing in the batch pipeline can call your customer database, so a request that depends on a tool_result would simply never receive one.
rationales.B: This overstates the limitation into something the documentation contradicts: tool use, including every server tool, is explicitly listed among what can be batched. The constraint is about client-side execution mid-request, not about tools existing in the request.
rationales.D: Suppressing tool use and then running 200,000 synchronous follow-up calls reintroduces the full-price traffic the batch was meant to remove, and leaves each extraction split across two passes that cannot see each other's context.

items.objective: 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
items.stem: A CI job generates a database migration and then, in the same session, asks Claude to review the migration it just wrote. Every review comes back clean. The team first rewrote the review instruction to demand adversarial self-critique against a named list of failure classes, and the reviews stayed clean; they then enabled extended thinking on the review turn, and the reviews stayed clean at four times the cost. Two of those migrations later failed in staging on a constraint the model had itself introduced. What does this evidence indicate?

options.text: Both remedies run inside the session that produced the migration, so the review still rests on the reasoning that justified the constraint rather than on the artefact alone.
The review instruction is still too general, and naming the specific constraint classes this team has been bitten by, with a worked example of each, would let the same in-session review catch them.
The migration is too large for a single review turn, so the review should be split into a per-statement pass for local problems plus an integration pass over the migration as a whole.

The two remedies were never given a fair test because they were applied one at a time, and combining the adversarial self-critique instruction with extended thinking on the same turn would compound their effect.

items.explanation: A model that reviews its own work in the same session still holds the reasoning that produced it, and is correspondingly unlikely to question the decisions it just justified. The guide states the consequence directly: independent review instances, without the prior reasoning context, are more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking. Two failed in-session remedies are exactly that claim being demonstrated, so the evidence points at the retained context rather than at the wording or the depth of the review turn.

rationales.B: The instruction was already specific: it named the failure classes to look for. Precision in the wording does not remove the reasoning the session is sitting on, and the reviewer keeps clearing the decision it argued for a few turns earlier.
rationales.C: Splitting into passes is the documented remedy for attention dilution across a wide review, and the symptom there is inconsistent or contradictory findings. Here a single local constraint in one artefact is being missed by a reviewer that is not independent, and narrower passes inside the same session inherit the same context.
rationales.D: Two in-session remedies stacked are still two in-session remedies. Both draw on the same retained reasoning, so combining them compounds cost rather than independence.

items.objective: 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
items.stem: You implement the independent reviewer as a Claude Code subagent defined in .claude/agents/migration-reviewer.md. To give it enough context, the delegating prompt pastes in the generator's full plan and its written reasoning about the trade-offs it chose. The subagent's reviews still endorse the decisions that later proved wrong. What is the flaw in this design?

options.text: The subagent frontmatter does not constrain tools to Read, Grep and Glob, so the reviewer spends its turns writing and editing files in the working tree instead of analysing the migration it was delegated to review.

Pasting in the generator's reasoning recreates the context that the isolated window exists to exclude, so the reviewer inherits the generator's justifications instead of judging the artefact on its own.
A subagent already loads the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, so project conventions are present and the pasted plan simply crowds them out of a window that is now carrying redundant material.
The reviewer subagent has no model override in its frontmatter, so it runs on the session's current model instead of a stronger one, and a weaker reviewer defers to a confidently argued plan.

items.explanation: The mechanism that makes a subagent useful as a reviewer is its isolated context window: it loads its own system prompt, the delegation message, the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and preloaded skills, and not the main session's history. Hand-feeding the generator's plan and rationale into the delegation message puts the very reasoning back in that the isolation was removing, and the reviewer evaluates the argument instead of the code.

rationales.A: Unconstrained tools are a real hardening gap and a read-only reviewer is good practice, but nothing here suggests the subagent is editing files. It is producing reviews; the problem is what those reviews are based on.
rationales.C: A subagent does load the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, so the first half is accurate, but crowding is not the failure. The reviewer is not short of project conventions; it is agreeing with an argument it should never have been shown.
rationales.D: Model choice is configurable in a subagent's frontmatter and can matter for hard reviews, but it is not what makes this reviewer agree: it is agreeing with an argument it should never have been shown, and the same plan pasted in front of any model produces the same deference.

items.objective: 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
items.stem: To cut false positives an engineer runs the review agent three times over each diff and posts only the findings that appear in at least two runs. The false-positive rate halves. Over the following month three production incidents are traced to findings that exactly one run had reported and the filter discarded. Which change MOST effectively restores the missed findings without returning to the original false-positive volume?

options.text: Move to five runs and require agreement from three of them, which stabilises the vote and lowers the chance that a genuine finding is lost to one unlucky pair of runs on a noisy diff.
Keep the three runs but post every finding any run produced, ranked by how many runs produced it, leaving triage to the developer reading the pull request.
Keep the two-of-three vote but raise the sampling temperature on each run, so the three passes explore more distinct hypotheses about the diff.
Replace the vote with a verification pass that checks each candidate finding against the actual behaviour of the code and drops the candidates it cannot substantiate.

items.explanation: Running the same prompt several times is documented as a way to detect inconsistency, not as a filter for suppressing it. Agreement is a weak proxy for truth, and intermittently detected bugs are exactly the ones a vote discards. Anthropic's own multi-agent review architecture instead follows the finding agents with a distinct verification step that checks each candidate against real code behaviour before it is reported.

rationales.A: More voters make the filter more stable, not more correct. A subtle bug that only one run in three notices is even less likely to clear a three-of-five bar, so the recall problem that caused the incidents gets worse rather than better.
rationales.B: Publishing everything restores the recall that was lost but abandons the precision goal entirely, returning the team to the false-positive volume that motivated the change and pushing the whole triage burden onto reviewers.
rationales.C: More divergent sampling widens the candidate pool but it also widens disagreement, so the vote discards more of the intermittently detected findings rather than fewer. It makes the recall problem that caused the incidents worse while leaving the filter itself unchanged.

items.objective: 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
items.stem: One prompt extracts 41 fields spanning six sections of a 90-page reinsurance treaty, and four of those fields can legitimately be sourced from more than one section. Fields owned by sections 4 to 6 come back null or populated from a neighbouring clause. Re-running the same prompt against the same treaty with only section 5's fields in the schema returns those fields correctly, and the treaty sits well inside the context window. Which restructuring BEST addresses the cause this evidence points to?

options.text: Split the treaty into six per-section documents and run the same 41-field schema against each of them, then merge the results by taking the first non-null value returned for each field.
Keep the single pass but place the treaty text above the instructions and schema, and close the prompt with an instruction to re-read sections 4 to 6 before answering.
Run one focused pass per section against only the fields that section owns, then a reconciliation pass over the merged record for the four fields more than one section can supply.
Keep the single pass and add a retry that names each field that came back null in the follow-up message, allowing up to three attempts per treaty before the document is queued for review.

items.explanation: The diagnostic re-run does the work. Section 5's fields are extracted correctly when they are the only thing asked for, on the same document, well inside the context window, so the information is present and the model can read it: what fails is one pass carrying 41 fields across six sections at once. Narrowing each pass to a section and the fields that section owns removes that dilution. The four fields with more than one possible source are a relationship no local pass can see, which is why a reconciliation pass over the merged record is needed on top of the focused ones.

rationales.A: Chunking the document without narrowing the schema asks every chunk the same 41-field question, so five sixths of each pass is a request for fields that are not in front of it. Merging on first non-null then locks in whichever chunk guessed first, which is precisely how a field ends up filled from a neighbouring clause.
rationales.B: Placing longform data above the query is sound prompting practice, but the re-run already showed the model can read section 5 when asked narrowly. Neither the ordering nor a closing reminder reduces what a single pass is being asked to hold, and neither compares the four multi-source fields.
rationales.D: Retrying names the missing fields without changing the conditions that lost them, and re-running the same 41-field pass reproduces the same dilution. It also does nothing for fields that came back populated from the wrong clause, because those never register as null.

items.objective: 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
items.stem: An independent verification pass checks every claim your synthesis subagent puts in a report against the cited source, producing about 9,000 verified claims a week. Analysts can hand-check roughly 600 of them. The team already holds 1,200 claims that analysts adjudicated as supported or unsupported last quarter. Which design routes the analysts' limited capacity to the claims MOST likely to be wrong?

options.text: Have the verification pass return a confidence value with each claim and send everything below 0.9 to the analysts, taking 0.9 as the point at which the model is reliably sure of a claim it has checked.
Have the verification pass report a confidence value with each claim, then use the 1,200 adjudicated claims to set the routing threshold where reported confidence actually tracks correctness.
Route by report section, sending analysts every claim drawn from the methodology and results sections, which is where unsupported claims have historically been found most often in past reports.
Run the verification pass three times per claim and route to the analysts only those claims on which the three runs disagreed about whether the source supported them.

items.explanation: The guide names verification passes in which the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding precisely so review effort can be routed. The word carrying the weight is calibrated: a reported confidence is only a ranking until it has been checked against ground truth, and 1,200 adjudicated claims are exactly the material for that check. Measuring how reported confidence tracks adjudicated correctness converts the score into a threshold that spends the 600 available checks on the claims most likely to be wrong, and the same labelled set shows whether the score separates them at all.

rationales.A: The mechanism is right and the threshold is invented. A cut-off like 0.9 means nothing until it has been compared against adjudicated outcomes, and with a labelled set already in hand there is no reason to guess: it may route far more or far fewer than 600 claims, and it may not concentrate the errors where the analysts are looking.
rationales.C: A section heuristic is a fixed prior that ignores what the verification pass actually found on each claim. It sends well-grounded methodology claims to the analysts while passing over an unsupported claim in the discussion, and it cannot be tuned to a 600-claim capacity.
rationales.D: Repeated sampling detects instability, not incorrectness. A claim the verifier gets confidently and consistently wrong produces no disagreement at all and is therefore routed away from the analysts, and the approach triples verification cost for a signal that is only a proxy.

items.objective: 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
items.stem: A 22-file pull request is reviewed by splitting the work: one subagent analyses each module for local issues, then a separate integration pass looks for cross-module data-flow problems. The integration pass keeps reporting nothing, or re-reporting problems the module passes already flagged. What must the coordinator hand the integration pass for it to do its job?

options.text: The merged list of findings from every module pass, ranked by severity, so that the integration pass can consolidate them into a single ordered report for the pull request.
Nothing beyond the pull request number and the review instruction, so that the integration pass forms a view uncontaminated by the module passes' conclusions.
Each module pass's findings together with the interface facts it established: the signatures it exposes and the shape of the data it emits and consumes.
The complete diff again with an instruction to concentrate on cross-module concerns, since the integration pass needs to see the same material the module passes saw.

items.explanation: A cross-file integration pass can only reason about data flow across a boundary if it is told what the boundaries are. Each local pass discovers that as it works -- signatures, emitted and consumed shapes, assumptions about callers -- and none of it survives into a later pass on its own, because a subagent's window holds its own definition and delegation message rather than what another subagent read. Forwarding the interface facts alongside the findings is what turns the second stage into an integration pass instead of a summariser.

rationales.A: Findings are conclusions, not contracts. A ranked list of local issues says nothing about what each module emits or expects, so the integration pass can only re-rank and restate them, which is the behaviour the team is already seeing.
rationales.B: Independence is worth protecting against the generator's reasoning, not against the facts a later pass needs to do its work. Starved of the interface information, the integration pass has to re-derive 22 modules' worth of local context, which is the attention dilution the split was meant to remove.
rationales.D: Handing back the whole diff rebuilds the wide single pass the split was designed to replace. Attention is diluted again and the cross-module relationships are no more visible than they were before the work was split.

items.objective: 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
items.stem: You are adding a verification stage between the extractor and the ledger loader for invoices above 50,000 dollars. Which THREE properties should that verification stage have? (Select THREE)

options.text: It runs as a separate invocation that receives the source document and the extracted record, and carries none of the extraction run's reasoning in its context.
It must cite a supporting quote from the source document for each field it confirms, and mark as unverified any field it cannot ground in such a quote.
It continues the extraction conversation, so the verifier can ask the extractor why a particular value was chosen before it decides whether to confirm the field.
It reports a confidence value per field against a cut-off the team picked by intuition, auto-approving anything above it and logging the rest for a review that happens monthly.
Disagreements between extractor and verifier are routed to a human queue rather than settled by accepting whichever value the verifier happened to produce.
It runs the extraction prompt three more times and confirms any field returned identically by at least two of those runs, discarding the rest as unstable.

items.explanation: An effective verification stage is independent, grounded and conservative about disagreement. Independence means a separate invocation that never sees the extractor's reasoning, since a model holding its own justifications is unlikely to overturn them. Grounding means each confirmed field is tied to a quote from the source, with anything unquotable marked unverified. And because a verifier disagreeing with an extractor is evidence that neither reading is safe, the disagreement belongs in a human queue rather than being silently resolved.

rationales.C: Continuing the extraction conversation reinstates exactly the reasoning context that independence is meant to exclude, and lets the extractor's justification of a value drive the verifier's decision about it.
rationales.D: Confidence routing is a documented verification technique, but only once the cut-off has been calibrated against a labelled sample; a number chosen by intuition sorts records by nothing in particular. The monthly log is the larger fault: it removes the human from the write path that the 50,000 dollar threshold exists to protect, so a wrong value surfaces weeks after the ledger has been posted.
rationales.F: Repeated sampling of the same prompt detects inconsistency but does not verify anything against the document. Requiring two matching runs also discards correct values that the model reads reliably only some of the time.

items.objective: 5.1 Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
items.stem: An extraction service runs an interactive review loop on the Messages API: an operator sends a supplier invoice, the model returns the extracted fields, and the operator corrects individual values over several turns before approving the record. To hold down per-request cost the wrapper stores every turn in its own database and sends only the newest operator message, alongside the system prompt and the document, in the messages array of each call. Operators report that corrections made two turns earlier come back undone in the next extraction, and that the model re-asks which currency a total is denominated in after having been told. What is the fix?

options.text: Send the newest operator message together with a system-prompt paragraph that restates the last three exchanges in condensed prose, which gives the model the recent context without paying for the raw turns, and keep the full record in the database for audit.

Capture the id returned on the first response and pass it on every subsequent request so the service reattaches the stored conversation server-side, leaving the wrapper to send only the newest operator message each time.

Put a cache_control breakpoint on the system prompt and the document so the shared prefix is cached, since a cached prefix is what carries earlier turns across requests without their having to be re-sent.
Send the complete messages array, every prior operator and assistant turn included, on every request: the Messages API is stateless and keeps nothing between calls.

items.explanation: The Messages API is stateless, so each request is answered only from the content it carries and the full conversational history has to be sent every time. Dropping earlier turns to save tokens removes the operator's corrections and the answers the model already gave, which is exactly the incoherence being reported. Rebuilding the whole messages array from the stored turns on each call restores coherence, and cost is then managed by other means such as caching the stable prefix.

rationales.A: A condensed restatement is a summary, and corrected field values are precisely what a summary blurs; it also puts a rewritten version of the operator's instructions in front of the model instead of what the operator actually wrote.
rationales.B: There is no server-side conversation to reattach. The API keeps no state between requests, and the id on a response identifies that single message rather than a stored session.
rationales.C: Caching changes what a re-sent prefix costs, not whether it is sent. A cache hit still requires the same content to be present in the request, so caching does not let the wrapper omit the turns it is dropping today.

items.objective: 5.1 Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
items.stem: A research coordinator collects nine subagent reports of 3,000 to 6,000 tokens each and concatenates them, in completion order, into a single prompt for the synthesis agent. Reviewers find that the finished report reliably covers the first two reports and the last one, while correct and relevant findings from reports three through seven are simply absent. The individual subagent transcripts show those findings were produced correctly. Which change most directly addresses the omission pattern?

options.text: Raise the synthesis agent's maxTurns and add an instruction telling it to read every section of the aggregated input in order and confirm it has covered each one before it starts writing the report.

Have each subagent score its own report for relevance against the coordinator's rubric and sort the concatenated reports by that score in descending order, so the material most likely to matter sits nearest the top of the input.

Have each subagent write its full report to a file and pass only the file paths to the synthesis agent, so the synthesis agent reads each report on demand and never holds all nine in its context at once.
Place a key-findings summary drawn from all nine subagents at the beginning of the aggregated input, then organise the detailed reports beneath it under explicit per-subagent section headers.

items.explanation: The symptom is the classic position effect: a model processes the beginning and the end of a long input reliably and omits material buried in the middle. The documented mitigation is structural placement rather than more instruction or more budget. Key findings are hoisted to the front of the aggregated input, where recall is strongest, and the detail below is made navigable with explicit section headers so the synthesis step can locate what it needs.

rationales.A: More turns and a stronger instruction do not change where the material sits in the input; the omitted findings are still in the middle, and an instruction to be thorough is not a mechanism for making them salient.
rationales.B: Sorting changes which reports occupy the middle without removing a middle: whatever ranks fourth to seventh still lands where recall is weakest. The findings being dropped today are correct ones, so reordering the same nine blocks does not make them visible.
rationales.C: Paths are a just-in-time retrieval pattern that helps a token budget, but the synthesis agent must still choose to open all nine files, and nothing in the design makes it more likely to notice the reports it is currently skipping.

items.objective: 5.1 Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
items.stem: An extraction workflow processes batches of supplier invoices in one long-running session. Its fetch_document_record MCP tool returns the full stored record for each document: 63 fields including the complete OCR text layer, per-page image metadata, an audit history array and workflow status flags. The extraction step reads five header fields from it and never touches the OCR text layer. After roughly 30 invoices in a session, field-level accuracy falls and the window is close to full. What is the most appropriate first change?

options.text: Trim the tool's response to the fields the extraction step actually consumes (document_id, doc_type, page_count, issuer, invoice_number), leaving the full record retrievable by id when a specific case needs it.

Add a context_management block with a clear_tool_uses_20250919 edit and a trigger of 30,000 input tokens, so older tool results are replaced with placeholder text once the accumulated context passes the threshold.
Process one invoice per session and start a fresh session for each document, so tool results from earlier invoices can never accumulate in the window of a later one.

Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling the agent to ignore the audit history array, the per-page image metadata and the workflow status flags in every fetch_document_record result, and to read only the five fields that the extraction schema actually requires.

items.explanation: Tool results accumulate tokens out of all proportion to their relevance, and the documented remedy is to trim verbose tool output to the relevant fields before it ever enters the context. Returning five fields instead of 63 removes the cause rather than managing the consequence, and the full record remains available by identifier for the rare case that needs it.

rationales.B: Clearing is a recovery valve for results already in the window, not a substitute for not putting 58 irrelevant fields there; it also fires only after the threshold is crossed, invalidates the cached prefix each time, and can remove a result the agent still needs.
rationales.C: One session per document discards batch-level state and cross-document consistency, and pays the full system prompt and instruction cost again for every invoice, which is a large price for a problem caused by a single oversized tool response.
rationales.D: An instruction to ignore fields does not stop those fields being sent, so every token is still consumed; CLAUDE.md supplies context, not enforcement over what a tool returns.

items.objective: 5.1 Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
items.stem: A team drives Claude Code through the Agent SDK for refactoring runs that last several hours, with settingSources: ["project"] configured. The opening prompt of each run says "never edit anything under vendor/, and add a CHANGELOG entry for every change". Short runs comply. Runs that pass the two-hour mark start editing vendor files and stop touching the CHANGELOG, with no configuration change in between. What is the documented fix?

options.text: Increase maxTurns for the run, because the loop is hitting its turn ceiling mid-refactor and restarting without the constraints that were established in the earlier part of the session.

Have the wrapper count assistant turns and re-send the two constraints as a fresh user message every twenty turns, so that the rules are always among the most recent messages in the transcript rather than the oldest ones.

Move the two rules into the project CLAUDE.md, because CLAUDE.md content is re-injected on every request while an initial prompt is part of the message history that automatic compaction replaces with a summary.
Switch the run to permissionMode: "plan" so that no file is written until a plan restating both constraints has been approved, which puts the rules in front of the model before each write.

items.explanation: Automatic compaction replaces older messages with a summary, so instructions given only in the initial prompt may not survive a long run. CLAUDE.md, loaded through settingSources, is re-injected on every request, which makes it the documented home for rules that must hold for the whole session.

rationales.A: Hitting maxTurns ends the query with an error subtype rather than silently continuing with different behaviour, so it does not explain a run that keeps working while ignoring its constraints.
rationales.B: Periodic re-injection by the wrapper is a hand-rolled version of what CLAUDE.md already does automatically, and it is brittle: the interval is guesswork and the re-sent messages become summarizable history themselves.
rationales.D: Plan mode changes the approval workflow rather than what survives compaction, and it converts an unattended multi-hour refactor into one that stops for a human at every step.

items.objective: 5.1 Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
items.stem: In a multi-agent research system, six retrieval subagents feed one synthesis subagent whose entire input arrives through the Agent tool prompt string. Each retrieval subagent currently returns its full reasoning chain plus the raw text of every page it opened. The synthesis subagent's context budget is exhausted before it has read all six inputs, so the last two retrieval results are truncated and never reach the report. Which TWO changes to the retrieval subagents' output contract MOST directly reduce what the synthesis subagent must hold while keeping its input usable? (Select TWO)

options.text: Have each retrieval subagent write its complete transcript to a shared working file and pass the synthesis subagent the list of file paths instead of the content.
Raise the retrieval subagents' maxTurns so each has room to investigate more thoroughly before it reports back to the coordinator.
Have each retrieval subagent return a structured result per finding (claim, source identifier, supporting excerpt, relevance) rather than prose reasoning chains and raw page text.
Have the coordinator forward each retrieval subagent's output to the synthesis subagent verbatim rather than reading it first, so nothing is lost in an intermediate pass.

Have each retrieval subagent apply the coordinator's relevance rubric to its own findings and return only the three that rank highest, so a fixed and predictable number of findings from each subagent consumes the synthesis budget.

Require each finding to carry a compact metadata header (publication or data-collection date, source location, retrieval method) in the structured output, so the synthesis subagent can date and place what it receives without pulling the underlying pages back into its own context.

items.explanation: When a downstream agent has a limited context budget, upstream agents should return structured data (key facts, citations, relevance) instead of verbose content and reasoning chains, and should include metadata such as dates and source locations in that structured output. Together the two changes cut the volume that reaches the synthesis step and keep what does arrive interpretable on its own, so the last inputs are no longer squeezed out by reasoning chains and raw page text.

rationales.A: Paths reduce what is passed but not what must eventually be read; the synthesis subagent still has to load the same raw volume to do the work, so the budget is consumed at the point of reading instead of the point of hand-off.
rationales.B: More retrieval turns increase the volume flowing downstream, which makes the budget problem worse, and thoroughness was never the failure: the findings are produced correctly and then never reach the report.
rationales.D: The coordinator is not the bottleneck being described, and forwarding six verbose transcripts unchanged is precisely the situation that is overflowing the synthesis subagent today.
rationales.E: A fixed cap trims the count but not the shape: each surviving finding still arrives as a reasoning chain plus raw page text, so the same verbose form consumes the budget. A hard top-three also discards material on any topic where one subagent legitimately found ten relevant items.

items.objective: 5.1 Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
items.stem: A contract-abstraction service works through a 180-page master services agreement inside a single Messages API conversation, extracting obligations section by section, and an operator then asks questions about the whole document at the end. Values captured early (effective date 2026-04-01, liability cap 2,500,000, notice period 90 days) come back at the end as "an early-2026 effective date and a multi-million cap". The operator's closing questions deliberately span sections, so per-section isolation is not acceptable. Which design change preserves the exact values?

options.text: Maintain an application-side extracted-facts record: after each section, append the confirmed field values to a structured block that the application re-sends as its own content block on every subsequent request, outside the history that gets summarized.
Enable server-side compaction and supply an instructions field telling the summarizer to keep every date, monetary amount and duration verbatim while condensing the surrounding narrative.

At the end of the run, prompt the model with "list every date, monetary amount and duration you extracted, together with the section number it came from" so that the full set of values is reconstructed from the conversation history before any of the operator's questions are answered.
Split the work into one conversation per section, extract independently, and concatenate the per-section outputs into a final document that the operator's questions are then asked against.

items.explanation: Precise values must be held in a layer that summarization cannot touch. Accumulating confirmed field values into a structured facts block that the application owns and re-sends on every request keeps the exact dates and amounts addressable for the whole run, while the narrative history remains free to be summarized.

rationales.B: A compaction instructions string completely replaces the default summarization prompt rather than adding to it, so a replacement must also restate the required output structure; more fundamentally, a summary is still a lossy rewrite and cannot be relied on to carry every value exactly.
rationales.C: Reconstruction happens after the loss, so the model is asked to recall values that have already been condensed away, and a plausible but wrong figure is exactly the failure being reported.
rationales.D: Per-section isolation is ruled out by the requirement that the closing questions span sections, and concatenating independent extractions gives no shared state for cross-references such as a cap defined in one section and qualified in another.

items.objective: 5.2 Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
items.stem: A customer opens a chat with the resolution agent and writes: "I have already explained this twice on chat today. Put me through to a person now." The agent has get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human available, and the account is in good standing. What should the agent do?

options.text: Make one resolution attempt first: look up the most recent order, offer the refund the customer is likely to want, and escalate only if the customer repeats the request afterwards.
Score the message for frustration and escalate only if the sentiment score crosses the configured threshold, so that routine requests phrased firmly are still handled by the agent.
Ask a clarifying question about which of the customer's issues needs a human, so the escalation is routed to the right queue rather than to general support.
Call escalate_to_human immediately, acknowledging the request and attaching the conversation so far, without attempting to investigate or resolve the issue first.

items.explanation: An explicit customer request for a human agent is one of the documented escalation triggers, and it is honoured immediately without first attempting investigation. Acknowledging the request and attaching context makes the handoff useful without delaying it.

rationales.A: Acknowledging frustration and offering to resolve applies when the customer is unhappy but has not asked for a human; here the customer has explicitly asked, and investigating first ignores a stated preference that has already been repeated twice.
rationales.B: Sentiment scoring is an unreliable proxy for whether escalation is warranted, and it is the wrong signal entirely here because the customer has stated the requirement in plain words rather than implied it.
rationales.C: The customer has asked to stop explaining, so another question before the handoff repeats the experience they complained about; routing detail can be derived from the transcript that accompanies the escalation.

items.objective: 5.2 Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
items.stem: The resolution agent's system prompt carries a pricing policy that covers exactly one case: a price drop on the company's own site within 14 days of purchase is refundable as the difference. A customer asks for the difference against a competitor's lower price on the same item. Competitor pricing is not mentioned anywhere in the policy, and the policy document contains no exclusion or "no other adjustments" clause. Audit shows the agent has been inventing a goodwill partial refund and calling process_refund for these requests. What behaviour should the design require instead?

options.text: Deny the request and cite the pricing policy, on the basis that a policy which authorises only own-site adjustments implicitly excludes every other adjustment it does not name.
Escalate to a human, because the policy is silent on the request rather than complex, passing on the customer's request and the policy section that was consulted.
Ask the customer for a link to the competitor listing and then apply the 14-day own-site rule by analogy, treating the competitor price as if it were a price drop.
Route on a policy-match confidence score whose threshold was calibrated on own-site price-drop cases, escalating only when a request scores below it.

items.explanation: Policy exceptions and gaps are a documented escalation trigger in their own right, distinct from cases that are merely complex. A request the policy neither authorises nor forbids is a decision for a human, and the escalation is more useful when it carries the specific request and the policy text that was checked.

rationales.A: Reading silence as prohibition is the agent making the policy decision by another route, and it commits the business to a refusal that no one authorised; a gap is for a human to close.
rationales.C: Extending the rule by analogy invents policy, which is the same failure as the goodwill refund already in the audit, only with a more respectable justification attached.
rationales.D: The threshold was fitted on cases the policy covers, so it has never seen a request the policy does not address and a score from outside that population means very little. The trigger here is a factual property of the policy text, which can be checked directly.

items.objective: 5.2 Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
items.stem: A caller gives their surname only. get_customer returns three records with different account ids, two of them in the same city, and all three with recent orders. The system prompt currently says "select the best match and continue". A quality review finds the agent has occasionally discussed one customer's orders with a different customer. What is the correct change?

options.text: Rank the matches by most recent order activity and continue with the top-ranked account, logging the two rejected candidates so a reviewer can spot a bad pick afterwards.
Escalate every multi-match result to a human, on the basis that identity resolution is a security decision that an autonomous agent should never make.
Instruct the agent to ask the customer for an additional identifier (order number, postcode, or the email on the account) and re-query, rather than choosing among the matches on a heuristic.
Change get_customer to return only the highest-scoring match so the model is never presented with an ambiguity it might resolve badly in the first place.

items.explanation: Multiple tool matches are an ambiguity to be resolved with the customer, not with a heuristic. The documented pattern is to ask for an additional identifier and re-query, which turns an unverifiable guess into a deterministic lookup and removes the possibility of discussing the wrong account.

rationales.A: Recency is exactly the kind of heuristic selection the pattern rules out; it produces a confident wrong answer whenever the other customer with the same surname happens to have ordered more recently, and after-the-fact logging does not prevent the disclosure.
rationales.B: Handing every common surname to a human throws away first-contact resolution for a case the agent can settle in one question, and escalation is reserved for explicit requests, policy gaps and genuine inability to progress.
rationales.D: Collapsing the result set moves the same guess into the tool and hides it from view, so the agent proceeds with false certainty and no signal that a decision was ever made.

items.objective: 5.2 Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
items.stem: A wrapper drives Claude Code through the Agent SDK for a large refactor in the main agent loop, with permissionMode: "dontAsk" and allowedTools: ["Read", "Edit", "Grep", "Glob", "AskUserQuestion"]. The requirement is that whenever a public API signature could reasonably change in two ways, the agent asks the maintainer to choose. In practice the agent never asks; it picks one and proceeds. What explains this and what fixes it?

options.text: AskUserQuestion is removed from any agent invoked through the Agent tool, so the signature decisions must be moved out of a delegated subagent and back into the main conversation loop before clarifying questions of any kind become possible.

dontAsk never prompts: it denies AskUserQuestion and tools marked as requiring user interaction even when they are in the allowed list. Run in default mode with a canUseTool callback that handles AskUserQuestion, which a tool requiring user interaction reaches even when an allow rule matches it.
Clarifying questions are raised only in plan mode, so the run should use permissionMode: "plan" to enable interactive requirement gathering before any signature is changed.
No canUseTool callback is supplied, and in the absence of a callback an unmatched tool call is denied, so the AskUserQuestion call is rejected before it can reach the maintainer.

items.explanation: dontAsk is defined by never prompting: pre-approved tools run and everything else is denied, including AskUserQuestion and MCP tools marked as requiring user interaction, even when they have been allowed. A workflow whose correctness depends on asking cannot use that mode. In a mode that does prompt, a tool requiring user interaction is routed to the canUseTool callback even when an allow rule matches, so default mode plus a callback that answers the question restores the behaviour.

rationales.A: The stripping of AskUserQuestion from subagents is real, but the stem states the refactor runs in the main agent loop, so it is not the cause here.
rationales.C: Clarifying questions are especially common in plan mode, which is why plan mode suits requirement gathering, but they are not exclusive to it; plan mode would also stop this run from applying any edit without an approved plan.
rationales.D: A missing callback is not what is happening: dontAsk denies the call before the callback step is ever reached, and the callback step is skipped entirely in that mode, so supplying one would change nothing while the mode stands.
